  - link "Featured · History The Matra dispute Two disputes thirteen years apart, usually told as one — the test-track fires an engineering change explains, the seventeen-year lawsuit Matra won, and the walkout that taught Taipei how to buy its next railway. Lokseng01 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons":
    - /url: /rail/history/matra-dispute/

about.snapshot:
- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - text: About
  - link "Back to the home page":
    - /url: /
  - heading "About" [level=1]
  - paragraph: An English-language reference for public transport across Taiwan — Taipei and New Taipei, Taoyuan, Taichung, Kaohsiung and the systems beyond them — written because the material exists in Mandarin and nowhere else in a form you can look something up in.
  - navigation "On this page":
    - paragraph: On this page
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - link "What this is":
          - /url: "#what-this-is"
      - listitem:
        - link "How it sources material":
          - /url: "#how-it-sources-material"
      - listitem:
        - link "Where it has got to":
          - /url: "#where-it-has-got-to"
      - listitem:
        - link "Corrections":
          - /url: "#corrections"
      - listitem:
        - link "How it is built":
          - /url: "#how-it-is-built"
  - heading "What this is" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Taiwan's transport network is unusually well documented — in Mandarin. Between 批踢踢 (PTT), Mobile01 and the Chinese Wikipedia there is detailed, argued-over coverage of rolling stock, depot allocations, signalling contracts and construction history, for systems from Taipei Metro to Kaohsiung Rapid Transit to the branch lines of Taiwan Railway. Some of it is better than anything published officially.
  - paragraph: "In English there is an encyclopedia article per line and a great deal of visitor-facing advice about which exit to use. What is missing is the layer in between: structured reference material you can look a fact up in, with the source attached, and covering the country rather than one city. That gap is what this site is for."
  - paragraph: It is independent and non-commercial. It is not affiliated with any transit operator — Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation, New Taipei Metro, Taoyuan Metro, Taichung Metro, Kaohsiung Rapid Transit, Taiwan Railway, Taiwan High Speed Rail, any city or county government, or any bus, ferry or bike-share operator — and it carries no advertising.
  - heading "How it sources material" [level=2]
  - heading "Official data where it exists" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: For the 198 stations the platform carries, names, codes, running order, coordinates, interchanges, route lengths and end-to-end times come from
    - link "TDX":
      - /url: https://tdx.transportdata.tw/
    - text: ", the Ministry of Transportation and Communications' open data platform. So do 10 of the 11 line colours, from the publishing operator's own line record. The exception is the Sanying Line, which opened in June 2026 and has no record on the platform at all; its colour was read instead from the operator's own line mark, and"
    - link "the line colours page":
      - /url: /data/line-colours/
    - text: says exactly which file and what it was checked against. TDX has no Sanying station dataset either, so LB01–LB12 are maintained in a separate hand-researched registry from the operator's station table and twelve information sheets. Every displayed Sanying fact links to that primary evidence, and coordinates remain TBC. The generated TDX registry itself is not hand-edited.
  - paragraph:
    - text: That decision has already paid for itself twice. Every English-language line colour we could find was wrong, including two cases where a confident correction citing an official map moved
    - emphasis: away
    - text: from the official value — the working is on
    - link "the colours page":
      - /url: /data/line-colours/
    - text: . And the route length this site published was 1.4 km too long, because it measured geometry that runs past both termini into depot leads, while the operator's own figure sat unread in a field nobody had looked in.
  - heading "Mandarin sources, synthesised rather than translated" [level=3]
  - paragraph: Where official data stops — fleet histories, depot facilities, the Matra contract dispute, why a line was built the way it was — the material is in Mandarin. The policy is to read it, cross-check it, and write it in English from scratch, citing the original in its own language rather than an English mirror of it. Translating a forum thread wholesale would be both a copyright problem and a way of importing its errors without noticing them.
  - paragraph: Where sources disagree, the intention is to record every value rather than pick the most plausible one and present it as settled.
  - heading "TBC rather than a guess" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: A figure marked
    - emphasis: TBC
    - text: means nobody here has traced it to a source worth citing. It does not mean the number is unknown to the world. It would be easy to fill those gaps with figures that are probably right, and the site would look more finished; it would also stop being usable as a reference, because you could no longer tell which numbers had been checked.
  - paragraph: The same applies structurally. A section that has not been researched yet says so on its own index page rather than being hidden or padded out. Where a figure has been settled since — the two underground Wenhu Line stations were marked “not established” for four builds and are now named, from the builder’s own record and an encyclopedia agreeing from different directions — the page says how it was settled rather than quietly filling the gap.
  - heading "Citations, and a count of what has none" [level=3]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Every page carries a source list, and a figure that rests on one says so with a numbered mark you can follow. Each entry records the title in English and in the original language, the publisher, the date the URL was read, and whether the source is
    - strong: primary
    - text: — the operator, the builder, a government department, a court — or
    - strong: secondary
    - text: ". That last field is required and has no default: this site has already found a case where a citation to an official route map was further from the published colour than the value it replaced, so who says a thing has to travel with the thing."
  - paragraph:
    - text: Everything cited anywhere is collected in the
    - link "bibliography":
      - /url: /data/sources/
    - text: ", with the primary-to-secondary ratio stated at the top. It is currently about a third primary, which is not good enough and is published anyway."
  - paragraph:
    - text: The build also counts statements that carry
    - emphasis: "no"
    - text: source at all, separately from those marked TBC, and refuses to let that number grow. A labelled gap and an unlabelled assertion are different failures, and only one of them is honest.
  - heading "What is not used" [level=3]
  - paragraph: No operator's route map, photography or signage artwork. Those are copyrighted. The maps on this site are drawn from published coordinate geometry, and the line colours are the published hex values — a colour specification is a fact, an operator's specific map is a design.
  - paragraph:
    - link "Data provenance":
      - /url: /data/provenance/
    - text: sets out field by field what is official, what is researched here, what is derived, and what is still open.
  - heading "Where it has got to" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Coverage grew outward from Taipei Metro's Wenhu Line, this site's first deep case study, and now spans metro and light rail systems in Taipei, New Taipei, Taoyuan, Taichung and Kaohsiung; the national bus network across several cities; Taiwan Railway and High Speed Rail groundwork; ferries to the outlying islands; and YouBike. Depth is uneven by design — a system gets a page per station and per line once it has been researched to that standard, and a section not yet at that depth says so rather than padding itself out. 0 of the 711 written pages still carry a stub flag, meaning some figures on them still need tracing to a primary source.
  - paragraph:
    - text: All 210 rail stations the platform carries are registered, so any station code on the site validates and any of them can be looked up on
    - link "the station records page":
      - /url: /data/stations/
    - text: ", with position, district, coordinates, interchanges and run times where the source publishes them. Where TDX does not publish structure, street exits or engineering numbers, some lines carry a hand-built overlay sourced from the operator directly instead — the station page for any given line says which kind of record it is."
  - heading "Corrections" [level=2]
  - paragraph: "Corrections are welcome, and specific ones are most useful: the page, the figure, and what it should be, with a source. A source in Mandarin is as good as one in English, and often better."
  - paragraph: The most valuable corrections are the ones that catch something stated confidently and wrongly, rather than something already marked TBC — a gap that is labelled is doing its job, but a wrong figure presented as checked undermines everything next to it.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Reporting a correction.
    - text: Open an issue on the repository this site is built from, quoting the page URL and the figure in question. If you would rather not use an issue tracker, the same information sent any other way is just as welcome — what matters is the source, not the channel.
  - heading "How it is built" [level=2]
  - paragraph: Content is Markdown; the site is generated as static HTML and served as files, with no server and no runtime API calls. Station code badges, Chinese language tagging, strip maps and geographic maps are all produced at build time from the data, which is why a station code that is not real fails the build rather than rendering as though it were.
  - paragraph: Station and line data retrieved from MOTC TDX on 2026-08-24. Government open data, used under the Open Government Data Licence.

    - heading "Bike-share service YouBike" [level=1]:
      - img "Bike-share service"
      - text: YouBike
    - paragraph: Taipei's bike-share ran three fare policies and two mutually incompatible dock generations before this page's writing, and the story English coverage tells — "free rides for transferring since 2018" — turns out to be the middle third of a longer, better-documented arc.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "\"The first thirty minutes are free if you are transferring from the metro\" is the version of YouBike most visitors hear, and it describes one six-year window in the system's life rather than the whole of it — and not even the current window"
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: . The fuller story, drawn from the city's own press releases and Taiwanese reporting, is a public bicycle system that has run three different fare policies and two mutually incompatible generations of hardware, in place, without ever closing.

    - heading "A BOT scheme that started with eleven stations" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: "'s public bicycle system began as a build–operate–transfer contract let to Giant under then-mayor Hao Lung-pin, piloted in Xinyi District from 11 March 2009"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
      - text: . Citywide operation started on 30 August 2012, and by the time that initial trial period ended on 30 November 2012 the system had already passed one million cumulative rides
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - heading "Free, then not free, then free for some, then free again" [level=2]
    - paragraph: This is the part almost nobody outside Taiwan gets right, because most accounts freeze on whichever policy was current when they were written.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: The system launched with the first 30 minutes free, and stayed that way until 1 April 2015
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: . Mayor Ko Wen-je's administration then introduced a flat NT$5 charge for that first half-hour, arguing the free period was subsidising recreational riding rather than commuting
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: . New Taipei, whose own network was still under construction, pointedly did not follow — it kept its first 30 minutes free through the rest of 2015, budgeting roughly NT$70 million a year to do so
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
      - text: ". What the 2015 change actually saved Taipei's budget is itself disputed: one account puts the monthly subsidy fall at NT$20 million to NT$8 million, another at NT$20 million to NT$13 million"
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
      - text: — the same policy, two different numbers, neither resolved here.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: A narrower discount followed in 2018
      - text: ": NT$5 off when transferring to or from a bus or the MRT, rather than a free period for everyone"
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: . This is the version of the story that made it into English coverage, and as a snapshot of 2018–2024 it isn't wrong — it is just not the whole arc, and it stopped being current on
      - strong: 28 February 2024
      - text: ", when Mayor Chiang Wan-an restored an unconditional first-30-minutes-free policy for registered members citywide and the transfer discount was cancelled the same day, since a universal free period made a transfer-specific one redundant"
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: . The city projected a 15% ridership increase and about 7,000 tonnes a year of avoided carbon emissions
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: . Ride a YouBike 2.0 in Taipei today and, if you are a registered member, that first half hour costs nothing regardless of where you are coming from; beyond it, the standard rate runs NT$10 per 30 minutes for up to four hours, NT$20 to eight hours, and NT$40 beyond
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: .
    - heading "Why there is a 2.0 at all" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The generational split is a genuinely engineering-driven story, and the city's own documents say so plainly. YouBike 1.0's docks needed a municipal power connection: the station-siting standard the transport department published on 23 March 2015 required, alongside a roughly 600-metre spacing principle and a minimum 2-metre clear sidewalk width, that a station sit near an existing power supply"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . That single requirement — road excavation, a utility connection, a minimum viable scale to justify it — was what capped how fast and how densely the network could grow
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: YouBike 2.0's answer was to move the intelligence off the dock and onto the bicycle. In the transport department's own words, the redesign 「免除市電需求，控制器移轉車機」 — removes the need for mains power and shifts the controller onto the bike itself
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: — which let station siting respond to terrain and sidewalk width instead of utility access
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: ". The physical dock changed too: 1.0 parked two bikes per post, 2.0 parks one"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . The trade was a lighter, cheaper, more flexible dock for total incompatibility with the existing fleet — a 1.0 card or bike could not use a 2.0 station, or vice versa, from the day the trial began.
    - paragraph:
      - text: That trial started at 10:00 on 15 January 2020, around
      - link "Gongguan":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g07/
      - text: "MRT Station and National Taiwan University: 102 stations sharing about 1,800 docks, and 500 new bicycles, according to the launch announcement"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . A follow-up release one month later, describing what reads as the same pilot area, instead gives 600 new bicycles
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: "— a discrepancy between two official releases six weeks apart that neither states an explanation for and that this page does not attempt to resolve. Full service across Taipei began at 10:20 on 8 May 2021: 160 new stations that day on top of the existing 103 in Gongguan and around NTU, for 263 total, with a year-end target of 750 stations and new batches of stations activated every Tuesday and Friday"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . New Taipei's own 2.0 network reached full service on 20 October 2021
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - heading "Retiring 1.0" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: By October 2022, YouBike 2.0 had already reached its 1,200-station citywide target, and 1.0 — the system that had carried Taipei's bike-share for thirteen years — accounted for just 8.5% of rides, turning over 1.8 times a day per bike
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . Taipei switched it off entirely at 00:00 on 3 December 2022, after more than 200 million cumulative rides
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: ". New Taipei kept its own 1.0 fleet running for a while longer, and the mismatch produced a real inconvenience at the boundary: a rider who picked up an orange 1.0 bike in New Taipei and carried it into Taipei after the cutover faced a NT$350 fee to have it collected, because there was nowhere in the city left to return it to"
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Retired 1.0 bicycles went three ways. The city transferred 1,106 to its own agencies, for neighbourhood patrols and school cycling-safety education, and donated 1,300 to Indigenous communities (原鄉)
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: ", marking the retirement with a memorial installation at MRT"
      - link "Taipei City Hall":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl18/
      - text: Station Exit 3 — the system's very first station
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: . Bicycles judged beyond further use were sold to a recycling contractor in late 2021 at NT$41 each; the city's own clarification states this reflects the cost of disassembly, transport, labour and disposal rather than an underpriced sale of public property
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . That NT$41 is a scrap value, not a replacement cost
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . The city's original unit purchase price remains TBC. Chinese Wikipedia gives NT$13,000 but carries no citation for it
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
      - text: .
    - heading "Electric assist, and where things stand" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "YouBike 2.0E — the electric-assist version — launched simultaneously in Taipei and New Taipei on 30 August 2024, giving a stated 80 to 100 km of range on a full charge on flat ground, with no free period or subsidy: a flat NT$20 per 30 minutes for the first two hours, NT$40 beyond, on the same docks and app as standard 2.0"
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: . It does not get the first-30-minutes-free benefit or the TPASS 基北北桃1200 discount that standard 2.0 carries in Taipei, with a carve-out only for holders of Taipei-issued senior or disability transit cards
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: — a distinction easy to miss if a source treats "YouBike" as one undifferentiated product.
    - paragraph:
      - text: As of a Taipei transport department release dated 14 August 2025, the city was operating 1,633 stations and 23,860 bikes, including 2,000 e-assist models, and was closing in on 400 million cumulative Taipei rides
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: ". That milestone came fast: 100 million to 200 million took about three and a half years, 200 million to 300 million took two and a half, and 300 million to 400 million took seventeen months — entirely inside the window opened by the February 2024 fare change"
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: . Across every Taiwanese city YouBike operates in, cumulative rides passed one billion on 4 June 2025
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . The same August 2025 release names a 2026 target of 2,000 stations and 4,500 2.0E bikes specifically
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: — narrower than the 27,500-bike, 2,000-station citywide target officials gave in February 2024 reporting
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: ". Their relationship remains TBC: the 4,500-bike target could be an e-assist subset of a still-current 27,500 total, or the plan could have changed, but nothing found restates the larger figure alongside the newer one."
    - heading "Static station snapshot" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A full TDX Bike Station/City pull retrieved on 23 August 2026 returned 1,794 Taipei station rows with a published capacity total of 50,877 docks
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: . The same pull returned 1,593 New Taipei rows and 48,355 published docks
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: .
      - link "Taoyuan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taoyuan/
      - text: returned 699 rows and 24,214 published docks
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Those three municipalities therefore contribute 4,086 static station rows in this dated build snapshot
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: . An earlier direct check recorded 1,790 Taipei rows, 1,593 New Taipei rows and 698 Taoyuan rows, for 4,081 in total; that is a dated retrieval conflict, not a reason to average the values
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The 25 August 2026 pull extends the committed layer to
      - link "Taichung":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taichung/
      - text: "and Kaohsiung: Taichung contributes 1,817 rows and 38,746 published docks, while Kaohsiung contributes 1,500 rows and 30,382 published docks"
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: . Together with the three earlier municipalities, the current five-city pull contains 7,403 rows and 192,573 published docks
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: . The three existing row counts are unchanged between the dated pulls, but Taipei's published capacity is 50,876 in the current pull rather than 50,877 on 23 August; both values remain published because they are separate live retrievals
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taichung's municipal open-data catalogue separately describes a citywide YouBike2.0 station and live-parking dataset with a ten-minute update frequency and station, address, coordinate and capacity fields
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
      - text: . Kaohsiung's catalogue likewise identifies a YouBike2.0 station/live-information dataset supplied by the city Transportation Bureau, including district, address, station-code, capacity, coordinate and operating-state fields
      - superscript:
        - link "[24]":
          - /url: "#ref-24"
      - text: . These catalogue records corroborate the operator/data-publication scope, while the committed static counts above come from the dated TDX Station/City pull
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The TDX Station/City records supply names, addresses, coordinates and published capacity, while current available bikes and return docks belong to a separate live availability feed and are not treated as static page facts
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: . Taichung and Kaohsiung rows with no usable district value remain explicitly unclassified; no district is inferred from a station name or address
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The 1,633 Taipei stations reported by the transport department on 14 August 2025 remain a separate dated official figure
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: . It measures a different time and publication scope from the 1,794-row TDX snapshot and is kept as a conflict rather than rewritten as a growth rate
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: .
    - heading "Conflicts in the static station snapshot" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The 23 August TDX snapshot records 4,086 rows across Taipei, New Taipei and Taoyuan, including 50,877 Taipei docks
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: . The 25 August snapshot records 7,403 rows across five municipalities, including 50,876 Taipei docks
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: ". These are different retrievals of a live-maintained feed: the later value adds Taichung and Kaohsiung and changes Taipei's returned capacity by one, so both values are published rather than averaged or selected as a definitive total"
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: .
    - heading "Open evidence" [level=2]
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: 1.0's exact fleet size at Taipei's retirement.
        - text: Chinese Wikipedia gives 13,072 bikes; no primary figure for the fleet at the 3 December 2022 cutover was found this run, so the specs table above marks it TBC
        - superscript:
          - link "[20]":
            - /url: "#ref-20"
        - text: .
      - listitem:
        - strong: The operator's ownership structure.
        - text: 微笑單車股份有限公司 runs the system under contract to Taipei's transport department
        - superscript:
          - link "[10]":
            - /url: "#ref-10"
        - text: ; its organisational relationship to Giant, and the systems-design firm reported to have built the electronics, were not independently confirmed against a primary source this run.
      - listitem:
        - strong: The 2018–19 New Taipei "E-YouBike" trial and the Putian, China variant
        - text: that reportedly reuses retired YouBike 1.0 docks. Both appear only in Chinese Wikipedia here, and no primary New Taipei or Giant/Kunshan source for either was located in the time available
        - superscript:
          - link "[20]":
            - /url: "#ref-20"
        - text: .
      - listitem:
        - strong: A primary source for the NT$350 cross-boundary fee.
        - text: It rests on one secondary account
        - superscript:
          - link "[19]":
            - /url: "#ref-19"
        - text: .
      - listitem:
        - strong: Contract and renewal terms
        - text: between Taipei City Government and Smile Bike Co. — nothing found this run addresses them.

The 1.0-era siting rules: ≥600 m station spacing, ≥2 m clear sidewalk width or ≥6 m clearance off it, a 30 m/15-dock minimum footprint, school approval near primary schools — and explicitly, a nearby power supply. The clause 2.0 was built to remove."
        - listitem:
          - link "Press release — Taipei's YouBike 1.0 system to retire fully, stopping operation 00:00, 3 December (Saturday)":
            - /url: https://dot.gov.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=D739A9F6B5C0AB95&sms=72544237BBE4C5F6&s=A310D64F8712A15D
          - text: "臺北市政府交通局-新聞稿-臺北市YouBike1.0系統將全面退場 111年12月3日（星期六）0時起停止營運 primary Taipei City Government, Department of Transportation accessed 2026-08-12 The retirement announcement: 2.0 had already hit its 1,200-station citywide target by October 2022, 1.0 was down to 8.5% of ridership with a 1.8 turnover, and the system closed for good at 00:00 on 3 December 2022 after 13+ years and 200 million-plus rides."
        - listitem:
          - link "Press release — Taipei's YouBike commemorative installation unveiled, retired bicycles donated to Indigenous communities":
            - /url: https://dot.gov.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=D739A9F6B5C0AB95&sms=72544237BBE4C5F6&s=9B82ECFCBB63CBEC
          - text: 臺北市政府交通局-新聞稿-臺北市YouBike紀念意象揭幕 退場車輛捐贈原鄉 primary Taipei City Government, Department of Transportation accessed 2026-08-12 1,300 retired 1.0 bicycles donated to Indigenous communities (原鄉), 1,106 transferred to city agencies for neighbourhood patrols and school cycling-safety education, and a memorial marker installed at MRT Taipei City Hall Station Exit 3, the system's first station.
        - listitem:
          - link "Clarification — on unusable, scrapped YouBike 1.0 vehicles":
            - /url: https://www.gov.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=74806083EBDF5A03&sms=72544237BBE4C5F6&s=1B3B7EC6424DC4D0
          - text: 臺北市政府全球資訊網-即時新聞澄清-YouBike1.0不堪用報廢車輛說明 primary Taipei City Government ( 臺北市政府 ) accessed 2026-08-12 Bicycles judged beyond further use were sold to a recycling contractor in late 2021 at NT$41 per bike; the city states this reflects disassembly, transport, labour and disposal costs rather than under-pricing. This is a scrap value, not a replacement cost — kept distinct from the unsourced 'NT$10,000 per bike' figure that had circulated.
        - listitem:
          - link "Public bicycles — introduction":
            - /url: https://dot.gov.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=44C34CB5F656CF90&s=2982E80C499FE909
          - text: 臺北市政府交通局-公共自行車介紹-簡介 primary Taipei City Government, Department of Transportation accessed 2026-08-12 Names 微笑單車股份有限公司 as the operating company under the department's contract, and confirms the citywide 2.0 upgrade completed by end of 2022 alongside 1.0's 3 December 2022 retirement.
        - listitem:
          - link "Press release — Taipei's free first 30 minutes drives a riding boom, cumulative rides about to pass 400 million":
            - /url: https://dot.gov.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=D739A9F6B5C0AB95&sms=72544237BBE4C5F6&s=3070537DD6D9C528
          - text: 臺北市政府交通局-新聞稿-臺北市YouBike前30分鐘免費引領騎乘風潮 累計騎乘次數即將突破4億人次 primary Taipei City Government, Department of Transportation accessed 2026-08-12 Dated 14 August 2025 (confirmed via search indexing). States 1,633 stations and 23,860 bikes (including 2,000 e-assist) in Taipei, that 400 million rides took only 17 months to reach after the Feb 2024 fare change versus 2.5 years for the prior 100 million, and a 2026 target of 2,000 stations with 4,500 2.0E bikes.
        - listitem:
          - link "FAQ — why doesn't the YouBike 2.0E electric-assist bike get the first-30-minutes-free or TPASS discounts?":
            - /url: https://www.gov.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=EEC70A4186D4C828&sms=87415A8B9CE81B16&s=AB88A9B746198352
          - text: 臺北市政府交通局-常見問答-電動輔助自行車YouBike2.0E為什麼沒有前30分鐘免費及TPASS都會通定期票優惠？ primary Taipei City Government, Department of Transportation accessed 2026-08-12 States plainly that YouBike 2.0E does not carry the free-30-minutes or TPASS 基北北桃1200 discounts in Taipei, with a carve-out for Taipei-issued senior/disability transit cards. Confirms 2.0's fare benefits do not simply extend to 2.0E.
        - listitem:
          - link "From 30 August 2024, YouBike 2.0E goes live in Taipei and New Taipei":
            - /url: https://www.youbike.com.tw/region/taipei/news/service/66cbf3b3f2a117dfe7056cf5/
          - text: "2024/08/30起，臺北市及新北市 YouBike 2.0E電輔車正式上線 primary 微笑單車股份有限公司 (Smile Bike Co., Ltd.) accessed 2026-08-12 The operator's own launch notice: 80–100 km range on a full charge on flat ground, tiered pricing (NT$20/30min for the first two hours, NT$40/30min beyond), no subsidy or free period, and shared docks/app with standard 2.0."
        - listitem:
          - link "From 28 February 2024, Taipei YouBike 2.0's first 30 minutes are free":
            - /url: https://www.youbike.com.tw/region/taipei/news/service/65dc48e2b507cedede07c6e2/
          - text: "2024/02/28起，臺北市YouBike 2.0 前30分鐘免費 primary 微笑單車股份有限公司 (Smile Bike Co., Ltd.) accessed 2026-08-12 The operator's own notice of the 2024 fare change: unconditional first 30 minutes free for registered members citywide, then NT$10/30min to 4 hours, NT$20/30min to 8 hours, NT$40/30min beyond."
        - listitem:
          - link "Taipei's free-first-30-minutes YouBike policy takes effect the 28th; bus/MRT transfer discount ends":
            - /url: https://www.cna.com.tw/news/aloc/202402270092.aspx
          - text: 北市YouBike前30分鐘免費28日起實施 轉乘公車捷運不再優惠 secondary 中央社 (CNA), 27 February 2024 accessed 2026-08-12 Confirms the transfer discount 「自107年上路」(began in the 2018 ROC year) and that it was cancelled the same day the unconditional free period began, plus the 1,338→2,000 station and 16,562→27,500 bike 2026 targets as stated by officials at the time.
        - listitem:
          - link "Chiang Wan-an restores YouBike's free first 30 minutes, estimated 7,000-tonne annual carbon cut":
            - /url: https://e-info.org.tw/node/238570
          - text: 蔣萬安恢復YouBike前30分鐘免費 估年減7000噸碳排 secondary 環境資訊中心 (Environmental Information Center), citing Taipei City Government accessed 2026-08-12 States the policy 'restores' (恢復) a free period that predates the transfer discount, names Ko Wen-je's April 2015 cancellation as the prior state, and gives the 15% ridership uplift and 7,000-tonne carbon estimates plus the 2026 fleet/station targets.
        - listitem:
          - 'link "Historical data feature: free-riding YouBike is back! Why did Ko Wen-je choose to take the criticism and charge NT$5?"':
            - /url: https://www.storm.mg/article/5033646
          - text: 歷史風數據》免費騎的YouBike回來了！柯文哲當年為何寧願挨罵也要收5元？ secondary 風傳媒 (Storm Media) accessed 2026-08-12 Fetched in full. Confirms the pre-2015 period was completely free, gives the Ko administration's stated commuting/leisure usage-shift rationale for the NT$5 fee, and states the city's subsidy fell from about NT$20 million to NT$8 million a month — a different saving figure from The News Lens's account of the same change.
        - listitem:
          - 'link "Taipei cancels YouBike''s free rides: NT$5 for the first 30 minutes, New Taipei does not follow"':
            - /url: https://www.thenewslens.com/article/13835
          - text: 北市YouBike免費取消：前30分收5元、新北不跟進 secondary 關鍵評論網 (The News Lens), 2015 accessed 2026-08-12 Fetched in full. Gives the exact effective date, 1 April 2015, and states New Taipei kept its own free first-30-minutes through the end of 2015 while still expanding its network, budgeting roughly NT$70 million/year to do so — a genuine policy divergence between the two cities, not just a lag.
        - listitem:
          - link "YouBike 1.0 in Taipei bows out 3 December; New Taipei riders forgetting to switch to 2.0 pay an extra NT$350":
            - /url: https://www.businesstoday.com.tw/article/category/183030/post/202211200003/
          - text: YouBike1.0台北市12/3起退場！新北市騎來忘換YouBike2.0 還車得多付350元 secondary 今周刊 (Business Today), 20 November 2022 accessed 2026-08-12 Source for the NT$350 cross-boundary misplacement fee for a 1.0 bike ridden from New Taipei into Taipei after Taipei's cutover — no Taipei DOT primary release stating this exact figure was found this run, so it rests on this secondary account alone.
        - listitem:
          - link "YouBike Smile Bike":
            - /url: https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-tw/YouBike微笑單車
          - text: "YouBike微笑單車 secondary 維基百科 (Chinese Wikipedia) accessed 2026-08-12 Used only for figures not found in a primary source and flagged as such: the 1.0 unit price (NT$13,000) and loss fee, the 13,072-bike fleet at 1.0's Taipei retirement, the 2018–19 New Taipei E-YouBike electric-assist trial, and the Putian, China variant built on retired 1.0 docks. None of these four independently verified against a primary source this run."
        - listitem:
          - link "TDX Bike Station City pull":
            - /url: "https://tdx.transportdata.tw/api/basic/v2/Bike/Station/City/{City}"
          - text: 交通部運輸資料流通服務平臺 — Bike Station/City primary Ministry of Transportation and Communications TDX / 交通部運輸資料流通服務平臺 accessed 2026-08-23 Build-time pull of the static station feed for Taipei, New Taipei and Taoyuan. Supports the dated station-row counts, published BikesCapacity totals and the fact that live availability is a separate feed.
        - listitem:
          - link "TDX Bike Station City pull — five-city snapshot":
            - /url: "https://tdx.transportdata.tw/api/basic/v2/Bike/Station/City/{City}"
          - text: 交通部運輸資料流通服務平臺 — Bike Station/City primary Ministry of Transportation and Communications TDX / 交通部運輸資料流通服務平臺 accessed 2026-08-25 Build-time pull of the static Station/City feed for Taipei, New Taipei, Taoyuan, Taichung and Kaohsiung. Supports the 25 August 2026 row and BikesCapacity totals, source-update timestamps and the fact that live availability is a separate feed.
        - listitem:
          - link "Taichung City Public Bicycle (YouBike2.0) Rental Station and Real-time Parking Space Data":
            - /url: https://opendata.taichung.gov.tw/search/6e38eb56-0e9a-4b9e-806d-23cd35d44d6b
          - text: 臺中市公共自行車(YouBike2.0)租借站&即時車位資料 primary Taichung City Government Transportation Bureau / 臺中市政府交通局 accessed 2026-08-25 The municipal open-data catalogue identifies the dataset as current Taichung YouBike2.0 station and live-parking data, with a ten-minute update frequency, station/address/coordinate/capacity fields and a citywide spatial scope.
        - listitem:
          - link "Kaohsiung YouBike2.0 Public Bicycle Rental Station Real-time Information":
            - /url: https://data.gov.tw/dataset/173477
          - text: 高雄YouBike2.0公共自行車租賃站即時資訊 primary Kaohsiung City Government Transportation Bureau / 高雄市政府交通局 accessed 2026-08-25 The national open-data catalogue identifies Kaohsiung's station/live-information dataset, lists district, address, station code, capacity, coordinates and operational-state fields, and states that it is provided by the Kaohsiung Transportation Bureau.

      - link "Operator service ratings Twice a year since 1992, Taipei has graded its bus operators 優/甲/乙/丙/丁 on 26 indicators — and the grade can cost an operator its routes. That structural fact — how many companies, how many routes, and the four city regulations that actually set out how the money moves — is explained in full on"
    - link "the joint-operation network":
      - /url: /bus/network/joint-operation/
    - text: .

    - text: Beyond Taipei and New Taipei, this section also covers the city bus networks of
    - link "Taichung":

    - text: ","
    - link "Kaohsiung":
      - /url: /bus/regional/kaohsiung/
    - text: ","
    - link "Tainan":
      - /url: /bus/regional/tainan/
    - text: and
    - link "Hsinchu":
      - /url: /bus/regional/hsinchu/
    - text: ", plus national"
    - link "intercity coach":
      - /url: /bus/intercity/
    - text: services — each with its own operators, fare structure and, where one exists, a rating or evaluation scheme distinct from Taipei's.
  - heading "What this section covers" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Network.
    - text: This site's
    - link "Network":
      - /url: /bus/network/
    - text: pages hold the joint-operation history, the route-numbering conventions, payment and ticketing infrastructure, the operator service-rating schemes (Taipei's since 1992, New Taipei's separate scheme, and others where a city runs one), and the 2030 electrification programme.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Operators.
    - text: The
    - link "TDX operator index":

    - text: lists the operator records in the committed pull, with route associations generated from the same data pull
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: ", deepened with ownership and corporate history where sources exist. The relationships between them — including who owns whom — are poorly documented in English, which makes this the part most likely to be worth reading rather than merely present."
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Routes.
    - text: Route pages are generated from the same TDX pull
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: ; this site explains the route-
    - emphasis: numbering system
    - text: separately so a bare number means something before any individual route page does.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Vehicles and garages.
    - link "Models":
      - /url: /bus/models/
    - text: covers electric, diesel and imported chassis with VSCC/MOTC type-approval records where they exist, and
    - link "Depots":
      - /url: /bus/depots/
    - text: covers garages and charging infrastructure — both report a field as TBC rather than filling it from an unverified fleet-list transcription.
  - paragraph:
    - strong: Fares and payment.
    - text: Section-based fares, the EasyCard transfer discount between bus and metro, and where the section boundaries actually fall — which is the thing visitors get wrong most often.
  - paragraph:
    - text: See

    - text: for how this site sources material.

bus-depots-charging-infrastructure.snapshot:
- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - link "Bus":
      - /url: /bus/
    - link "Bus depots and operating sites":
      - /url: /bus/depots/
    - text: Depot electrification and charging infrastructure
  - link "Back to Bus depots and operating sites":
    - /url: /bus/depots/
  - article:
    - heading "Transit depot Depot electrification and charging infrastructure" [level=1]:
      - img "Transit depot"
      - text: Depot electrification and charging infrastructure
    - paragraph: No consolidated national depot-charger registry exists — but named installations show buses sharing MRT depots at night, rationed charging bays, and a public-EV-charger boom that mostly isn't about buses at all.
    - region "Quick facts":
      - text: Depot electrification and charging infrastructure
      - term: National public chargers, end-Jul 2025
      - definition:
        - text: 12,334 connectors
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Ratio measured against
      - definition:
        - text: Registered electric passenger cars, not buses
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: National public chargers, Dec 2025
      - definition:
        - text: 13,482 connectors (scope not stated)
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
      - term: Charging standard
      - definition:
        - text: CCS1
        - superscript:
          - link "[7]":
            - /url: "#ref-7"
      - term: Beitou depot charging bays
      - definition:
        - text: "22"
        - superscript:
          - link "[4]":
            - /url: "#ref-4"
      - term: Muzha depot
      - definition:
        - text: 80% in 20 minutes
        - superscript:
          - link "[6]":
            - /url: "#ref-6"
    - navigation "On this page":
      - paragraph: On this page
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "National public-charger figures mostly aren't about buses":
            - /url: "#national-public-charger-figures-mostly-arent-about-buses"
        - listitem:
          - link "No dedicated depot-electrification budget line found":
            - /url: "#no-dedicated-depot-electrification-budget-line-found"
        - listitem:
          - link "Named installations":
            - /url: "#named-installations"
        - listitem:
          - link "Cost and delay, from named industry figures":
            - /url: "#cost-and-delay-from-named-industry-figures"
        - listitem:
          - 'link "Charging standard: CCS1"':
            - /url: "#charging-standard-ccs1"
        - listitem:
          - 'link "A city-level combined figure: Keelung"':
            - /url: "#a-city-level-combined-figure-keelung"
        - listitem:
          - link "Specifications":
            - /url: "#specifications"
        - listitem:
          - link "References":
            - /url: "#references"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taiwan publishes no consolidated national registry of bus depots and their chargers. This page is deliberately an overview built from named installations and city/national figures, not a census — see
      - link "bus depots and operating sites":
        - /url: /bus/depots/
      - text: for the per-depot pages this site does have.
    - heading "National public-charger figures mostly aren't about buses" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: MOTC reports 12,334 public charging connectors nationally as of end-July 2025 — but the figure is explicitly measured against 110,768 registered electric
      - strong: passenger cars
      - text: (電動小客車), giving a 9.0:1 ratio that says nothing about buses
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . A December 2025 report gives 13,482 connectors and an 8.8:1 overall ratio attributed to MOTC, but states no vehicle category at all
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: — it very plausibly continues the same largely-passenger-car series, but no source confirms this either way, and the figure should not be read as bus-specific charging capacity. The Forward-Looking Infrastructure Program's own NT$9.8 billion public-charger initiative states directly that its demand-assessment tool "specifically targets electric sedans," not buses
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . The programme's own July 2025 figure, from the same MOTC release quoted above, gives 4,768 chargers approved and 1,653 activated by that date
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: — a lower approved count than an unverified, unfetched search-summary figure of 4,865 approved by December 2024, an unreconciled and unsourced drop this page does not resolve.
    - heading "No dedicated depot-electrification budget line found" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The 2030 electric-bus programme's FY2025 budget, verified from a Legislative Yuan primary document, has four lines: vehicle-purchase subsidy (NT$5.92bn), operating subsidy (NT$797.2m), route-network optimisation subsidy (NT$130.8m) and maintenance-system support (NT$9.5m)"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: .
      - strong: None is labelled as charging-infrastructure or depot-electrification spending.
      - text: Route-network optimisation is the closest candidate but is not confirmed to cover charging installations.
    - heading "Named installations" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - strong:
        - link "Beitou":
          - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r22/
        - text: depot (
        - link "北投機廠":
          - /url: /rail/metro/depots/beitou-depot/
        - text: ),
        - link "Taipei":
          - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: — Taipei's electric buses gained a shared night-charging facility inside
      - link "TRTC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: "'s Beitou MRT depot on 2 July 2025: 11 charging posts, 22 bays, run by Danan Bus but open to any operator, coordinated with TRTC by the city's transport bureau"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: ". The rationale given is a genuinely elegant piece of infrastructure sharing: the metro draws its power mainly by day, electric buses charge mainly by night, so pairing the two uses the same land and grid capacity for both"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong: 南港站 (Nangang), Capital Bus
      - text: — 8 charging posts, 16 guns, with 30 buses rotating through them and each charge taking 3–4 hours
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong: 二重站, New Taipei
      - text: — roughly 38 buses sharing only 5 charging bays, requiring a charge after nearly every run
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . Which operator runs this depot is not stated by the source found.
    - paragraph:
      - strong:
        - text: 木柵二站 (
        - link "Muzha":
          - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br02/
        - text: "#2), Xinxin Bus"
      - text: — Taipei's first electric-bus fast-charging station, opened February 2023, reaching 80% charge in 20 minutes on a CCS1 connector — "matching what most of Taiwan's electric buses currently use" — and explicitly built as a shared facility under central policy, likened by its own coverage to a petrol-station model
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: .
    - heading "Cost and delay, from named industry figures" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A charger for a large electric bus costs roughly NT$3 million, "not counting the cost of the Taipower feed-in application process," per a named Taiwan Motor Transport manager
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . Converting a depot — removing fuel tanks, applying for a Taipower feed, installing transformers and chargers — typically takes one to two years of administrative process and tens of millions of NT dollars, per a named Capital Bus deputy manager
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . Taipower feed-in applications can sit unapproved for months, a real operational difficulty
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: .
    - 'heading "Charging standard: CCS1" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: An ITRI-led alliance of roughly 50 companies selected CCS1 as Taiwan's unified public fast-charging standard in March 2021, reasoning that Taiwan's electrical grid environment resembles the United States' and that CCS1 is compatible with the existing J1772 slow-charge base
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: ". That announcement addressed electric vehicles generally, not buses specifically — but bus-specific use is independently confirmed: Tron Energy's current"
      - link "RAC-700":
        - /url: /bus/models/rac-700/
      - text: bus charges via CCS1 with dual guns, and the Muzha depot above independently uses CCS1
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: .
    - 'heading "A city-level combined figure: Keelung" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: Keelung plans to replace its remaining 164 diesel city buses and build 8 charging stations by 2026, a combined NT$1.8 billion — an audit found the programme running significantly behind schedule
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . The source does not split the NT$1.8 billion between vehicles and charging infrastructure.

bus-intercity.snapshot:
- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - link "Bus":
      - /url: /bus/
    - text: National intercity coaches
  - link "Back to the previous page":
    - /url: /bus/depots/charging-infrastructure/
  - heading "National intercity coaches" [level=1]
  - paragraph: A source-backed snapshot of Taiwan's national intercity-coach operators, route variants, stops and published departure times.
  - navigation "On this page":
    - paragraph: On this page
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - link "What the national data actually publishes":
          - /url: "#what-the-national-data-actually-publishes"
      - listitem:
        - link "Route identities and terminals":
          - /url: "#route-identities-and-terminals"
      - listitem:
        - link "Frequencies and service days":
          - /url: "#frequencies-and-service-days"
      - listitem:
        - link "Operators, fares and transfer points":
          - /url: "#operators-fares-and-transfer-points"
      - listitem:
        - link "Coverage and conflicts":
          - /url: "#coverage-and-conflicts"
      - listitem:
        - link "What remains TBC":
          - /url: "#what-remains-tbc"
      - listitem:
        - link "References":
          - /url: "#references"
  - paragraph:
    - text: The national intercity-coach network is published as transport data rather than as a single English network map. The Highway Bureau's company directory is the right starting point for operators and booking links, while its open-data catalogue exposes the timetable as a separate daily dataset.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: The directory is dated 114-08-13 (13 August 2025), whereas the timetable catalogue records an update of 115-07-01 (1 July 2026); those dates describe different publications and are not a single network “last updated” value.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
  - heading "What the national data actually publishes" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: The timetable catalogue names the export as 客運時刻 and supplies a static CSV at the Taiwanbus timetable endpoint.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: Its documented fields include the operator, route number, branch, direction, Chinese and English route names, stop name, stop sequence, departure time, weekday flags, service-date bounds, stop coordinates and stop-position identifier.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - text: The committed snapshot is a full fetch of that CSV on 25 August 2026, not a transcription of search results or a sample of advertised routes.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: It contains 132,398 timetable rows, 44 distinct operator labels and 1,837 route variants after grouping by operator, route number, branch and the published Chinese and English route names.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
  - paragraph:
    - text: The route-summary file is available as
    - link "the committed national route-summary JSON":
      - /url: /data/intercity-bus-routes.json
    - text: .
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: It preserves the source fields and adds a compact direction summary so the site can expose the network without creating thousands of brittle route stubs.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: "The data layer is deliberately a dated snapshot: a later timetable export can add, remove or rename a route variant, so its retrieval date belongs beside every figure that is read from it."
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
  - heading "Route identities and terminals" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: “Route” is not one unambiguous key in the export. The same number can be separated by operator, branch, direction or published route name, and those distinctions are retained in the generated route variants.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: This is why the index reports 1,837 variants rather than silently collapsing the file to a smaller count of route numbers.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
  - paragraph:
    - text: For each direction, the data layer keeps the first and last distinct stops in the order presented by the source rows, together with stop count, coordinates where present and the source stop-position identifier.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: These are derived terminal summaries, not a separate operator-published field called “terminal”.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: A user should therefore treat a first or last stop as the timetable export's ordered boundary and follow the underlying route identity when a service has a short-working, branch or date-bounded variation.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
  - heading "Frequencies and service days" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: The direction summary counts distinct departure times found at the first stop and records the earliest and latest published times.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: It also retains weekday flags and the service-date values present in the export, which makes weekday-only, weekend and date-bounded services visible without pretending that a static timetable is a real-time feed.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: “Frequency” here means the number and span of published departures in the retrieved timetable, not an inferred headway between every pair of trips.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
  - paragraph:
    - text: The national data layer can therefore answer questions such as which operator publishes a route variant, which stops bound a direction in the export, how many departures are listed at its first stop, and which weekday flags or date bounds accompany those rows.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - text: It cannot yet answer whether a vehicle is running now, whether a listed trip is sold out, or whether an operator has made a temporary operational change after the static export was generated.
    - superscript:
      - link "[2]":
        - /url: "#ref-2"
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
  - heading "Operators, fares and transfer points" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: The Highway Bureau directory links operator names to online ticketing and company information, which is useful for moving from a normalized route identity to the operator's own booking surface.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - text: The current snapshot contains 44 operator labels with timetable rows; that is a count of labels in this export, not a claim that it is the bureau's complete regulated-company count.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
  - paragraph:
    - text: Fares remain TBC in this layer. The bureau's 2024 fare notice says the Ministry approved a basic-fare adjustment and that operators may adjust within the approved ceiling, file the result with the bureau and publish it for a week before it takes effect; the notice also explains the TPASS subsidy treatment.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: That rule is not a current fare table for every route, so no route-specific fare has been invented here.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - text: Current fares, reservation classes, concession rules outside the notice's scope, terminal facilities, luggage policy and guaranteed transfer arrangements need route-level operator or bureau records.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
  - paragraph:
    - text: TDX documents an InterCityBus API family alongside its other transport-data services.
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
    - text: This page uses the full public static timetable export for its committed snapshot; authenticated API coverage, real-time service status and any additional route-level fields remain outside the present data layer.
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
  - heading "Coverage and conflicts" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: The current snapshot's 1,837 route variants does not contradict the Highway Bureau plan's historical figure of 173 highway routes in May 2022, because the two values count different things.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: The snapshot splits operator, branch, direction-linked names and timetable identities, while the plan describes a historical route count in a vehicle-electrification planning context.
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - text: The same plan records 57 supervised operators and 3,130 highway vehicles for that May 2022 picture, so its 57 cannot be substituted for the current CSV's 44 timetable labels.
    - superscript:
      - link "[6]":
        - /url: "#ref-6"
    - superscript:
      - link "[3]":
        - /url: "#ref-3"
  - paragraph:
    - text: "The bureau's monthly 國道汽車客運概況 catalogue is another publication layer: it describes aggregate fields such as operator count, route count, trips, passengers, passenger-kilometres and revenue, but it is not the row-level timetable used for this index."
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - text: A national ridership and revenue series should be built from that monthly dataset once the full data file can be fetched and verified; until then, those figures stay TBC.
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
  - heading "What remains TBC" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: Current fares by route, live departures, historical route changes, operator fleet allocation, terminal-by-terminal facilities, route ridership, revenue and a stable transfer graph are not established by the committed static snapshot.
    - superscript:
      - link "[1]":
        - /url: "#ref-1"
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
    - text: The next evidence needed is a full route-level fare source, a successful authenticated or public TDX pull that can be checked end to end, the bureau's monthly statistics file, and operator or terminal primary pages for service details.
    - superscript:
      - link "[5]":
        - /url: "#ref-5"
    - superscript:
      - link "[4]":
        - /url: "#ref-4"
    - superscript:
      - link "[7]":
        - /url: "#ref-7"
  - region "References":
    - heading "References" [level=2]
    - paragraph: 7 of 7 sources on this page are primary — published by the operator, the builder or government.
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - link "Highway Bureau online ticketing and intercity-bus company directory":
          - /url: https://www.thb.gov.tw/cp.aspx?Create=1&n=312
        - text: 網路訂票暨客運公司資訊 primary Highway Bureau, Ministry of Transportation and Communications ( 交通部公路局 ) accessed 2026-08-25 The bureau's directory of intercity-bus companies and online booking links, updated 114-08-13.
      - listitem:
        - 'link "Highway Bureau open-data catalogue: bus timetable"':
          - /url: https://www.thb.gov.tw/News_Content_thbOpenData.aspx?n=13&s=599
        - text: 客運時刻 primary Highway Bureau, Ministry of Transportation and Communications ( 交通部公路局 ) accessed 2026-08-25 The daily timetable dataset catalogue, including the published CSV URL and field list; the catalogue records update 115-07-01.
      - listitem:
        - link "National intercity-bus static timetable export":
          - /url: https://www.taiwanbus.tw/TimeTableExport/timetable.csv
        - text: 公路客運客運時刻 CSV primary Highway Bureau public transport data portal ( 公路局公共運輸資料流通服務 ) accessed 2026-08-25 Full static export fetched on 2026-08-25 and used to generate data/intercity-bus/routes.json and the public route-summary copy.
      - listitem:
        - 'link "Highway Bureau open-data catalogue: national highway-bus overview"':
          - /url: https://www.thb.gov.tw/News_Content_thbOpenData.aspx?n=13&s=492
        - text: 國道汽車客運概況 primary Highway Bureau, Ministry of Transportation and Communications ( 交通部公路局 ) accessed 2026-08-25 Monthly aggregate dataset catalogue with operator count, route count, vehicle-kilometres, passengers, passenger-kilometres and revenue fields.
      - listitem:
        - link "Highway Bureau announcement on base-fare adjustment":
          - /url: https://www.thb.gov.tw/News_Content.aspx?n=87&s=245774&sms=13235
        - text: 交通部核定國道客運基本運價，票價微幅調漲 primary Highway Bureau, Ministry of Transportation and Communications ( 交通部公路局 ) accessed 2026-08-25 The 2024 base-fare adjustment notice, including the operator filing and passenger-notice rule and TPASS subsidy treatment.
      - listitem:
        - link "2030 electric intercity-bus plan":
          - /url: https://ws.thb.gov.tw/Download.ashx?icon=.pdf&n=6Zu75be06KiI55WrKOaguOWumuacrCkucGRm&u=LzAwMS9VcGxvYWQvNDM2L3JlbGZpbGUvMTMyOTEvMjQ4NDQxLzVmYjAzZDZhLTA5ZWQtNGNjYy04YmFlLWZlMGUwYmJlMjdlNC5wZGY%3D
        - text: "2030 年客運車輛電動化推動計畫 primary Highway Bureau, Ministry of Transportation and Communications ( 交通部公路局 ) accessed 2026-08-25 A May 2022 snapshot in the plan: 57 supervised operators, 173 highway routes and 3,130 highway vehicles."

        - listitem:
          - link "The one documented pilot":
            - /url: "#the-one-documented-pilot"
        - listitem:
          - link "No type-approval trail":
            - /url: "#no-type-approval-trail"
        - listitem:
          - link "What Taiwan actually ran instead":
            - /url: "#what-taiwan-actually-ran-instead"
        - listitem:
          - link "What remains open":
            - /url: "#what-remains-open"
        - listitem:
          - link "References":
            - /url: "#references"
    - paragraph: Taiwan's bus fleets never adopted compressed natural gas (CNG, 壓縮天然氣) at any scale this site could find evidence of. The one documented episode is small, undated beyond its year, and rests on a single source.
    - heading "The one documented pilot" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: introduced six CNG buses in 1999 and built a slow-fill refuelling station in
      - link "Neihu":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br19/
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: ". The source is a 2009 technical article by the Automotive Research & Testing Center (ARTC), a government-linked vehicle-testing body, reporting on the city's programme rather than being the city's own record of it:"
    - blockquote:
      - paragraph:
        - text: 台北市於民國88年引進6輛壓縮天然氣公車，並且在台北內湖蓋了一座慢速加氣站，但因為車輛保養不易、巡航距離較短、加氣站太少且加氣速度過慢、天然氣品質不穩定等因素導致計畫最後宣告失敗
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
        - text: 。
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The programme is described as a failure, for five stated reasons: vehicles were hard to maintain, cruising range was short, refuelling stations were too few and too slow, and gas quality was inconsistent"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . No operator, manufacturer, chassis brand or route number is named anywhere this source or any other found — the six-vehicle figure and the Neihu station are the whole of what is documented. A search across zh.wikipedia's general Taipei bus articles, the Taipei Environmental Protection Bureau's own published history timeline, and Taiwanese news archives found nothing that names this programme independently of the ARTC article, so the claim is carried at Medium confidence rather than confirmed by a second source.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The same ARTC article, on its own institutional work rather than Taipei's programme, states its diesel-engine laboratory had tested converting diesel engines to run on CNG conversion kits and compared emissions against unconverted diesel, with a liquefied-natural-gas test rig planned to help domestic manufacturers localise conversion kits
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . This frames CNG in Taiwan's bus context as a retrofit technology applied to existing diesel chassis, not a purpose-built model — which is consistent with no CNG entry existing in any vehicle type-approval register found.
    - heading "No type-approval trail" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Vehicle Safety Certification Center (VSCC), the body responsible for large-bus type-approval in Taiwan, publishes no CNG-specific qualified- model list. Its coach-chassis registry index names exactly three document sets, none referencing natural gas, and its only other large-bus register is the electric-bus promotion programme
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . This absence was checked against VSCC's own published index directly, not inferred from a search returning nothing.
    - heading "What Taiwan actually ran instead" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "This site has not independently verified it, so it is stated as an unconfirmed lead rather than a fact: search results describe an environmental-authority \"油氣雙燃料車\" (oil-gas dual-fuel vehicle) programme running roughly 2008 to 2012, using LPG rather than CNG, for taxis and light vehicles — not a bus programme. It is noted here only so the two fuels are not conflated, which one AI-generated search summary encountered during this research did do, wrongly attributing a taxi LPG conversion to the CNG bus claim. This site's own"
      - link "electric bus programme":
        - /url: /bus/network/electric-bus-programme/
      - text: page covers what actually reached Taiwan's city bus fleets at scale after 2020.
    - heading "What remains open" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Manufacturer, chassis brand, model designation, operating end date, and whether any of the six vehicles survive are all TBC. No Kaohsiung,
      - link "Taichung":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taichung/
      - text: or
      - link "Taoyuan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taoyuan/
      - text: CNG bus programme was found in this search, though the search for those cities was not exhaustive.
    - region "References":
      - heading "References" [level=2]
      - paragraph: 1 of 2 sources on this page is primary — published by the operator, the builder or government.
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "An old but enduring vehicle fuel — the application of natural gas in vehicles":
            - /url: https://www.artc.org.tw/tw/knowledge/articles/67
          - text: "古老、卻長遠的汽車燃料--天然氣在車輛上的應用 secondary Automotive Research & Testing Center ( 財團法人車輛研究測試中心 , ARTC) accessed 2026-08-28 ARTC (a MOTC-linked, government-affiliated testing body) reporting on Taipei City's own 1999 programme, not a primary record of it — no Taipei city, MOTC or news source corroborating this was found. Quoted directly: 「台北市於民國88年引進6輛壓縮天然氣公車，並且在台北內湖蓋了一座慢速加氣站，但因為車輛保養不易、巡航距離較短、加氣站太少且加氣速度過慢、天然氣品質不穩定等因素導致計畫最後宣告失敗。」 ARTC is primary for its own testing work on CNG conversion kits, described in the same article."
        - listitem:
          - link "Declared chassis suitable for coach bodywork, and vehicle-type qualification information zone":
            - /url: https://www.vscc.org.tw/Home/List/5
          - text: 宣告登錄可適性打造遊覽車之底盤車及合格證明車型資訊專區 primary Vehicle Safety Certification Center ( 財團法人車輛安全審驗中心 ) accessed 2026-08-28 VSCC's own coach-chassis registry index, fetched directly. Lists exactly three document sets, none referencing natural gas — the strongest available evidence that no CNG-specific type-approval list exists. VSCC's only other large-bus register found is the electric-bus programme (交通部電動大客車推動計畫專區).

- main:
