    - heading "Conflicts and gaps" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Xiaobitan’s work has three different primary-source figures. The general DORTS table gives NT$1,000,000; the dedicated DORTS work record gives approximately NT$35,900,000 plus a NT$1,000,000 first prize; and the DORTS technical book says the project was constrained by a NT$15,000,000 budget limit before the interior works were substantially reduced.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The sources describe different scopes or stages, but do not reconcile them, so all three values remain published.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Sanying sources also disagree. The 2025 announcement assigns 蘆花街燈 to
      - link "LB08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb08/
      - text: and 時光行旅 to
      - link "LB10":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb10/
      - text: .
      - superscript:
        - link "[33]":
          - /url: "#ref-33"
      - text: The 2026 announcement omits the
      - link "LB08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb08/
      - text: label, assigns 時光行旅 and 陶鄉 to
      - link "LB10":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb10/
      - text: ", and calls the programme 12 works."
      - superscript:
        - link "[34]":
          - /url: "#ref-34"
      - text: The full
      - link "LB08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb08/
      - text: art record instead names 陶鄉 at
      - link "LB08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb08/
      - text: . The table preserves each value rather than choosing a station allocation.
      - superscript:

          - /url: "#ref-33"

rail-krtc-facilities-accessibility.snapshot:
- main:
  - navigation "Breadcrumb":
    - link "Home":
      - /url: /
    - link "Rail & cable":
      - /url: /rail/
    - link "Kaohsiung Metro":
      - /url: /rail/krtc/
    - link "Facilities":
      - /url: /rail/krtc/facilities/
    - text: Kaohsiung Metro station accessibility
  - link "Back to the previous page":
    - /url: /rail/history/matra-dispute/
  - article:
    - heading "Kaohsiung Metro station accessibility" [level=1]
    - paragraph: The operator states every station has an accessible elevator — but not as a measured percentage, and not under any named regulation this page could find.
    - region "Quick facts":
      - text: Kaohsiung Metro station accessibility
      - term: Accessible elevator provision
      - definition:
        - text: stated as universal ("all stations"), not a measured completion percentage
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Accessible restrooms
      - definition:
        - text: in both men's and women's facilities at every station
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Accessible parking
      - definition:
        - text: one car/motorcycle space at stations with park-and-ride facilities
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Named regulatory basis
      - definition: TBC
    - navigation "On this page":
      - paragraph: On this page
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "What the operator states, and what it doesn't":
            - /url: "#what-the-operator-states-and-what-it-doesnt"
        - listitem:
          - link "The light rail is a separate question":
            - /url: "#the-light-rail-is-a-separate-question"
        - listitem:
          - link "What governs MRT station accessibility generally":
            - /url: "#what-governs-mrt-station-accessibility-generally"
        - listitem:
          - link "Remaining gaps":
            - /url: "#remaining-gaps"
        - listitem:
          - link "References":
            - /url: "#references"
    - heading "What the operator states, and what it doesn't" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: KRTC's own accessibility page states that every station provides an accessible elevator, framed to serve visually impaired, physically disabled, elderly and other temporarily mobility-limited passengers — those carrying heavy items or pushing strollers are named explicitly alongside disabled passengers.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: "This is a statement of universal provision in words, not a measured completion percentage: no \"100% of stations\" figure, or any numeric count, appears anywhere on the page."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The same page enumerates a defined set of facilities at every station: an accessible ticket gate and an accessible add-value/ticketing machine positioned near the non-paid-area elevator exit; accessible restrooms in both men's and women's facilities; accessible ramps that continue existing street-level infrastructure into the station as a connection point for wheelchair users; one accessible car or motorcycle parking space at stations that have park-and-ride facilities; and platform-level tactile guidance, accessible door-position signage, and audible door-closing warnings."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph: "Checked specifically: the same page cites no named law, regulation or design standard anywhere in its content — not Taiwan's general building accessibility code, not the public-transport accessible-facilities regulation, not the disability-rights protection act. This is recorded as not found on this page, not as confirmed absent from KRTC's practice more broadly; a KRTC internal policy document or tender specification might state one that this page did not reach."
    - heading "The light rail is a separate question" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: KRTC's accessibility page sits within the site's heavy-rail ("乘車指南") section. The separate
      - link "Circular Light Rail":
        - /url: /rail/krtc/lines/circular-light-rail/
      - text: station-guide pages checked for this page did not themselves mention accessibility, low-floor vehicles or wheelchair access. Whether the heavy-rail page's "all stations" statement is meant to cover the light rail too, or refers only to the Red and Orange Lines, is not stated by any source found and is not assumed either way here.
    - heading "What governs MRT station accessibility generally" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: KRTC's own page names no regulation, but a different Taipei-region operator's page does.
      - link "TRTC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: "'s station-facilities page states directly that its MRT elevators comply with the Ministry of the Interior's Building Accessibility Facility Design Code (建築物無障礙設施設計規範), the general public-building accessibility standard issued under Article 167 of the Building Technical Regulations."
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: This establishes what governs MRT station buildings generally in Taiwan; it does not itself confirm that KRTC's own stations were built or audited against this specific code, since KRTC's own page does not name it.
    - heading "Remaining gaps" [level=2]
    - paragraph: No numeric elevator-completion figure was found in any source read for this page. Whether KRTC's own stations were designed or audited against the Building Accessibility Facility Design Code specifically is TBC. Whether the Circular Light Rail is covered by the same "all stations" statement is TBC.
    - region "References":
      - heading "References" [level=2]
      - paragraph: 2 of 2 sources on this page are primary — published by the operator, the builder or government.
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Accessibility Facilities":
            - /url: https://www.krtc.com.tw/Guide/safety_guide?id=12828c60abbc465bac2d2c608f4cab0a
          - text: 無障礙設施 primary Kaohsiung Rapid Transit Corporation ( 高雄捷運股份有限公司 ) accessed 2026-08-27 Full operator page, read directly. States universal elevator provision and enumerates other station facilities; checked specifically and confirmed to cite no named law, regulation or design standard.
        - listitem:
          - link "Station elevator facilities":
            - /url: https://www.metro.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=C0EB9D07B84907D9&s=4FDC24D931DE6050
          - text: 站內無障礙設施 primary Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation ( 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 ) accessed 2026-08-29 A different Taipei-region operator's own page, fetched twice with identical results. States directly that its MRT elevators comply with the Ministry of the Interior's Building Accessibility Facility Design Code (建築物無障礙設施設計規範). Establishes what governs MRT station buildings generally in Taiwan; does not itself confirm KRTC's own stations were built or audited against this code, since KRTC names no regulation on its own page.
    - paragraph: "Last updated: 2026-08-28"

    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Xindian Line A former 10.4 km Wanhua–Xindian railway, bought by the state in 1949, withdrawn in 1965 and later overlapped by roads and the Taipei Metro.":
        - /url: /rail/history/xindian-line/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Zhonghe Line A former 6.5 km freight-only TRA branch from Banqiao to Zhonghe that opened in 1965, stopped service in 1990 and was physically dismantled in 1993.":
        - /url: /rail/history/zhonghe-line/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Fengyuan–Dongshi Line A former 14.1 km TRA branch built in 1958, opened in 1959 and withdrawn after its final train on 31 August 1991.":
        - /url: /rail/history/fengyuan-dongshi-line/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Tanzi–Shengang Line An 8.7 km route listed in TRA's construction table alongside a roughly 14 km municipal greenway whose official histories disagree about the former railway's administrative identity.":
        - /url: /rail/history/tanzi-shengang-line/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Ruifang–Shen'ao Line A 6.3 km operator-table route with conflicting 1961 and 1965 opening records, passenger and freight service stopped in 1989, and passenger service restored on a shorter surviving route in 2014.":
        - /url: /rail/history/ruifang-shenao-line/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Houtong–Sandiaoling Double Track A 2.5 km double-track construction segment recorded by TRA as built in 1967 and opened in 1968, within the present Yilan Line corridor between Houtong and Sandiaoling.":
        - /url: /rail/history/houtong-sandiaoling-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Changhua–Minxiong Double Track A 71.7 km TRA construction-history segment recorded as built in 1957 and opened in 1970 with a double-track extension, kept separate from the current Western Main Line data layer.":
        - /url: /rail/history/changhua-minxiong-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Chiayi–Xinshi Double Track A 50.1 km TRA construction-history segment recorded as built in 1957 and opened in 1970 with a double-track extension, kept separate from the current Western Main Line data layer.":
        - /url: /rail/history/chiayi-xinshi-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Jianan–Taichung Port Construction Record A 7.8 km TRA construction-history record for Jianan–Taichung Port, recorded in the operator PDF as constructed in 1973 and opened in 1974, while the current HTML history table omits the row.":
        - /url: /rail/history/jianan-taichung-port-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Xinpu–Tongxiao Double Track A 5.8 km TRA construction-history segment recorded as built and opened in 1974 with an added second track, kept separate from the current Western Main Line data layer.":
        - /url: /rail/history/xinpu-tongxiao-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Yuanli–Rinan Double Track A 7.8 km TRA construction-history segment recorded as built and opened in 1974 with an added second track, kept separate from the current Western Main Line data layer.":
        - /url: /rail/history/yuanli-rinan-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Jianan–Qingshui Double Track A 6.0 km TRA construction-history record preserved in the operator PDF as built and opened in 1974 with an added second track, while the current HTML history table omits the row.":
        - /url: /rail/history/jianan-qingshui-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Dajia–Jianan Double Track A 5.3 km TRA construction-history segment recorded in the operator PDF as built in 1974 and opened in 1977 with an added second track, kept separate from the current station and line data.":
        - /url: /rail/history/dajia-jianan-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Dongshan–Su'aoxin Double Track A 5.4 km TRA construction-history segment recorded in both operator presentations as built in 1974 and opened in 1977 with an added second track, while current TDX data places Xinma between its named endpoints.":
        - /url: /rail/history/dongshan-su-aoxin-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Sijiaoting–Ruifang Double Track A 5.8 km TRA construction-history segment recorded in the operator's records as built in 1974 and opened in 1977 with an added second track, while current TDX data gives a separate 5.0 km endpoint-distance interval.":
        - /url: /rail/history/sijiaoting-ruifang-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Mudan–Shuangxi Double Track A 3.1 km TRA construction-history segment recorded in the operator's records as built in 1974 and opened in 1978 with an added second track, while current TDX data gives a separate 3.4 km endpoint-distance interval.":
        - /url: /rail/history/mudan-shuangxi-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Hualien–Hualien Port Records The operator records two Hualien–Hualien Port entries—4.0 km before Retrocession and 5.8 km for the later TRA construction completed in 1979—while a 2005 operating table retains the 5.8 km section.":
        - /url: /rail/history/hualien-hualien-port/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Hualien–Heping Construction Record The operator records Hualien–Heping as a 39.4 km project opened in 1979 after construction in 1978, while its historical and current tables disagree on the constructor and current TDX endpoints measure 39.6 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/hualien-heping/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Heping–Su'aoxin Construction Record The operator records Heping–Su'aoxin as a 39.8 km project opened in 1980 after construction in 1973, while its historical and current tables disagree on the constructor and current TDX endpoints measure 39.9 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/heping-su-aoxin/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Hualien–Taitung Widening Record The operator records the Hualien–Taitung widening as a 162.2 km project opened in 1982 after work in 1978, while current TDX endpoint fields cover 150.9 km between Hualien and Taitung.":
        - /url: /rail/history/hualien-taitung-widening/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Hanben–Hualien Double-track Record The operator records Hanben–Hualien as a 42.5 km Railway Reconstruction Bureau project built in 1992 and opened in 2003 with double-tracking, electrification, heavier rail and PC sleepers; current TDX endpoint fields measure 44.0 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/hanben-hualien-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Hualien–Ruisui Reconstruction Record The operator records Hualien–Ruisui as a 70.5 km Railway Reconstruction Bureau project built in 1992 and opened in 2003 with heavier rail and PC sleepers; current TDX endpoint fields measure 62.8 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/hualien-ruisui-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Su'aoxin–Hanben Double-track Record The operator records Su'aoxin–Hanben as a 36.7 km Railway Reconstruction Bureau project built in 1993 and opened in 2004 with double-tracking; current TDX endpoint fields measure 35.5 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/suaoxin-hanben-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Hualien Port Line Reconstruction Record The operator records Hualien Port Line as a 10.5 km Railway Reconstruction Bureau project built in 1992 and opened in 2004 with heavier rail and PC sleepers; current TDX data supplies no named Hualien Port passenger endpoint.":
        - /url: /rail/history/hualien-port-line-reconstruction/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Songshan–Nangang Underground Record The operator records Songshan–Nangang as a 7.7 km Railway Reconstruction Bureau project built in 1998 and opened in 2008 as railway underground; current TDX endpoint fields measure 2.8 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/songshan-nangang-underground/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Keelung Station Track-removal Records The operator's historical PDF contains two TRA Keelung Station records—2.9 km from 1978 and 2.0 km from 1969—both tied to 27 April 2010 track removals; current TDX identifies Keelung as Western Main Line position 1.":
        - /url: /rail/history/keelung-station-track-removal/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Zhuzhong–Liujia Double-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 3.1 km Railway Reconstruction Bureau Zhuzhong–Liujia double-track project with 2005 and 2011 year fields; current TDX keeps the two stations as the LJ line's 3.1 km ordered pair.":
        - /url: /rail/history/zhuzhong-liujia-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Tao-yuan Station Track-removal Record The operator's historical PDF records a 3.1 km Tao-yuan Station subject with 1969 and 1969 year fields and a May 2012 removal explanation for tracks 5–11, the loading line and the flour line.":
        - /url: /rail/history/taoyuan-station-track-removal/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Longtian–Shanhua Double-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 3.8 km Longtian–Shanhua double-track subject with 2001 and 2013 year fields and a Zeng-Wun River Bridge new-construction explanation; current TDX fields span 6.8 km via Baling.":
        - /url: /rail/history/longtian-shanhua-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Xinshi–Yongkang Double-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 2.9 km Xinshi–Yongkang double-track subject with 2009 and 2013 year fields and a Yan-shui River Bridge new-construction explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 5.0 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/xinshi-yongkang-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Wuhe–Sanmin Single-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 1.6 km Wuhe–Sanmin single-track subject with 2013 and 2013 year fields and a Hualien–Taitung railway electrification explanation; current TDX exposes Sanmin but no Wuhe endpoint record.":
        - /url: /rail/history/wuhe-sanmin-single-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Sanmin–Yuli Single-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 4.1 km Sanmin–Yuli single-track subject with 2013 and 2013 year fields and a Hualien–Taitung railway electrification explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 10.8 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/sanmin-yuli-single-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Dongli–Dongzhu Single-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 2.1 km Dongli–Dongzhu single-track subject with 2012 and 2013 year fields and a Hualien–Taitung railway electrification explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 6.0 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/dongli-dongzhu-single-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Dongzhu–Fuli Single-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 2.9 km Dongzhu–Fuli single-track subject with 2012 and 2013 year fields and a Hualien–Taitung railway electrification explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 6.1 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/dongzhu-fuli-single-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Chishang–Haiduan Single-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 0.3 km Chishang–Haiduan single-track subject with 2012 and 2013 year fields and a Hualien–Taitung railway electrification explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 5.7 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/chishang-haiduan-single-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Haiduan–Ruiyuan Single-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 4.6 km Haiduan–Ruiyuan single-track subject with 2010 and 2013 year fields and a Hualien–Taitung railway electrification explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 16.7 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/haiduan-ruiyuan-single-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Shanli–Taitung Double-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 7.3 km Shanli–Taitung double-track subject with 2010 and 2013 year fields and a double-tracking explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 8.2 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/shanli-taitung-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Huatan–Shetou Double-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 4.3 km Huatan–Shetou double-track subject with 2006 and 2014 year fields and a Yuan-Lin Railway elevated explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 15.3 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/huatan-shetou-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Jinlun–Taimali Single-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 1.9 km Jinlun–Taimali single-track subject with 2010 and 2014 year fields and a South-Taimail Bridge reconstruction explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 10.9 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/jinlun-taimali-single-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Pingtung–Chaozhou Double-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 16.3 km Pingtung–Chaozhou double-track subject with 2009 and 2015 year fields and a south-of-Pingtung railway-elevation explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 15.0 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/pingtung-chaozhou-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Shoufeng–Nanping Double-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 12.0 km Shoufeng–Nanping double-track subject with 2014 and 2015 year fields and an extension-to-double-track explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 11.2 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/shoufeng-nanping-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Taoyuan Station Switching Record The operator's historical PDF records a 0.3 km Taoyuan Station subject with 2015 construction and operation-start fields and a temporary-station switching explanation; current TDX places Taoyuan at Western Main Line position 21.":
        - /url: /rail/history/taoyuan-station-switching/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Japanese-era trunk line, 1895–1945 How 臺灣總督府鐵道部 built the west-coast trunk line that became TRA — a 1908 completion at a gauge fixed years earlier under the Qing, two named stations lost to demolition and bombing, and a ten-week gap before the Republic of China's own railway administration took over.":
        - /url: /rail/history/japanese-era-trunk-line/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Shoufeng–Fengtian Double-track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 2.7 km Shoufeng–Fengtian double-track subject with 2015 and 2016 year fields and an extension-to-double-track explanation; current TDX endpoint fields span 2.8 km.":
        - /url: /rail/history/shoufeng-fengtian-double-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Haikeguan–Badouzi Reopening Record The operator's historical PDF records a 0.4 km Haikeguan–Badouzi subject with 2015 and 2016 year fields and a resumption-of-service explanation; current TDX places the two stations 0.4 km apart on the Shenao Line.":
        - /url: /rail/history/haikeguan-badouzi-reopening/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Sugar Railway network A 762 mm network that reached roughly 3,244 km by 1952, carried passengers for 74 years until 1982, and survives today as five short tourist lines plus one still-working cane-hauling branch at Huwei.":
        - /url: /rail/history/sugar-railway/
    - listitem:
      - link "Forestry railways beyond Alishan Taipingshan, Baxianshan and the Luodong connector — three logging railway systems that moved timber out of Taiwan's mountains for six decades before ending in the 1960s-80s, with one short tourist stretch still running at Taipingshan.":
        - /url: /rail/history/forestry-railways/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Shanhua Station Platform Record The operator's historical PDF records a 0.3 km Shanhua Station subject with 2017 construction and operation-start fields and an Add platform explanation; current TDX places Shanhua at Western Main Line position 84.":
        - /url: /rail/history/shanhua-station-platform/
    - listitem:
      - link "Coal and mineral mining railways The private colliery railway that became the Pingxi Line, and the separate gold and copper networks at Jinguashi and the coal railway at Houtong — three industrial systems whose Japanese-era origins are still visible in today's TRA branch and heritage sites.":
        - /url: /rail/history/mining-railways/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Sanmin Station Track Record The operator's historical PDF records a 2.1 km Sanmin Station subject with 2010 construction and 2017 operation-start fields and an Add track explanation; current TDX places Sanmin at Eastern Main Line position 52.":
        - /url: /rail/history/sanmin-station-track/
    - listitem:
      - link "Port rail connections — Kaohsiung, Keelung, Taichung Kaohsiung's century-old harbour line closed in 2018 and was partly reused for light rail; Keelung's went silent by 2015; only Taichung's port branch still runs freight today, on a construction date that conflicts with its own operator's two histories.":
        - /url: /rail/history/port-rail-connections/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Donggang Line A wartime naval branch to Pingtung County's coast, closed in 1991 after a bridge ended its reason to exist — and whose own operator record cannot currently be read.":
        - /url: /rail/history/donggang-line/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Old Mountain Line The original, earthquake-scarred Sanyi–Houlong alignment, bypassed in 1998 because it was too difficult to double-track — now run by Miaoli County as a rail-bike attraction rather than by TRA.":
        - /url: /rail/history/old-mountain-line/
    - listitem:
      - link "The Ten Major Constructions and the THSR BOT crisis Six transport projects launched in the 1970s under one banner, and a fundamentally different procurement model 25 years later for high speed rail — whose 2009 financial crisis a Control Yuan investigation called a \"knockoff BOT\" that left the government carrying nearly all the risk.":
        - /url: /rail/history/ten-major-constructions/

    - listitem:
      - link "Railway electrification chronology and achievements":
        - /url: https://www.railway.gov.tw/tra-tip-web/adr/about-achievement-1?selectIndex=0
      - text: 臺鐵電氣化沿革及歷年建設 primary National Taiwan Railways Corporation / former Taiwan Railway Administration ( 國營臺灣鐵路股份有限公司／臺灣鐵路管理局 ) accessed 2026-08-27 The full operator achievement page gives the electrification chronology, Western Main Line phases, later branch and regional extensions, substation milestones and the 2001 centralised SCADA power-dispatch arrangement. Cited by
      - link "Taiwan Railways electrification":
        - /url: /rail/tra/technology/electrification/
    - listitem:
      - link "Railway Locomotive and Rolling Stock Inspection Rules":
        - /url: https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawSingle.aspx?pcode=K0030003&flno=8
      - text: 鐵路機車車輛檢修規則 primary Ministry of Transportation and Communications, via Laws & Regulations Database ( 交通部 , 全國法規資料庫 ) accessed 2026-08-27 Article 8, read directly. Defines TRA's four-level rolling-stock inspection system, a different framework from the five-level metro-depot facility grade this project has documented elsewhere. Cited by
      - link "Taiwan Railways maintenance workshops":
        - /url: /rail/tra/rolling-stock/maintenance-depots/
    - listitem:
      - link "Railway Operating Rules":
        - /url: https://law.moj.gov.tw/LawClass/LawAll.aspx?PCode=K0030005
      - text: 鐵路行車規則 primary Laws & Regulations Database, Ministry of Justice ( 全國法規資料庫 , 法務部 ) accessed 2026-08-27 Full regulation text, read directly. Confirms the national operating regulation does not contain the intensity-graduated post-earthquake speed rule widely attributed to TRA in news coverage. Cited by
      - link "Taiwan Railways seismic design and earthquake response":
        - /url: /rail/tra/technology/seismic-design/
    - listitem:
      - link "Railway roads changing shape — the urban texture formed by railways (3)":
        - /url: https://www.dorts.ntpc.gov.tw/documentary/articleInfo/Qw92VjrK2jOk
      - text: 鐵路馬路變變變—鐵道型塑的都市紋理（三） primary New Taipei City Government Department of Rapid Transit Systems ( 新北市政府捷運工程局 ) accessed 2026-08-26 Full municipal history page. It identifies the Zhonghe Line as freight-only, dates operation from 5 March 1965 and says it stopped and was dismantled in 1990 as coal demand fell and the city developed. Cited by
      - link "The Taiwan Railways Zhonghe Line":
        - /url: /rail/history/zhonghe-line/

      - text: 鐵道技術 primary Alishan Forest Railway and Cultural Heritage Office ( 阿里山林業鐵路及文化資產管理處 ) accessed 2026-08-25 Operator technical history for the 1912 opening, 762 mm gauge and mountain methods. Cited by

        - /url: /rail/alishan/lines/alishan-forest-railway/

      - text: 淡水信義線／淡水線路線說明 primary Taipei City Government, Department of Rapid Transit Systems ( 臺北市政府捷運工程局 ) accessed 2026-08-10 The builder's own project record. The whole alignment in one sentence — 淡水線北起淡水站沿原北淡鐵路南行至北投以北之貴子坑溪為地面段；自貴子坑溪堤起高架南行跨基隆河，過民族西路下降進入地下至中正紀念堂站，全長約23.8公里(含北投至新北投路段約1.2公里)，設22座車站及1座主機廠 — plus 另新北投支線為北投站至新北投站, the 1986 approval and NT$444.4bn budget, the 13 design and ~120 construction contracts, the opening and inspection dates in ROC years, and 最早CT107標北投機廠土方工程，自77年1月19日簽約開始施工. Its station table carries a 工程編號 column distinct from the passenger codes. Cited by

  - heading "What this page does not tell you" [level=2]
  - paragraph:
    - text: It lists what is cited, not what is asserted. A page can carry a figure with no citation at all, and that figure will not appear here — which is precisely why the build counts those separately. Run
    - code: npm run claims
    - text: for the count of statements on this site that currently rest on nobody’s authority.
  - paragraph:
    - text: Nor does it tell you whether a source is
    - emphasis: right
    - text: . This site has already found one case where a citation to an official route map was further from the published colour than the value it replaced. Primary means “first hand”, not “correct”.

    - heading "Scope and built form" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Kaohsiung’s Circular Light Rail is a 22.1 km surface-light-rail loop with 38 stations in the city government’s completed-route description.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: Its alignment uses the former harbour-rail corridor, port roads, Pier-2, the west-side railway corridor, the Museum of Fine Arts area and Dashun roads before returning through the south-western corridor.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: The operator’s English guide map lists the same C1–C37 plus C21A station identity, while the current TDX Metro pull contains only the Red and Orange metro lines.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The approved planning page gives a combined construction cost of NT$211.16 billion, including NT$70.13 billion in central support and NT$141.03 billion borne by the city, including self-financing revenue.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: It describes a surface B-type right of way with the track separated from the road, 1,435 mm standard gauge, 100% low-floor vehicles, and platforms 2.5–4 m wide and 35 cm high.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The government route page lists transfers to the Red Line at C3 and C24, to the Orange Line at C14 and C32, and to TRA at C18 and C30.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - heading "Two-phase construction and delay" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The approved plan divided construction because the C17–C20 railway-garden section depended on the Kaohsiung urban railway-undergrounding project, while the C32–C36 corridor depended on the release of land from the Taiwan Railways East Harbour Line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: Phase 1 was defined as 8.7 km from the Qianzhen shunting yard to Sizihwan, while Phase 2 covered the remaining 13.4 km.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The planning page’s original schedule expected Phase 1 to finish by the end of ROC year 106 and Phase 2 to follow the 2017 railway-undergrounding schedule; those are planning milestones, not the eventual opening dates.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The second phase became a public dispute rather than a routine continuation. DORTS says the route had been planned since the 1990s, but when construction entered the site in ROC year 106, residents repeatedly protested the route and construction method.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The city published five “reassurance” measures in July 2018, but opposition continued, and the mayor announced on 18 January 2019 that the disputed second-phase works should pause for broader public hearings.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS then held five public hearings in February and March 2019 and recorded 1,874 opinion forms.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The support submissions cited accessibility, relief of road and commercial-area congestion and connections to the Red and Orange lines; the opposition submissions cited lower capacity, slower speed, traffic effects, loss of curb parking and a preference for underground or elevated metro.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The bureau appointed nine rail and transport experts to examine nine alternatives, including the original alignment and method, elevated, underground, a Tongmeng Road diversion, C-type right of way and cancellation.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The expert committee’s recommendations retained the southern noncontroversial section, proposed resident participation and human-centred streetscape treatment for the Art Museum Road and Dashun Road section, and suggested a future northward extension toward
      - link "Taiwan High Speed Rail":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/lines/thsr/
      - link "Zuoying":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/zuoying/
      - text: .
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: DORTS said the committee judged elevated or underground alternatives less economically suitable because of cost, construction risk and later operation, but that is the bureau’s account of the committee’s assessment rather than an independent finding by this page.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - heading "Environmental revision and completion" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The 2021 environmental-difference review recorded more than 44 public briefings and 20 expert meetings before the city retained the basic route with design changes.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: Those changes included a larger curve radius, moving the Art Museum Road alignment north, preserving four road lanes, adding C21A, adding a pedestrian bridge for Chung-Hua Arts School and placing a station in the United Hospital setback.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: DORTS said the changes reduced noise, preserved emergency access and road service, and did not increase environmental impacts compared with the approved environmental assessment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - text: KRTC’s current operator Q&A records the result as a 1 January 2024 full-circle trial with service expanded to all 38 stations, followed by formal full-line operation from 26 February.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: It also records the change from a flat fare to distance-based charging and identifies C1 as both termini for the circular service.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: The planning schedule and the operating record therefore show a clear conflict between the original 2017-era completion expectation and the actual 2024 full-line service date; neither is silently substituted for the other.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - heading "Station sequence and data boundary" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The government station table contains C1 through C37 plus C21A, so C21A Neiwei Arts Center and C21 Kaohsiung Museum of Fine Arts remain separate records.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"

    - heading "Red Line in the current data" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: TDX identifies this route as the Red Line with line ID R; the line record supplies the Traditional Chinese name 紅線.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The operator’s English guide map uses the same line identity and lists the same station-code family from R3 to RK1.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: This page keeps the line record, route record and station-of-route record separate because they answer different questions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The direction-zero StationOfRoute record contains 25 ordered members.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: The reverse-direction record is also present in the raw pull, but this page uses direction zero as the reader-facing sequence so that the order is stable and explicit.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: The sequence is a data relationship; it does not claim that every train service stops identically at every time of day.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - heading "Construction and opening chronology" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The government’s network history places the Red and Orange lines in the first stage of Kaohsiung’s first-period MRT development plan, approved in ROC80, and says that the two routes were completed and opened in ROC97.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: "KRTC’s company history gives a more granular institutional chronology: the city invited private participation on 1 February 1999, the China Steel-led application was selected on 10 May 2000, the company received its licence on 28 December 2000, and the construction and development agreements were signed on 12 January 2001."
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: KRTC records construction beginning in October 2001 and describes the concession as 36 years from the start of construction, comprising more than six years of construction before the Red and Orange lines entered service.
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "MTBU treats the Red and Orange network as one private-participation construction and operating project: its page gives six years of construction, 30 years of operation and a 36-year concession, with a planned 42.7 km and 38 stations, three depots and a total construction cost of NT$183.963 billion."
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: KRTC records the Red Line’s regular service opening on 9 March 2008 and the Orange Line’s opening on 14 September 2008; the latter date marks the full operation of the original cross-shaped network, not the first Red Line service.
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The historical service-indicator document is a separate design snapshot. It describes a Red Line of 28.3 km, with 19.8 km underground and 8.5 km elevated, and 23 stations at the time of that document.
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: The current government page reports 28.3 km and 24 Red Line stations, while the TDX route pull reports 29.72 km and its current sequence includes R24 and RK1.
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: Those values are retained as different dated or structured boundaries rather than made to agree by arithmetic.
    - heading "Extensions, interfaces and depots" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: R24 was not part of the original 2008 station opening.
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: MTBU’s delivery study says the station contract began on 3 January 2011, that overall progress reached 79.55% by the end of June 2012, and that the project had initially fallen behind because approval timing was later than expected and KRTC had declined to invest in the electrical and mechanical works on financial-difficulty grounds.
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: The same study describes the response as a contract change with more finely divided milestone payments and records the target of substantive completion and system integration by the end of 2012.
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: The government’s 109-year statistical report records R24 ’s opening on 23 December 2012.
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
    - paragraph:
      - text: R11 Kaohsiung Main Station was a second interface with another major project. The temporary co-constructed station opened with the Red Line in ROC97, while the permanent station had to follow the city railway-undergrounding programme; MTBU records the switch from the temporary station to the permanent station’s initial operating area on 5 September 2018.
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: This is why a Red Line opening date alone does not describe every station’s final architectural or systems completion.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The first Gangshan–Lujhu extension phase added RK1 north of R24 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: MTBU records free trial operation from noon on 30 June 2024, a connection to TRA Gangshan Station and planned joint development around the new interchange.
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: The free trial ended and formal operation and charging began on 1 September 2024.
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
      - text: The current second phase is split into 2A and 2B; the government reports RK2–RK6 Phase 2A at 33.59% on 20 May 2026 and identifies relocation of a 2,000 mm water main under Provincial Highway 1 as a major construction constraint.
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The joint project planned two Red Line depots and one Orange Line depot, a distinction also recorded in the statistical report.
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: KRTC places the South Depot at the Red Line’s southern end around R4A , with a 26-hectare site, a Level 3 maintenance function and the network control centre.
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: It places the North Depot at the Red Line’s northern end across Gangshan and Ciaotou districts.
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
    - heading "Systems evidence and boundary" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The historical service-indicator document lists rolling stock, signalling, DC traction power, AC power, platforms, communications, automatic fare collection, lifts, escalators and depot equipment as the integrated system components.
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: "The checked modern system record is more specific for the RK1 extension than for the original line: MTBU describes train, power, signalling, communications, fare collection and platform-door testing, including the interlock between the doors and signalling."
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: Its power notice records RK1 traction supply extended from BSS5 through the North Depot, with a 22 kV feeder and 380/220 V station supply.
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: These extension records establish the interface and power arrangement for the new section, but they do not establish the original Red Line signalling supplier, generation, headways, full-line platform-door retrofit history or per-station accessibility inventory; those remain TBC.

      - link "Taipei Metro ridership 2.1 million average daily riders in 2025, recovered to 97% of the pre-pandemic level — from TRTC's own performance report, plus NTMC's separately published per-line figures showing the Circular Line and its two light-rail lines all posting record ridership a year after a 2024 earthquake shut the Circular Line down.":
        - /url: /rail/metro/operations/ridership/
    - listitem:
      - link "Taipei Metro fares A 10-band distance fare from NT$20 to NT$65 — with the operator's own site stating plainly that an EasyCard costs exactly the same as a paper token today, contradicting the common assumption that stored-value cards are cheaper, plus a genuine conflict between TRTC and NTMC over how many social-welfare points a senior or disability card carries each month.":

      - link "Taipei Metro accessibility The first mass-transit system in Taiwan to adopt accessibility facilities, per the operator's own account — set against a 2023 city inspection that found every one of 81 checked accessibility facilities failed, and a Control Yuan finding that TRTC fined a disabled passenger without reviewing the footage that would have cleared him.":
        - /url: /rail/metro/facilities/accessibility/
  - paragraph: "The 捷運 network as this site files it: TRTC's lines, New Taipei Metro's Circular, Sanying and light rail lines, and Taoyuan Metro's Airport MRT. Three companies, and from a rider's point of view one railway — one stored-value card, one interchange network, one station-numbering scheme, one map."
  - paragraph: "That is the boundary this system draws, and it is the boundary the fare system draws. It is not drawn by technology: the network contains rubber-tyred metro, steel-wheel metro and street-running light rail, and none of those is a reason to file a line somewhere a rider would not look for it. Taiwan Railway and high speed rail are outside it because they are separate networks with separate ticketing, separate stations and separate operators — not because they are a different kind of train."
  - paragraph:
    - text: The
    - link "ridership":

    - text: and
    - link "fare":
      - /url: /rail/metro/operations/fares/
    - text: records cover what TRTC and NTMC each publish about their own networks — including a genuine, unresolved conflict between the two operators over a widely-used social-welfare benefit. The
    - link "accessibility record":

    - heading "Overview" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Beitou Depot, 北投機廠, is the
      - link "Tamsui–Xinyi Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/tamsui-xinyi-line/
      - text: "'s main depot, on the south side of Zhongyang North Road Section 3 in"
      - link "Beitou":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r22/
      - text: District.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: DORTS classifies the steel-wheel facility at level five, the highest grade shown in its operating-depot inventory.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: A separate DORTS history calls it the network's largest maintenance depot.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - link "TRTC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: "'s current organisation places Beitou workshop management in Vehicle Plant One. That unit maintains Tamsui–Xinyi trains, depot equipment and track-maintenance vehicles."
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: The operator does not publish a current model-by-model stabling roster on that page, so present fleet allocation remains TBC rather than being inferred from the line's rolling-stock history.
    - heading "Construction history" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Two official dates describe different starts. DORTS says CT107, the Beitou Depot earthworks contract, was signed and began construction on 19 January 1988; it calls this the earliest construction contract on the
      - link "Tamsui":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r28/
      - text: Line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: A later DORTS history dates the depot's formal groundbreaking to 22 July 1988.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: The January contract commencement and July ceremony are therefore retained as separate milestones, not forced into a single start date.
    - heading "Site and ground conditions" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The depot occupies a long strip on the
      - link "Guandu":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r25/
      - text: alluvial plain. DORTS describes a site about 350 metres north–south and 1,720 metres east–west, bounded by Guizikeng Creek to the east and Zhongyang North Road to the north.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: Before filling, most of it was farmland with ponds and a small number of one- and two-storey houses; the surface fell from northeast to southwest.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
    - paragraph:
      - text: That ground dictated the earthworks. Beneath the depot, highly compressible, water-rich clay thickens from about 15 metres on the north side to 50 metres on the south.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: DORTS says the site had to be raised for flood protection and later recorded maximum settlement of about 1.46 metres in the western part of fill area seven, with differential movement damaging or impairing power, communications, fire, drainage and track facilities.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - heading "Area and capacity" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Official figures disagree unless their labels are preserved. The geotechnical manual twice describes approximately 40 hectares, while the network-planning inventory and depot-equipment table publish 41 hectares.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: No opened source reconciles the one-hectare difference, so both values are reported; rounding or boundary choice is possible but not established.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Capacity has a second, more explicit difference. The planning inventory gives 33 trainsets of 儲車空間—storage space—while the equipment table gives 30 駐車軌列數, stabling-road positions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: Those are differently named measures and are not converted into one generic capacity figure.
    - heading "Maintenance equipment" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS lists a larger package family here than at the other initial-network depots. CT309A supplied 28 categories of main maintenance equipment; CT309B four dual electric/battery locomotives; CT309C twelve work cars; and CT309D 65 road–rail and auxiliary-equipment items.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: CT309E, CT309F, CT309G and CT501A covered small tools, a driving simulator, maintenance test instruments and track-maintenance machinery, with seven further kinds of special track vehicle funded through TRTC.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The equipment table also records a test track.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: These procurement records establish what the depot was equipped to do, but not which original machines remain in service or which current train model occupies each road. Those live asset details remain TBC.

    - heading "Overview" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Tucheng Depot, 土城機廠, is the
      - link "Bannan Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/bannan-line/
      - text: "'s main depot, on the east side of Huanhe West Road and Baijiebao Road in"
      - link "Tucheng":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl03/
      - text: District.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: DORTS's detailed route account places it on former Dahan River flood-control land, with Xinxing Bridge to the north, the newer Tucheng levee to the west and the industrial district and river authority to the east.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The site works with
      - link "Nangang Depot":
        - /url: /rail/metro/depots/nangang-depot/
      - text: to provide the maintenance needed for the whole Bannan Line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - link "TRTC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: currently groups both workshops under Vehicle Plant Two, the unit responsible for Bannan rolling-stock maintenance.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: Neither source publishes a current model-by-model stabling roster, so depot fleet allocation remains TBC.
    - heading "Planning and construction" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS says planning began in 1990.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: "'s metro construction supervision meeting approved the scheme on 14 December 1990, a provincial–city coordination meeting followed on 9 January 1991, and the proposal went through the Ministry of Transportation and Communications on 25 March 1991."
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The Executive Yuan approved the construction plan on 18 October 1993.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The project used two section contracts. DORTS defines CD550 as covering civil and building-services work from
      - code: BL2
      - text: to Tucheng Depot and line-wide track and electromechanical systems—including the depot—as well as rolling stock.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: CD551 covered a different station section.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: The route page says CD551 was the first main works contract signed, on 29 April 1999, but does not identify that as the depot's start.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: Exact CD550 award, depot start, handover and commissioning dates remain TBC.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Tucheng Line from
      - link "Xinpu":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl08/
      - text: to
      - link "Yongning":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl02/
      - text: opened on 31 May 2006 after preliminary inspection beginning 21 April and final inspection beginning 20 May.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: Those are line milestones and are not relabelled as depot acceptance dates.
    - heading "Site and functions" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS consistently gives an area of approximately 26.8 hectares.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The route description identifies Tucheng as one of the principal sites for stabling, washing and maintaining trains used across the Banqiao, Tucheng and Nangang sections.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The planning inventory classifies it as a level-four steel-wheel depot.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
    - heading "Capacity and equipment" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Capacity differs by table heading. The network-planning inventory publishes storage space for 34 trainsets, while the equipment table gives 36 stabling-road positions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: No opened source converts between those measures or explains the two-position difference, so both remain labelled rather than collapsed into one capacity.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The equipment table records no test track.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: DORTS's procurement list identifies CD319A as a package of twelve categories of main maintenance equipment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: That establishes original equipment scope, not a current inventory; the active machinery and division of heavy work between Tucheng and Nangang remain TBC.

    - heading "Overview" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Muzha Depot, 木柵機廠, sits in Wenshan District between Xinguang Road Section 2 and the
      - link "Jingmei":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g05/
      - text: River, beside the
      - link "Taipei Zoo":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br01/
      - text: end of the original
      - link "Muzha Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: .
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: DORTS gives its area as approximately 6.2 hectares and lists vehicle storage, maintenance, operations control, train washing, wayside maintenance and parts warehousing among its functions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The depot began as the Muzha Line's main facility.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: When
      - link "Neihu":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br19/
      - text: Depot entered the operating arrangement, DORTS reclassified
      - link "Muzha":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br02/
      - text: as the Wenhu Line's secondary depot and Neihu as the main depot.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: The line itself opened on 28 March 1996, but the opened records do not isolate the depot's civil-work start, handover or commissioning dates.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - heading "Role and capacity" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Two DORTS manuals describe capacity in different units that should not be combined. The network-planning inventory publishes room for 84 two-car married pairs.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: The depot-equipment table publishes 12 stabling roads, along with a 25-train fleet context and a test track.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The 84-pair figure is therefore storage capacity, while 12 counts the roads used to provide it; neither is a count of four-car trains.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The pair capacity is larger than the 51 pairs procured for the original Matra fleet, but DORTS does not explain in these pages whether the surplus represents operational flexibility, shared Wenhu storage, maintenance positioning or a different planning horizon.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: Current vehicle allocation by fleet and active/reserve status remains TBC.
    - heading "Maintenance equipment" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS's equipment inventory identifies CM350 as the turnkey package containing complete heavy-maintenance equipment for 102 cars.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: It also lists CM351A for non-VAL-system test instruments and CM351B for non-VAL small maintenance equipment and tools.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: "Those records correct the former page's suggestion that heavy overhaul might not happen here: the official inventory explicitly says complete heavy-maintenance equipment was procured for the original fleet."
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph: The opened material does not establish which of that equipment remains active, what work has migrated to Neihu, or how responsibilities are divided for the Bombardier fleet. Those current workshop allocations remain TBC rather than being inferred from the depots' main/secondary labels.
    - heading "Relationship with Neihu Depot" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS says the two depots support one another and share Wenhu train storage and maintenance.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: That wording establishes a paired maintenance system, not a one-fleet-per-depot assignment. Neihu provides the principal function and Muzha the secondary function, while the current fleet split is not published in the opened records.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
    - paragraph: The page's diagram locates the junction at BR01 from the project's curated depot-join record. No opened prose source independently states that station code, so the exact named junction remains a structured-data fact rather than a claim about current workshop allocation.

    - heading "Overview" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Xinzhuang Depot, 新莊機廠, is the
      - link "Zhonghe–Xinlu Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/zhonghe-xinlu-line/
      - text: "'s secondary depot, beside O21"
      - link "Huilong":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/o21/
      - text: and spanning the New Taipei–Taoyuan boundary.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: DORTS classifies it at level three and lists storage, inspection, maintenance, washing, and storage for line power and track-maintenance equipment among its functions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - link "TRTC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: groups
      - link "Xinzhuang":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/o18/
      - text: with
      - link "Luzhou":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/o54/
      - text: and
      - link "Xindian":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g01/
      - text: workshops under Vehicle Plant Three.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: That unit maintains trains for two trunk lines and two branches, but the page is not a depot-level roster. Current fleet allocation at Xinzhuang therefore remains TBC.
    - heading "Losheng Sanatorium" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The depot occupies part of the historic Losheng Sanatorium site. The Ministry of Culture's heritage record says the institution opened in 1930 as Taiwan's first public Hansen's-disease prevention and isolation facility.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: Its compound combined hospital, residential, work, religious and community functions, reflecting the coercive isolation policy then used for Hansen's disease.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The same official history says the government selected Losheng as the depot site in 1994, while new hospital construction and depot planning proceeded together.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: Metro work began in 2002; preservation and resident rights disputes then interrupted and reshaped the project.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: "This page does not reduce that history to a generic “heritage delay”: it changed the depot's physical footprint and completion sequence."
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - heading "Redesign and site area" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS says the original site was approximately 17.4 hectares and was reduced to 13.9 hectares to accommodate the Losheng preservation plan.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: Another paragraph on the same route page describes the earlier depot at approximately 17.5 hectares, while the depot-equipment table gives 17.2 hectares without dating or defining that design stage.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The 17.4/17.5 values are original-layout approximations and 13.9 is explicitly post-redesign; the unexplained 17.2 value remains an unresolved intermediate or different-boundary measurement.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Ministry of Culture records the 30 May 2007 preservation decision as 39 buildings retained in place and six demolished.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: Its overview says nine buildings were to be rebuilt, while its longer history says ten were to be relocated/reassembled or rebuilt.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: That internal nine-versus-ten conflict is published rather than silently corrected.
    - heading "Facilities and capacity" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The pre-reduction DORTS description lists a train wash, entry and exit tracks, maintenance and civil/track workshops, a test track, stabling, perimeter road, car park, electrical facilities, administration/training and a wastewater plant.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: A later equipment table says “no” test track.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The records may describe different layouts, but the opened source does not say when the test-track provision changed; both statements are retained as a design-stage conflict.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The planning inventory gives storage space for 16 trainsets, while the equipment table lists 17 stabling-road positions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: CK379A supplied fourteen categories of main maintenance equipment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - heading "Delayed activation" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS explicitly says preservation-driven facility rearrangement prevented the depot from being completed when the Xinzhuang main line opened.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The line reached Huilong on 29 June 2013, but the depot did not undergo preliminary inspection until 25 October 2020 or final inspection until 23 December 2020.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: It entered operation on 4 January 2021, more than seven years after trains reached the terminus.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS calls it the only initial/final inspection case without an associated route section.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: Exact civil contract completion and current equipment allocation remain TBC; the dated inspections and activation are the official commissioning milestones recovered in this search.
