      - code: A14a
      - text: for
      - link "Airport Hotel Station":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/a14a/
      - text: — plain
      - code: A14
      - text: is reserved for the still-unbuilt Terminal 3 station
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: TDX's A1 route records 51.76 km to A22 , while the New Taipei DORTS project record gives the line as 51.03 km and describes 22 stations, 15 elevated and seven underground
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . DORTS further describes approximately 10.92 km of underground alignment and 40.11 km of elevated alignment, running from Taipei through
      - link "Sanchong":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/o15/
      - text: ", the airport and the"
      - link "Taoyuan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taoyuan/
      - text: HSR area to the Zhongli side
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . Those are different published measurements; the sources do not identify which engineering boundary accounts for the 0.73 km difference
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: .
    - heading "Planning and approvals" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Sources disagree about when this line's history starts because different bodies mean different things by "planning." The first fully verified institutional milestone is the central government's October 1996 decision to build it as a BOT (build–operate–transfer) concession, and Long Life International Development Co. won that concession in 1998
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . The BOT model collapsed on 31 December 2002, when Long Life and the High Speed Rail Bureau agreed to terminate the contract
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: ". Government took over: MOTC designated the High Speed Rail Bureau as the project's builder on 28 October 2003, and the central government approved the construction plan on 9 March 2004"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: .
    - heading "Construction history" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Construction of the Sanchong–Airport– Zhongli section and its E&M systems formally started 27 February 2006
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: ; TYMC's own history page instead marks 26 June 2006, the date of a ceremonial groundbreaking presided over by the Premier
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: — two different milestones in the same year, not a contradiction. DORTS records that Taipei rejected the originally elevated Sanchong–Taipei section on urban-design and land-use grounds; Taipei City agreed to fund the extra cost of underground construction, and that section formally started on 25 September 2006 after its design and construction were assigned to DORTS
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . The detailed design ran from March 1998 through 2002, according to the same project chronology
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The opening date itself moved repeatedly. The earliest announced target was January 2009; by March 2016 it had changed six times
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: . The fetched report gives that count but not a complete dated list of each change. The line finally opened
      - strong: 2 March 2017
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . TYMC's chronology records the 99% system-stability test on 20 November 2016, Ricardo's safety certification on 2 December, initial inspection on 3–4 December, final inspection on 29–30 December, the operating permit on 25 January 2017 and trial service from 2 February
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: .
    - heading "Engineering and contract disputes — two figures confirmed, a widely repeated total not found anywhere" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The main electromechanical contract (ME01) went to a consortium led by the Japanese trading house
      - strong: Marubeni
      - text: (丸紅), with Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Hitachi as named subcontractors. In January 2017, weeks before opening, the High Speed Rail Bureau announced it would impose a
      - strong: NT$2.5 billion delay penalty
      - text: — the contract's maximum, calculated at 0.05% of contract value per day of delay — and had already
      - strong: withheld roughly NT$1.9 billion in performance bonds
      - text: ", over Marubeni's unauthorised subcontracting of the signalling system, which its contract required it to design itself, to a British firm"
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: . Marubeni's own counter-claim against the Ministry, seeking NT$12.9 billion over repeated design changes, was reported in the same account
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: . Both of the Bureau's figures were independently corroborated by two further contemporaneous reports naming the same amounts and the same reasons.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: A combined "NT$7.2 billion" total for this dispute circulates widely.
      - text: NT$2.5 billion plus NT$1.9 billion is NT$4.4 billion, not NT$7.2 billion, and no primary or secondary source read for this page — not the three contemporaneous 2017 news accounts, not zh.wikipedia's own article on the line, which contains no Marubeni monetary figures at all — states a combined total of any kind. The NT$7.2 billion figure appeared repeatedly in this research run's own search-engine result summaries, never inside a quoted source sentence, and in one case alongside an unrelated, later, and much smaller 2021 dispute — the Railway Bureau withheld NT$726.93 million from Marubeni that year for missing express-train travel-time, speed and headway targets
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: — that shares a leading digit and may be the source of the confusion. The two confirmed figures, and Marubeni's name, are published here on the strength of three independent contemporaneous accounts; the total is not, because it could not be found stated anywhere.
    - heading "Operations and service patterns" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Two services share the same track. The
      - strong: express (直達車)
      - text: ", in purple, calls at A1 , A3 , A8 , A12 and A13 ; a peak-only enhanced express additionally serves A18 and A21"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: — zh.wikipedia names this pattern the Huanbei Express, giving it a run time of about 64 minutes against roughly 39 minutes for the base A1 – A13 express
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . The
      - strong: commuter (普通 車)
      - text: ", in blue, calls at every station from A1 to A22 ; the A21 – A22 section between Huanbei and Laojiexi carries commuter trains only"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "This site's TDX pull cannot show the skip-stop pattern directly: every route TDX defines for this line lists consecutive stops through every intervening station, so the shorter \"A-2\" and \"A-3\" routes in the underlying data are all-stops services over part of the line, not the express — the express pattern above rests on TYMC's own timetable page rather than the generated station data"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: .
    - paragraph
    - figure "A1 Taipei Main Station, the line's Taipei terminus. Littlebtc, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons":
      - img "The underground platform at A1 Taipei Main Station, trains standing on both sides"
      - text: A1 Taipei Main Station, the line's Taipei terminus. Littlebtc, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
    - paragraph
    - heading "Depots" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The fully read line account names Luzhu Depot (蘆竹機廠) and Qingpu Depot (青埔機廠) as the two maintenance bases serving the Airport MRT
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . The source does not publish a current set-by-set allocation between them, so that operational detail remains TBC.
    - heading "Rolling stock" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Two fleets, two manufacturers, sharing the same 1,435mm gauge and DC 750V third-rail supply
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The
      - strong: express fleet (2000-type, purple)
      - text: is built entirely by
      - strong: Kawasaki Heavy Industries
      - text: ", delivered 2011–2013 for the 2017 opening: 11 five-car sets, 55 cars, each set four passenger cars plus a dedicated luggage car"
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: . Transverse seating, overhead luggage racks, WiFi and USB charging are fitted; wireless charging pads are noted in one source as currently suspended, rather than the always-on feature sometimes described
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: . Capacity is around 855 per set, with 206 seats and eight wheelchair spaces
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: .
    - paragraph
    - figure "Inside an express (2000-type) train. Cheng-en Cheng from Taichung City, Taiwan, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons":
      - img "Passengers seated in the purple transverse seating of an Airport MRT express train, luggage racks and a route display overhead"
      - text: Inside an express (2000-type) train. Cheng-en Cheng from Taichung City, Taiwan, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons
    - paragraph
    - paragraph:
      - text: The
      - strong: commuter fleet (1000-type, blue)
      - text: "was built under an industrial- cooperation arrangement: Kawasaki built the prototype set and three later sets (101, 118–120); the rest, sets 102–117, were assembled domestically by"
      - strong: Taiwan Rolling Stock Co.
      - text: (台灣車輛股份有限公司)
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: . There are currently 20 four-car sets, 80 cars, with longitudinal seating for higher standing capacity
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: . Per-set seating is 188 — one source's own summary prose describes this as "per car," which its own per-car table contradicts (44+47+50+44 seats across the four cars, summing close to 188), so this page publishes the per-set reading
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Both fleets run at 100 km/h in service, with a 110 km/h design maximum
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: .
    - heading "Stations and passenger facilities" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Free advance check-in and baggage drop operate at two stations:"
      - strong: A1 Taipei Main Station
      - text: ", on B1, 06:00–21:30, and"
      - strong:
        - text: A3
        - link "New Taipei Industrial Park":
          - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y20/
        - text: Station
      - text: ", on 1F, 09:00–16:00, both closing 3 hours before flight departure"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: ". TYMC's own page does not itself list participating airlines and links onward to the airport operator's page for the current list; that page returned an access error to this site's tooling, so the airline list below rests on secondary aggregation rather than a primary fetch, checked 12 August 2026:"
      - strong: A1 — China Airlines, Mandarin Airlines, EVA Air, UNI Air, Cathay Pacific and Starlux; A3 — China Airlines, Mandarin Airlines, EVA Air, UNI Air, Tigerair Taiwan, and the AirAsia group.
      - text: Treat this list as liable to change without notice, and reconfirm with the airline or station before relying on it.
    - heading "Extensions and depot interface" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: A22 Laojiexi
      - text: opened
      - strong: 31 July 2023
      - text: ", the same day its operating permit was issued"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: ". MOTC's own account gives three causes for the delay together, not one: COVID-era disruption to foreign electromechanical suppliers through 2020–2022, high technical difficulty integrating the extension's newer signalling generation with the existing line (requiring extended testing), and design changes needed to coordinate with the separate Taoyuan rail-undergrounding project"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . Total project cost was NT$17.302 billion
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Two further extensions are in progress:"
      - strong:
        - code: A23
        - text: Zhongli
      - text: ", which would connect directly with the Taoyuan Metro Green Line, and"
      - strong:
        - code: A14
      - text: ", a new underground station serving the airport's Terminal 3."
      - strong: Both extensions' opening dates and budgets are TBC.
      - text: News reporting circulates a July 2028-to-around-2029 slip for
      - code: A23
      - text: ", attributed to a platform redesign for the Green Line connection, and a late-2027 target for"
      - code: A14
      - text: ", each with its own NT$ budget figure — none of it established from a source read in full here, still TBC. No fetched Railway Bureau project page or dated full article establishes either opening date or budget; settling them needs one of those primary records rather than a summary."
    - heading "Ridership and finances" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: TYMC's finances went from a NT$706 million negative net worth and a NT$1.067 billion bank loan in 2022 to record profitability within three years. 2023 was the company's first profitable year, though no source found here gives a precise NT$ figure for that year specifically. 2025's surplus reached
      - strong: NT$679 million
      - text: ", a record, with"
      - strong: ridership over 46 million, up 12% on 2024
      - text: ", and the bank loan"
      - strong: fully repaid in April 2025
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: . Taoyuan Mayor 張善政 described pre-2022 operations as "pitiful" (悽慘) and the company as now debt-free (零負債)
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "2024's figures do not fully agree between sources: one report, published nine days before the end of 2024, gives a NT$500 million surplus for that year"
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: ; a later, retrospective account instead gives "over NT$400 million"
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: — plausibly because the earlier figure was a projection rather than a final result. Neither source gives an exact 2023 figure; one implies roughly NT$124 million for 2023 through a "fourfold increase to NT$500 million" framing of its 2024 number, but that implied figure cannot be checked against any other source
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: .
    - heading "Fares and ticketing" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A single journey from Taipei Main Station to either airport terminal costs NT$160, the line's maximum single fare; a NT$10 system-wide discount that applied until January 2025 was withdrawn from 2 January 2025, cited to rising electricity costs
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: ". Express and commuter trains are priced identically. Combination tickets pair an airport-line return with a Taipei Metro pass: NT$520 with a 48-hour pass, NT$600 with a 72-hour pass"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: .
      - link "EasyCard":
        - /url: /ticketing/guides/cards-passes-and-fares/
      - text: ", iPass and icash 2.0 are all accepted, and the line is covered by the cross-city 基北北桃1200都會通 monthly pass at unchanged pricing"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: .
    - heading "Sources" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Station codes, sequence, coordinates and route length come from
      - strong: Taiwan MOTC's TDX platform
      - text: ", operator TYMC — government open data, retrieved 12 August 2026"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . TDX has no way to represent this line's skip-stop express pattern, so service-pattern detail throughout this page comes from TYMC's own timetable instead. Everything else is cited inline and listed above; where a figure rests on a search-engine synthesis rather than a page fetched and read in full, the source note says so.

Built 2011–2012 and again 2015. 4-car sets (4M), 20 sets currently (80 cars). Longitudinal seating. Same power supply and gauge as the express fleet. The article's summary prose reads as 188 seats per car, but its own per-car table (44+47+50+44=185) shows 188 is the per-set total, not per car — checked here rather than repeated as written."

          - link "Taoyuan Metro's surplus reached a record NT$679 million last year, with nearly NT$1.1 billion in debt fully repaid":
            - /url: https://news.ltn.com.tw/news/Taoyuan/breakingnews/5332661
          - text: 桃園捷運去年盈餘6.79億元創新高 近11億債務全清償 secondary 自由時報 accessed 2026-08-12 Published 4 February 2026. 2025 surplus NT$679 million (盈餘6.79億元創新高), a record; nearly NT$1.1 billion in bank debt fully repaid (近11億債務全清償); 2025 ridership over 46 million, up 12% on 2024 (去年全年運量來到4600多萬人次，相較2024年增加12%).
        - listitem:
          - link "How did a money-loser become a golden goose? Taoyuan Metro is profitable — Mayor Chang Shan-cheng on three keys, and NT$1 billion in debt fully repaid":
            - /url: https://www.storm.mg/lifestyle/11101286
          - text: "賠錢貨如何變身小金雞？桃園捷運賺錢了！張善政曝3關鍵：10億債務全還清 secondary 風傳媒 Storm Media ( 李伊晴 ) accessed 2026-08-12 Published 6 February 2026. Corroborates the 2025 NT$679 million surplus figure exactly. Adds: 2022 negative net worth of NT$706 million (淨值-7.06億元) forced a NT$1.067 billion bank loan; 2023 was the first profitable year (no NT$ figure given for 2023 itself); 2024 profit 'over NT$400 million'; the loan was fully repaid 去年4月 — 'April of last year' relative to this February 2026 article, i.e. April 2025, not April 2026. Includes a direct quote from Mayor 張善政 describing pre-2022 operations as 悽慘 (pitiful) and the company as now 零負債 (zero debt)."
        - listitem:
          - link "Taoyuan Airport MRT's 2024 surplus hit a record NT$500 million — why cancel the system-wide NT$10 fare discount?":
            - /url: https://city.gvm.com.tw/article/117975
          - text: 桃園機場捷運2024盈餘5億創新高！為何全線取消車票10元優惠？ secondary 城市學 (GVM) accessed 2026-08-12 Published 22 December 2024 — nine days before year-end, so its 2024 figures likely a projection rather than a final result, which may explain why they do not match Storm Media's later 'over NT$400 million' figure for the same year. States the NT$10 discount ends 2 January 2025, per Chairman 陳志長, citing rising electricity costs. States 2024 daily ridership 114,289.
        - listitem:
          - link "Taoyuan Metro Corporation":
            - /url: https://zh.wikipedia.org/zh-tw/桃園捷運公司
          - text: 桃園捷運公司 secondary 維基百科 (Chinese Wikipedia) accessed 2026-08-12 Read in full. Founded 6 July 2010, capital NT$3 billion, ownership split Taoyuan 64.01% / New Taipei 29.32% / Taipei 6.67% by original construction-cost share. Renamed 25 December 2014 when Taoyuan County became a municipality. Headquarters at the Qingpu Depot site, 251 Linghang North Road Section 4, Dayuan District — beside A17 Linghang, not A18 Taoyuan HSR.

      - text: Anxin Bridge, near the Ankeng LRT's route. Tze Chiang Hao, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
    - paragraph
    - heading "Overview" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The line begins beside Ankeng Depot at the junction of Antai and Anyi roads, runs north along Anyi Road through the valley, turns onto the Anhe branch road and Anhe Road, then crosses National Freeway 3, the Zhong-An Bridge approach, the New Taipei Expressway and the Xindian River before reaching Shisizhang.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: DORTS describes the built railway as a mixed at-grade and elevated system; the passenger service covers about 7.5 km between K01 and K09 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The project gave the Ankeng district a direct rail interchange with the wider Taipei network at Shisizhang.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: "Its alignment required very different civil works within one short line: street-level track, viaduct, a depot lead through Shuang'an Tunnel, vibration-isolated track beside housing, and the long An-Xin Bridge over the Xindian River."
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
    - heading "Route and alignment" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: From the depot, the alignment reaches K01
      - link "Shuangcheng":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/k01/
      - text: near the Antai Road–Anyi Road junction. K02
      - link "Rose China Town":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/k02/
      - text: stands on viaduct, while K03 Taiping Temple, K04 Cardinal Tien Hospital
      - link "Ankang":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/k06/
      - text: Branch and K05 Jingwen University of Science and Technology form the at-grade middle of the valley route.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: The railway rises again for K06 Ankang and remains elevated through K07 Yangguang Sports Park and K08
      - link "Xinhe Elementary School":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/k08/
      - text: to K09 Shisizhang.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The final approach turns east near the Water Resources Agency's Xindian office, then north on a new road before the railway crosses the expressway and river on An-Xin Bridge.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: K09 stands in the Shisizhang redevelopment area, where the light rail terminates beside Circular Line station Y08 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - heading "Planning and approvals" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Executive Yuan approved feasibility on 1 July 2013.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: New Taipei then began comprehensive planning that June, held public hearings on 27 and 30 December, and sent the plan to the Ministry of Transportation and Communications on 7 May 2014.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: After ministry reviews in September and November 2014 and National Development Council review on 18 May 2015, the Executive Yuan approved the comprehensive plan on 8 June 2015.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Environmental review had a longer history. The original environmental-impact statement was placed on record on 14 October 2003; later difference analyses covered design changes in 2016 and changes to depot layout and earthworks in 2020.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The urban-plan changes for the route took effect on 24 January 2018, followed by a separate change affecting the river zone on 18 November 2019.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - heading "Construction history" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The civil and track design-build contract was awarded on 3 March 2016, and main construction began on 6 April.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: An official project-management paper identifies Sinotech Engineering Consultants as the project and construction manager and MOH and Associates as supervising consultant; its figures show both the government and consultant site teams expanding as the work moved from civil construction into railway systems.
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Testing and commissioning closed the gap between construction and public service. Stability testing was complete on 7 November 2022, initial inspection followed on 11 December, and the project team reported its corrective work complete on 27 December.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The Ministry of Transportation and Communications conducted final inspection on 14 January 2023 and issued the operating permit on 2 February; public service began eight days later.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
    - paragraph:
      - text: New Taipei's opening account says labour shortages, material shortages and the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted delivery.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: Those statements describe the builder's account of the schedule pressure; the cited page does not quantify a separate delay attributable to each cause.
    - heading "Engineering" [level=2]
    - heading "Track, tunnel and vibration control" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Shuang'an Tunnel lies between K01 and Ankeng Depot, on the depot lead rather than between two passenger stations.
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: "DORTS describes it as Taiwan's first combined road-and-light-rail tunnel: road bores flank the light rail bore, and the tracks contain a crossover at grade inside the tunnel so trains can change direction during depot movements."
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Near K07 and K08 , homes beside the railway made vibration and secondary noise a design concern.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: "DORTS records three floating-slab track installations totalling 800 m across both running directions: two sections around K08 total 300 m each, and the section beside the Anhe fire brigade totals 200 m."
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: Elastic pads separate the heavy track slab from the bridge deck or structural invert, lowering the system's natural frequency and reducing vibration transferred into the supporting structure.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - heading "An-Xin Bridge" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Between K08 and K09 , An-Xin Bridge crosses a roughly 400 m-wide reach of the Xindian River.
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: Flood-management requirements limited the crossing to two river piers, leading to a 502 m, three-span structure with a 225 m main span.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: Its structural system combines an asymmetric cable-stayed bridge with a steel truss; the 130 m pylon and water-bird-wing profile form the line's most conspicuous landmark.
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Wind was a specific design load. DORTS says the bridge was checked for wind speeds up to 80 m/s—above the 61.2 m/s threshold it gives for Beaufort force 17—and tested with a 1:60 wind-tunnel model.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: The same source explains the name 安心 as a pairing of 安坑 and 新店 as well as a promise of reassurance.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The bridge's design-build team used building-information modelling from detailed design through construction.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: The official technical paper describes collision checks between structural elements, coordinated shop and construction drawings, drone-derived three-dimensional terrain for the K08 – K09 area, simulations of the bridge coating colours, and model-based quantity calculations.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: Its handover table also includes models, records and manuals intended for the operating stage, making the model a project record rather than only a presentation image.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The bridge's record claim varies by source. DORTS calls its 225 m main span the longest span in a Taiwanese rail transport system; its comparison gives 120.7 m for Danhai's Blue Sea Bridge and about 96 m for Kaohsiung's Love River Bridge.
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: CNA instead quotes a named Sinyi Construction Development project director calling the whole 502 m structure Taiwan's longest rail bridge and reports a pylon weight of about 3,450 tonnes.
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: These are different superlatives—span and total bridge—and remain attributed to the sources that make them.
    - heading "Stations and interchange" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Nine stations carry codes K01 to K09 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: Five are elevated— K02 and K06 through K09 —and four are at grade— K01 and K03 through K05 —according to the route description and DORTS's K02 station record.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: At K09 , riders may board from either side platform before transferring to the Circular Line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: K04 's full official name is
      - link "耕莘安康院區":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/k04/
      - text: ", Cardinal Tien Hospital Ankang Branch. New Taipei's station-naming panel settled on that form in December 2017, and it appears consistently in NTMC's station page, its full station list and the TDX station record."
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph
    - figure "K04 Cardinal Tien Hospital Ankang Branch station. S8321414, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons":
      - img "The canopied platform at Cardinal Tien Hospital Ankang Branch station, overhead wire and open track running beside it"
      - text: K04 Cardinal Tien Hospital Ankang Branch station. S8321414, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
    - paragraph
    - heading "Route-length records" [level=2]
    - paragraph: Three figures circulate for this line's length, and they are not simple duplicates of each other.
    - table:
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Figure What it measures Source":
          - columnheader "Figure"
          - columnheader "What it measures"
          - columnheader "Source"
      - rowgroup:
        - row "7.5 km NTMC's own published length, matching TDX's RouteLength field for route K-1 exactly NTMC[2], TDX[1]":
          - cell "7.5 km":
            - strong: 7.5 km
          - cell "NTMC's own published length, matching TDX's RouteLength field for route K-1 exactly":
            - text: NTMC's own published length, matching TDX's
            - code: RouteLength
            - text: field for route K-1 exactly
          - cell "NTMC[2], TDX[1]":
            - text: NTMC
            - superscript:
              - link "[2]":
                - /url: "#ref-2"
            - text: ", TDX"
            - superscript:
              - link "[1]":
                - /url: "#ref-1"
        - row "7.1 km TDX's own station-to-station chainage, K01 to K09 TDX CumulativeDistance[1]":
          - cell "7.1 km"
          - cell "TDX's own station-to-station chainage, K01 to K09"
          - cell "TDX CumulativeDistance[1]":
            - text: TDX
            - code: CumulativeDistance
            - superscript:
              - link "[1]":
                - /url: "#ref-1"
        - row "7.67 km zh.wikipedia's total route length zh.wikipedia[29]":
          - cell "7.67 km"
          - cell "zh.wikipedia's total route length"
          - cell "zh.wikipedia[29]":
            - text: zh.wikipedia
            - superscript:
              - link "[29]":
                - /url: "#ref-29"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The three published length figures use incompatible labels. TDX gives 7.5 km as
      - code: RouteLength
      - text: but 7.1 km as the cumulative station-to-station distance at K09 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Chinese Wikipedia labels 7.67 km as total route length and 7.5 km as operating length, while describing the route as beginning at Ankeng Depot rather than K01 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[29]":
          - /url: "#ref-29"
      - text: DORTS independently publishes “about 7.5 km” for the line but does not define its measurement boundary.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Chinese Wikipedia also divides 7.5 km into 2.8 km at grade, 4.3 km elevated and 0.4 km underground including a portal.
      - superscript:
        - link "[29]":
          - /url: "#ref-29"
      - text: DORTS, by contrast, describes the passenger system simply as elevated and at grade, while placing Shuang'an Tunnel between the depot and K01 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: The sources therefore do not establish whether the 0.4 km is counted within the K01 – K09 passenger route or on its depot connection.
    - heading "Rolling stock" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taiwan Rolling Stock Company built the fleet with Germany's Voith Engineering Services.
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: "NTMC's fleet page groups the Danhai and Ankeng orders together: thirty trains of the design were built, fifteen allocated to each line."
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: Each five-car, fully low-floor train has a stated capacity of 265 passengers—62 seated and 203 standing—and a maximum speed of 70 km/h under overhead wire or 50 km/h on an unwired section.
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
    - paragraph
    - figure "An Ankeng LRT tram's interior. Wctaiwan, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons":
      - img "The empty interior of an Ankeng LRT tram, longitudinal seats and a centre grab pole running the length of the car"
      - text: An Ankeng LRT tram's interior. Wctaiwan, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
    - paragraph
    - paragraph:
      - text: The gold livery, 光耀金, was selected by a public vote.
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: Chinese Wikipedia records the other 2018 ballot options as red-gold, purple and green, but the NTMC fleet page confirms only the winning colour.
      - superscript:
        - link "[29]":
          - /url: "#ref-29"
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
    - heading "Depot" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Ankeng Depot sits on the hillside beyond K01 and connects to the passenger line through Shuang'an Tunnel.
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
      - text: DORTS divides its rail facilities into a nine-track stabling yard and a five-track maintenance shop, with the latter used for inspection, testing, maintenance and cleaning; the administration building houses train control, dispatch and staff-training functions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The depot's boarding platform carried two weekday morning passenger departures during a trial from July through December 2024.
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: The 06:28 and 07:16 trains ran toward K09 , used a portable fare reader, and charged as if the rider had boarded at K01 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: New Taipei said the trial was an input to evaluating whether the platform should be proposed for conversion to a normal station.
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
    - heading "Operations" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Two service patterns run the line. The full-line service, K01 to K09 , takes about 21 minutes; a short working, K06 to K09 , takes about 9 minutes
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . Baseline headways were about 7.5 minutes peak on the overlapping K06 – K09 section and 10–15 minutes peak on the non-overlapping K01 – K05 section, both about 15 minutes off peak
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: By February 2024 the line had carried 2 million cumulative passengers, averaging 5,600 a day, with growth concentrated on the non-short-working stretch between K05 Jingwen University of Science and Technology and K01 Shuangcheng
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: ". From 26 February 2024 the peak short workings became full-line services: morning-peak headway tightened to 6–8 minutes, evening-peak to 8–10 minutes"
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: . Off-peak sections were left unchanged.
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
    - heading "Fares" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Fares are stepped by distance, matching
      - link "Danhai LRT":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/danhai-lrt/
      - text: ": NT$20 base, NT$25 maximum"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . A 常客回饋金 (frequent-rider) rebate returns NT$50 for every NT$200 accumulated on an e-ticket, stated in NTMC's own Ankeng-specific announcement rather than only a general New Taipei light-rail scheme
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The line is covered by the TPASS 基北北桃1200 monthly pass: MOTC's programme table lists light rail among the covered modes across the four participating municipalities."
      - superscript:
        - link "[28]":
          - /url: "#ref-28"
      - text: The published sales locations conflict. MOTC's 2022 sales-point table names
      - strong: K09 Shisizhang
      - text: directly
      - superscript:
        - link "[28]":
          - /url: "#ref-28"
      - text: ", but NTMC's own current page listing sales locations for the pass names only Circular Line stations and two Danhai LRT stations — no Ankeng LRT station appears on it."
      - superscript:
        - link "[24]":
          - /url: "#ref-24"
      - text: The sources establish different lists at different publication dates, not whether K09 currently sells the pass.
    - heading "Incidents and ridership" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The line was affected by the 3 April 2024 Hualien earthquake: immediately afterward, K09 – K06 ran single-track bidirectional and K06 – K01 ran a partial service, before the whole line returned to normal running at 16:30 the same day, at a 15-minute headway"
      - superscript:
        - link "[25]":
          - /url: "#ref-25"
      - superscript:
        - link "[26]":
          - /url: "#ref-26"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: NTMC's full-year release says the line carried more than 2.03 million journeys in 2025.
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
      - text: The same release gives more than 6.01 million for Danhai LRT and 22.04 million for the Circular Line, within a New Taipei Metro total exceeding 30.09 million journeys.
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
    - heading "Naming and place" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Ankeng's old name was 暗坑 (Hokkien Àm-kheⁿ), and the district was renamed in 1801 by Lin Deng-xuan, grandson of the pioneer settler Lin Tian-cheng, because the old name meant “dark valley” and was considered inauspicious.
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
      - text: The modern line name therefore preserves the district's later name rather than inventing a separate railway identity.

    - heading "Overview" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Bannan Line is the
      - link "Taipei Metro":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: network's continuous east–west trunk, running from BL01 Dingpu in
      - link "Tucheng":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl03/
      - text: to BL23 Nangang Exhibition Center through 23 stations.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: "Its present identity joins five construction projects: the Nangang, Banqiao and Tucheng lines, the Nangang eastern extension and the Dingpu extension."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: Those projects opened in eight passenger-service stages between 1999 and 2015, and DORTS describes every one as underground.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The line carries two overlapping services: BL23 – BL01 over the whole route and BL23 – BL05"
      - link "Far Eastern Hospital":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl05/
      - text: over the busier eastern and central section.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: The operator schedules service from 06:00 to 24:00 and publishes journey times of about 48 minutes for the full route and 38 minutes for the short working.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - heading "Route and alignment" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: From Dingpu the railway remains underground through Tucheng and Banqiao, crosses below the
      - link "Xindian":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g01/
      - text: River between
      - link "Jiangzicui":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl09/
      - text: and
      - link "Longshan Temple":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl10/
      - text: ", then follows Heping West Road, Zhonghua Road and the Zhongxiao corridor across central"
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: .
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: East of
      - link "Kunyang":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl21/
      - text: ", shield tunnels continue below Zhongxiao East Road to Nangang, cross the high-speed and conventional-rail tunnels, and reach Nangang Exhibition Center beneath Nanxi Park east of Academia Road."
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The western alignment was not the scheme first studied.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: From 1987 DORTS examined alternatives on both sides of the Xindian River and a river-bottom tunnel before the Executive Yuan accepted a 1989 revision that changed the originally elevated western Blue Line to underground construction and extended it towards Tucheng.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: "The eastern end also changed: the 1986 initial-network approval had the Blue Line running from Banqiao to"
      - link "Songshan":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g19/
      - text: ", before the Executive Yuan accepted an extension to Nangang on 21 January 1988."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: That eastern proposal still contained elevated and surface railway beyond the Dongxin Street tunnel portal.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Taipei City Council asked in December 1989 for the roughly 1.75 km Xiangyang–Nangang section to be put underground, and a 1992 Executive Yuan public-works meeting directed that the main and branch routes east of
      - link "Houshanpi":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl20/
      - text: ", Kunyang station and the route to it would be underground, with Kunyang becoming the initial network's operating terminus."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The committed TDX route measures 26.65 km between BL01 and BL23 and 20.48 km between BL05 and BL23 on the short working.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: Its longest inter-station gap is 3.08 km between BL09 Jiangzicui and BL10 Longshan Temple, across the Xindian River, while the shortest is 0.65 km between BL06
      - link "Fuzhong":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl06/
      - text: and BL07 Banqiao.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
    - heading "Planning, contracts and opening" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The original Blue Line formed part of the 70.3 km initial network approved by the Executive Yuan on 4 April 1986; the NT$444.4 billion figure on the DORTS page is the approval total for that six-line initial network, rather than a Bannan-only cost.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Tucheng planning began in 1990 and its route was approved on 18 October 1993 as about 5.6 km with four underground stations and a depot.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The eastern extension's route plan was approved on 17 June 1998, its financial plan on 13 June 2001, and its published total budget was NT$15.735 billion.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS divided the early Nangang works into numerous civil, building-services and systems packages, including rolling stock, signalling, power, communications, lifts, escalators, fare collection and depot facilities.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: "Procurement strategy varied with the work: DORTS says technically demanding Nangang packages used international joint bids, others required foreign technical cooperation, and the security-sensitive CN251 and CN252 works through the Bo'ai special district were negotiated with the Veterans Engineering Agency."
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: The same retrospective records that political representatives and private contractors criticised negotiated-price awards to public construction bodies, after which the Banqiao Line abandoned that route to contract award.
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
    - table:
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Opened Passenger section Construction project":
          - columnheader "Opened"
          - columnheader "Passenger section"
          - columnheader "Construction project"

        - row "25 December 2008 Kunyang–Nangang Nangang eastern extension[5]":
          - cell "25 December 2008"

            - text: Nangang eastern extension
            - superscript:
              - link "[5]":
                - /url: "#ref-5"
        - row "27 February 2011 Nangang–Nangang Exhibition Center Nangang eastern extension[5]":
          - cell "27 February 2011"
          - cell "Nangang–Nangang Exhibition Center"
          - cell "Nangang eastern extension[5]":
            - text: Nangang eastern extension
            - superscript:
              - link "[5]":
                - /url: "#ref-5"
        - row "6 July 2015 Yongning–Dingpu Dingpu extension[6]":
          - cell "6 July 2015"
          - cell "Yongning–Dingpu"
          - cell "Dingpu extension[6]":
            - text: Dingpu extension
            - superscript:
              - link "[6]":
                - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS says the Municipal Government–Ximen and Ximen–Longshan Temple works were rushed to early completion so the east–west railway could form the 雙十 network with the
      - link "Tamsui":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r28/
      - text: ", Xindian,"
      - link "Zhonghe":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y12/
      - text: and
      - link "Muzha":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br02/
      - text: lines.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: The eastern extension was deliberately designed to open in two stages because its two-station tunnel was being delivered by the Railway Underground Project Office while DORTS's own civil work was split into CE730A and CE730B.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: Its seven systems packages—trains, signalling, power, communications, digital radio, fare collection and track—were bundled with the Xinzhuang–Luzhou Line systems to preserve compatibility and intellectual-property continuity while controlling cost.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The 2 km Dingpu extension was approved on 16 February 2007, began construction on 31 December 2009 and cost NT$7.627 billion according to the project page.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: Initial inspection occurred on 6 June 2015, final inspection on 23 June and passenger service on 6 July.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - heading "Engineering and construction" [level=2]
    - heading "Shield tunnelling below the Xindian River" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS identifies the shield tunnels below the Xindian River bed as both technically difficult and large enough in scale and cost to drive joint bidding for the CP261, CP262 and CP263 packages.
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: Its construction-management volume calls the Banqiao Line approximately 7 km long, where the current project page says approximately 7.1 km.
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: CP261 extended 2,063 m from the south end of Ximen station along Zhonghua Road and Heping West Road to a ventilation shaft below Huajiang Bridge, including Longshan Temple station and twin running tunnels.
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
      - text: The tunnels used earth-pressure-balance shields with soil conditioning.
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
    - paragraph:
      - text: On 28 April 1995, while workers were breaking out the launch face for the westbound tunnel, a small seep observed at 06:45 became a large water-and-sand inflow at 07:15.
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: From 08:10 the ground developed a void about 6 m across and a nearby ten-storey residential building tilted slightly.
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: DORTS locates the leak about 2.5 m above the shaft base at the boundary between more permeable silty fine sand and silty clay, where water pressure was greatest within that part of the Songshan Formation.
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The emergency response pushed the shield into its steel bulkhead, pressurised the chamber, injected water-stopping material, backfilled the street void, grouted the surrounding ground at low pressure and increased monitoring.
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: DORTS says the inflow was stopped by 13:00 and traffic then reopened; engineers later selected low-pressure grouting from five assessed methods to correct the building while minimising disruption to its structure and residents.
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
    - heading "Underground stations and the central corridor" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS's structural manual says initial-network underground stations including those on Bannan were designed by cut-and-cover construction.
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: It describes the basic station form—not a dimension schedule for every station—as a two-level rectangular box roughly 200 m long and 18 m wide, with a concourse above the platform and tracks.
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The builder classifies Nangang as one of the more difficult routes because it crossed dense commercial districts with heavy traffic beside Taipei Main Station, the Executive Yuan and the Control Yuan, while CN253B shield tunnels passed beneath the first-grade
      - link "Beimen":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g13/
      - text: monument.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Its tunnel manual later stated that CN253B had been completed without affecting Beimen, a claim from the builder rather than a separately published monitoring dataset.
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
    - paragraph
    - figure "The concourse at Taipei Main Station, platform 3, the interchange every east–west Bannan rider passes through. Bigmorr, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons":
      - img "The concourse at Taipei Main Station, ticket gates and destination signage overhead"
      - text: The concourse at Taipei Main Station, platform 3, the interchange every east–west Bannan rider passes through. Bigmorr, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
    - paragraph
    - heading "The three-railway eastern work" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: East of Kunyang, DORTS records about 725 m of the extension inside Taiwan Railways land and describes a 三鐵共構 arrangement.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The same sentence names high-speed rail and 地鐵 after its preceding alignment text has named the high-speed and Taiwan Railways tunnels, so the source's wording is preserved as an internal anomaly rather than silently normalised.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The extension placed Nangang station south of the former TRA freight yard and carried the route beneath the high-speed and conventional-rail tunnels before turning towards Nangang Exhibition Center.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The tunnel between the two new stations was designed and built on DORTS's behalf by the Taipei Railway Underground Project Office, now incorporated into the Railway Bureau.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - heading "Traction-cable faults" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A later DORTS technical paper records successive DC traction-cable incidents on the Bannan and Tucheng lines.
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: TRTC's inspection found a small number of cables with low insulation resistance caused by moisture carrying soil into insufficiently waterproof joints, or by water entering through damaged outer jackets.
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: The response standardised the construction method and material selection for joints between 500 mm² and 240 mm² DC cables.
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
    - heading "Stations and architecture" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS says the Nangang stations were designed around their relationship with the existing urban and commercial environment rather than a single monumental architectural style.
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
      - text: High land values and scarce sites led the surface entrances and ventilation structures to use restrained forms that minimised their mass in the streetscape.
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
      - text: The Tucheng stations likewise prioritised functional interiors and the relationship of entrances and vents with their surroundings.
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Dingpu's design translates the area's change from mining and industrial production towards high-technology research through a sequence of “light” elements across concourse, platform, ceiling, floor and walls.
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
      - text: At Nangang, the “nostalgia and technology” concept uses lake green for the district's former ponds, ceramic floor tiles and historic imagery on glass, while each side of the platform carries a 62.5 m art wall based on Jimmy Liao's work.
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
      - text: Nangang Exhibition Center instead adopts “digital space, e-station,” with dawn blue, metal finishes and barcode-like surface patterns tied to the nearby software park, trade centre and Academia Sinica.
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
    - heading "Rolling stock" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The line's verified fleet comprises the Siemens 321 and 341 series.
      - superscript:
        - link "[24]":
          - /url: "#ref-24"
      - text: DORTS says all 36 trains procured under the Xindian/Nangang/Zhonghe contract and all six trains procured for Tucheng operated on Bannan.
      - superscript:
        - link "[24]":
          - /url: "#ref-24"
      - text: "Its electrical and mechanical history identifies both as six-car fleets: 216 cars in 36 321 trains and 36 cars in six 341 trains."
      - superscript:
        - link "[25]":
          - /url: "#ref-25"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The 321 fleet uses 750 V DC third-rail power, VVVF-GTO control, regenerative and disc-friction braking, and ATC incorporating ATO, ATP and ATS; DORTS gives an 80 km/h maximum operating speed and capacity of 2,200 passengers.
      - superscript:
        - link "[25]":
          - /url: "#ref-25"
      - text: The 341 trains were manufactured by Siemens in 2003 and delivered to DORTS from September through November 2004 for the Tucheng opening.
      - superscript:
        - link "[25]":
          - /url: "#ref-25"
      - text: Their changes included bellows-style gangway covers, larger front destination text, later side destination displays, IGBT traction and static inverters, a revised motor coupling, self-cooled braking resistors and updated current collection equipment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[25]":
          - /url: "#ref-25"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "A contemporaneous CNA report adds a procurement dispute: civil contractor Continental Engineering bought the six trains after DORTS rejected its proposed KOROS equipment, then obtained Siemens trains for more than NT$2.248 billion at a reported unit price about 50% above DORTS's earlier Siemens purchase."
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: That account is secondary evidence for the price and disagreement, while the DORTS technical publications independently establish the manufacturer, fleet size, delivery period and assignment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - superscript:
        - link "[25]":
          - /url: "#ref-25"
      - superscript:
        - link "[24]":
          - /url: "#ref-24"
    - heading "Depots" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Nangang depot occupies about 7.83 hectares east of Xiangyang Road and Dongxin Street, south of Zhongxiao East Road Section 7 and north of Muzhi Mountain, providing stabling, inspection and washing.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: DORTS says the roof slab above its stabling area reserved development rights.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Tucheng depot occupies about 26.8 hectares on former Dahan River flood-control land.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: It is the principal stabling, washing and maintenance works for the trains of the Banqiao, Tucheng and Nangang sections.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - heading "Operations and crowding" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: At weekday peaks from 07:00–09:00 and 17:00–19:30, TRTC publishes a whole-route headway of about six minutes and an overlapping-section headway of about three minutes.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: Its densest published interval is about 2 minutes 15 seconds from Longshan Temple towards Kunyang between 08:00 and 09:00.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: Off-peak service is every 8–10 minutes over the full route and 4–5 minutes on the overlap; after 23:00, full-length trains alone run every 8–12 minutes.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The published peak figures conflict.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: TRTC's route page gave 2 minutes 15 seconds when accessed on 10 August 2026, while CNA reported a two-minute interval from Far Eastern Hospital towards Nangang Exhibition Center during the 08:00–08:30 half-hour and said that interval would start at 07:30 from 10 November 2025.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: CNA attributed about 1,500 extra places to the earlier start, or about 2,000 when six trains with more standing space were counted.
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "TVBS reported another peak measure in August 2025: four extra trains began at Far Eastern Hospital, with the 08:07 and 08:16 workings running empty to Jiangzicui before boarding passengers."
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: The report quoted TRTC saying trains were already 2 minutes 15 seconds apart and additional frequency was not available, so four peak trains would instead have fewer seats from 20 August.
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
    - paragraph:
      - text: TRTC's public ridership series combines Bannan with the other three high-capacity lines rather than giving it a separate total.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: The operator separately publishes monthly station-entry and exit spreadsheets back to 1996 and whole-system totals, including 62,471,614 journeys in June 2026, but that system figure is not a Bannan value.
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: The daily-ridership fact therefore remains TBC.
    - heading "Dingpu joint development" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Control Yuan's 2026 investigation distinguishes construction of the operating station from the joint-development project above and beside it.
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
      - text: It found no illegality in the 2009 urban-planning procedure or the original landowner's agreement, while recommending that future projects consider less burdensome ways to deliver planning returns and whether local conditions justify adjusting their proportion.
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
    - paragraph:
      - text: After development tenders failed in August 2016 and February 2017, DORTS paused the process citing co-construction with
      - link "Sanying":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/sanying-line/
      - text: station
      - code: LB01
      - text: and an urban-plan change, then held the third tender on 2 May 2024.
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
      - text: The Control Yuan found those two factors had limited effect on tendering and said it was difficult to deny delay; it also criticised the earlier failure to settle the disputed planning-return procedure thoroughly before land acquisition.
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
    - heading "Conflicting measurements and records" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The operating and construction lengths do not describe the line with one number.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: TDX measures 26.65 km from BL01 to BL23 and English Wikipedia rounds that to 26.6 km, while Chinese Wikipedia gives 28.2 km.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: "The five DORTS project lengths also sum to 28.2 km: about 11, 7.1, 5.6, 2.5 and 2 km respectively."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: DORTS's construction-management volume introduces a further rounding by calling Banqiao about 7 km rather than the project page's 7.1 km.
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The final-inspection date for the first 1999 opening also differs between DORTS pages.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: The parent Nangang record says 13 December 1999, while the Banqiao record says 23 December for Ximen–Longshan Temple; both give passenger service on 24 December.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
