      - text: TRTC's published
      - link "Bannan Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/bannan-line/
      - text: pattern gives a 06:00–24:00 service window, overlapping peak patterns and different one-way run times for the two operating patterns.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: The page is useful precisely because it states service as an operator responsibility; it does not turn those Bannan values into a claim about every TRTC line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Construction, project approvals and civil-package history remain with the relevant
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: or New Taipei rapid-transit engineering bureau.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The operator inherits and runs those assets, and the source family here does not support a single consolidated TRTC procurement history for every line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: Where a contract, incident or opening date is line-specific, it is cited on that line or vehicle page rather than attributed to the corporation in the abstract.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"

      - text: The sources read for this operator entry do not publish a current all-depot fleet allocation, a single company-wide headway table or a complete shareholder and governance history. Those fields remain TBC. The durable facts established here are the operating role, the vehicle-plant responsibility boundary and the operator-published example of a line-specific service pattern.
      - superscript:

    - text: "Every line the site carries, each labelled with its code at both ends — colour alone does not identify a line. Bannan blue and Airport MRT purple are indistinguishable to a reader with protanopia, and Tamsui red against Danhai red is the closest pair on the network even in normal colour vision, which is why every line carries its code. Interchange stations are ringed in black; termini are the outer dots. Branch track is drawn as a pale core of its parent's colour inside a hairline of the same colour darkened — a branch belongs to its line rather than being a line of its own, and the hairline is what gives the pale core a defined edge on the paper. 4 lines have one: Tamsui-Xinyi, Songshan-Xindian, Zhonghe-Xinlu and Danhai LRT. Where a line appears broken, the alignment across the gap is missing from the published geometry — those breaks are holes in the source data, not features of the network, and are left unbridged rather than joined with track we cannot evidence. A dashed line is not surveyed track: it joins that line's published station points in order and says nothing about the route between them. Sanying is drawn that way, having no published route geometry at all."

  - paragraph:
    - strong: Length is official; Measured is ours.
    - text: "The operators publish a route length through TDX — as a running total against the last station of each route, not in the route-length field, which is zero throughout. Measured is computed independently from the surveyed geometry, taken between the outermost stations because the published alignment runs on past both termini into depot leads and tail track. The two agree to within about 150 m on every line whose geometry is continuous, which is the point of printing both: the check is visible rather than asserted. Both columns describe the trunk route only, so a line's branch is excluded from each. A ≥ marks a line whose geometry arrives in discontinuous runs — the track crossing each gap is absent from the source, so our figure is a floor, and the shortfall against the official column measures how much is missing: 0.8 km on the Tamsui–Xinyi Line, 2.8 km on the Circular. End-to-end times are MOTC's own."
  - paragraph:
    - strong: A † marks a figure that is not the platform's.
    - text: MOTC's data holds no record of the Sanying Line of any kind — not a line record, not a station, not a metre of geometry — so its station count, length and end-to-end time on this table are the operator's own, from New Taipei Metro's own opening announcement, 30 June 2026, and are cited on its
    - link "line page":
      - /url: /rail/metro/lines/sanying-line/
    - text: . The length bar is drawn to the same scale as every other, because a published route length is the same quantity whoever published it; what the dagger marks is that this row was assembled from a different source than the 10 above it, not that it is worth less. Its colour is the operator's too — see
    - link "the line colours page":
      - /url: /data/line-colours/
    - text: for where that was read and what it was checked against.

    - heading "TOD and joint development" [level=1]
    - paragraph: The station-area buildings, land rights, public returns and disputes that sit beside Taipei-region rail.
    - region "Quick facts":

    - heading "What TOD means here" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Taipei-region primary record uses land development and joint development as the operative terms, rather than treating every station-area building as a generic TOD project.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The mechanism combines a station, entrances, depot or other rail facility with offices, shops, housing or public space, and the development record is therefore about land rights and interfaces as much as about architecture.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: The page uses TOD as a reader-facing label, but keeps the official categories and site names in the tables below.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - heading "How value and risk are allocated" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: "'s FAQ says the authority and landowners each receive half of the actual design incentive floor area created under the applicable MRT and planning rules, unless a different agreement or law applies."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Its separate value-conversion explanation subtracts the authority's incentive-volume value from the building's total value and treats the investor's assessed construction, tax and expected-profit contribution as a conversion value, rather than publishing a single investor revenue percentage.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Taipei also states that rent, sale and operating income from returned property can support MRT construction finance.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "New Taipei publishes a different sequence: after planning designation and negotiated acquisition, the authority selects an investor, then proceeds through design, permits, construction and rights allocation before transferring property according to the agreed allocation."
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: Its value rule starts with the completed building's total value, subtracts the authority's allocated value, and uses the balance to calculate landowner and investor values.
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: The public record therefore supports a process comparison, not a single Taipei-wide revenue-share ratio.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
    - heading "Completed and operating cases" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The DORTS technical journal records Daan Forest Park J2 as a 2,994 m² private site with 34,644.77 m² of non-MRT floor area, 62 homes, and an occupancy permit in ROC 99; its station entrance is integrated into the building.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: The same case records an estimated NT$56.77 million saving in land-acquisition cost at the stated valuation basis, which is a case-specific estimate rather than a general return.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: The adjacent Daan J3 case has an 890 m² site, 12,650.72 m² of non-MRT floor area, 31 commercial units and an occupancy permit in ROC 101; its station entrance is also built into the development.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: These cases link to
      - link "Daan Park ( R06 )":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r06/
      - text: and
      - link "Daan ( R05 )":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r05/
      - text: ", while the source-era labels J2 and J3 remain the development identifiers."
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The Daan Forest Park design book shows why completion cannot be inferred from a drawn station plan: its basic design proposed 23,499.96 m², while the investor's building-permit design showed 34,644.77 m² and a different building height and use mix."
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The source also makes the station entrance a programme constraint, with completion targeted before the Xinyi Line opening so that passenger access and evacuation would not be delayed.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Zhongshan has at least two separately numbered development cases. The J1 record gives a 1,468.58 m² site, 18,228.12 m² of planned non-MRT floor area, a retail, office and residential mix, and 95.40% construction progress at the end of July 2017; it does not settle a final completion date in that page.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The J2 design record instead gives a 1,681 m² site and 24,070.77 m² total floor area, including 1,164.14 m² of MRT facilities, with exit 6 integrated into the building.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: The current registry links the station to
      - link "Zhongshan ( R11 )":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r11/
      - text: and
      - link "Zhongshan ( G14 )":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g14/
      - text: ; the source's
      - link "G16":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g16/
      - text: label is an engineering-era label, not a current station code.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current DORTS rental table shows the returned-property side of this system, not just the construction side. It lists, for example, one
      - code: BR4
      - text: Zhongxiao Fuxing shopping-mall property at 2,036.38 ping and NT$3,869 per ping per month, and a
      - link "G02":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g02/
      - text: Xindian District Office development with 25 office units listed and 25 leased.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: The table also records a range of areas and rents for Daan, Daan Park, Xinpu, Guting and other sites, but it is not a complete construction history or a developer register.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - heading "Current and advancing portfolio" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taipei's public-land register supplies contract dates and named private investors for newer cases while leaving many area, completion and revenue fields to their individual project records.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: Its current list includes the
      - link "Xinpu adjacent site ( BL08 )":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl08/
      - text: signed with 旺泰建設 and 忠泰長虹建設 on ROC 110-07-05, the
      - link "Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall site R08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r08/
      - text: and
      - link "G10":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g10/
      - text: signed with 愛山林建設 and 宏匯 on ROC 114-05-22, and future-labelled
      - code: Y26
      - text: and
      - code: Y21
      - link "Circular Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/circular-line/
      - text: development cases with named investors.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: The contract list is evidence of an investor agreement, not evidence that construction or occupancy has finished.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS's current land-development office page shows that its work now spans investor selection, design review, contract management, construction-cost assessment, rights allocation and post-handover defects; it names current work at
      - code: Y26B
      - text: ","
      - code: Y37
      - text: ","
      - code: Y21B
      - text: ","
      - code: Y20B
      - text: ","
      - code: Y23B
      - text: ", CKS Memorial Hall, Xinpu and"
      - link "Xindian":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g01/
      - text: District Office sites.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: Those future Circular labels cannot be silently converted into current station pages because the committed station registry does not yet contain every planned code.
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
    - heading "New Taipei scale and public return" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: New Taipei's Circular Line integrity platform identifies ten planned land- development stations and says four—
      - link "Xiulang Bridge":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y09/
      - text: ","
      - link "Jingping":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y10/
      - text: ","
      - link "Zhonghe":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y12/
      - text: and
      - link "Zhongyuan":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y14/
      - text: —had investors performing contracts when the page was fetched.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: For the six sites placed on the integrity platform, the same official page publishes an estimated NT$7.287 billion contribution to self-financing funds, NT$176.072 billion in total building value, NT$60.883 billion in investment and NT$67.937 billion in public benefit including public landowners.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: These are the authority's estimates for that portfolio, not realized revenue. The source also says the Circular Line itself completed and entered service on 31 January 2020, while the ten development sites remained a separate land- development programme.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
    - paragraph:
      - text: New Taipei's current financial account says its authority had 37 development cases, had selected investors for 13, and had completed two when the article was updated; it describes returned-property rents and sales as a principal source for repaying self-financing debt.
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: A separate
      - link "Sanying":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/sanying-line/
      - text: depot news record gives a 14.1-hectare depot-and-
      - link "LB05":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb05/
      - text: site, says about 80% of agreeing landowners had chosen participation or retained development rights, and leaves the investor-selection stage ahead.
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: It is therefore an advancing land-rights case, not a completed building.
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
    - heading "Meihe City and the legal dispute" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Meihe City is the region's essential caution against treating joint development as an uncomplicated financing success. New Taipei's official 2014 account says the review lasted more than 15 years, reduced an original 26-building design to 13 buildings, and required greater setbacks and public space after urban-design and environmental review.
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: A later New Taipei government research report instead describes 16 towers, 2,220 units, about 400,600 m² of floor area, and Rich Development as the selected private developer.
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: Those are conflicting project descriptions from different official records; the site publishes both rather than choosing one.
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The legal issue is not just a design disagreement. Judicial Interpretation No. 743 states that land expropriated under MRT Law Article 6 cannot be used in the same plan for Article 7 joint development, and that transfer to a third party requires clear legal authority.
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: The interpretation records the underlying Xindian depot case, the different statutory purposes of expropriation and joint development, and the disagreement among the Control Yuan, executive agencies and courts before the interpretation.
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: Meihe City is therefore published here as a legal and governance conflict as well as a large-scale station-area project.
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
    - heading "What the inventory still cannot say" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The fetched primary material does not provide one reconciled table containing every site's developer, site area, total floor area, completion date, realized revenue share and dispute history.
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: It provides detailed case records, current rental inventory, contract lists, portfolio estimates and legal records in separate families.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: The missing values stay TBC until the project contract, occupancy record, rights-allocation decision or audited revenue statement is fetched for that specific site.
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"

      - text: Look at the boundary. The Neihu section is BR13 to BR24 — twelve stations. The B series has eleven.
      - strong: BR13 Songshan Airport is a Neihu-section station carrying a Muzha-section number
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":

      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The chronology says why it might be. Songshan Airport was not in the original scheme: MOTC directed a study on serving the airport directly in February 2000, the Executive Yuan agreed in principle on 1 August 2001, and the funding was approved on 4 January 2002"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":

      - text: . By then the Neihu section's B series had been allocated to the stations that already existed on paper.

    - paragraph:
      - strong: That last step is this site reading the table, not DORTS explaining it.
      - text: The addition date is the builder's; the inference about the numbering is ours, and it is offered as a reading rather than a fact. What the table shows without interpretation is that the number is in the wrong series for the section the station is in.
    - heading "Why any of it matters" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taipei's network was not designed and then built. It was built project by project, each with its own budget, contractor, systems supplier and drawing set, and then operated as one railway afterwards. Almost every oddity on this site traces back to that — two incompatible fleets on one line, a depot in the wrong district for its name, station numbers that jump 29 places on the
      - link "Zhonghe–Xinlu Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/zhonghe-xinlu-line/
      - text: .
    - paragraph: The numbering is the cleanest evidence of it, because it is the seam left visible in the paperwork. The signs were made to be read by passengers on a finished railway. The drawings were made by two teams, working outward from their own starting points, years apart.

      - superscript:

Every number on this page is transcribed from it. The same page also carries the Songshan Airport station's chronology — MOTC directs a study in February 2000, the Executive Yuan agrees in principle on 1 August 2001, the Public Construction Commission approves the funding on 4 January 2002."

- main:

  - article:
    - heading "Why the Wenhu Line looks the way it does" [level=1]
    - paragraph: The official design logic behind the Wenhu Line's steel-and-glass stations, its three Neihu architectural vocabularies, and its river-in-the-sky idea.
    - navigation "Wenhu Line strip map":
      - list:
        - listitem: BR01 Taipei Zoo
        - listitem: BR02 Muzha
        - listitem: BR03 Wanfang Community
        - listitem: BR04 Wanfang Hospital
        - listitem: BR05 Xinhai
        - listitem: BR06 Linguang
        - listitem: BR07 Liuzhangli
        - listitem: BR08 Technology Building
        - listitem: BR09 Daan
        - listitem: BR10 Zhongxiao Fuxing
        - listitem: BR11 Nanjing Fuxing
        - listitem: BR12 Zhongshan Junior High School
        - listitem: BR13 Songshan Airport
        - listitem: BR14 Dazhi
        - listitem: BR15 Jiannan Rd.
        - listitem: BR16 Xihu
        - listitem: BR17 Gangqian
        - listitem: BR18 Wende
        - listitem: BR19 Neihu
        - listitem: BR20 Dahu Park
        - listitem: BR21 Huzhou
        - listitem: BR22 Donghu
        - listitem: BR23 Nangang Software Park
        - listitem: BR24 Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center
      - text: Serves all 24 stations
    - region "Quick facts":
      - link "BR":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/wenhu-line/
      - link "Wenhu Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: 文湖線
      - term: Muzha station language
      - definition:
        - text: Steel and glass with simple forms
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Neihu design vocabularies
      - definition:
        - text: Three
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Neihu design theme
      - definition:
        - text: Lake City Story
        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: Underground stations
      - definition:
        - text: BR13
        - link "Songshan Airport":
          - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br13/
        - text: and BR14
        - link "Dazhi":
          - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br14/
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
    - navigation "On this page":
      - paragraph: On this page
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - 'link "Muzha: lightness under constraint"':
            - /url: "#muzha-lightness-under-constraint"
        - listitem:
          - 'link "Neihu: three architectural dialects"':
            - /url: "#neihu-three-architectural-dialects"
        - listitem:
          - link "The bridge and the space beneath it":
            - /url: "#the-bridge-and-the-space-beneath-it"
        - listitem:
          - link "Which stations are underground?":
            - /url: "#which-stations-are-underground"
        - listitem:
          - link "Specifications":
            - /url: "#specifications"
        - listitem:
          - link "References":
            - /url: "#references"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The
      - link "Wenhu Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: "does not have one station style repeated twenty-four times. Its visual change is deliberate: the"
      - link "Muzha":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br02/
      - text: section and the
      - link "Neihu":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br19/
      - text: section were designed around different briefs, and the builder describes both rather than calling the difference an accident.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - 'heading "Muzha: lightness under constraint" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: The original Muzha section is elevated and passes through the city on a route whose sites are mostly in existing roads. DORTS says that the urban setting made the design form highly constrained, while the single-column support system limited the load available for decoration.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The stations therefore use steel and glass with simple forms, positioned as an expression of modern urban architecture, and their volumes are kept as far as possible from roadside buildings.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: That is a useful explanation of the line's familiar visual economy. The minimalism is not presented by the builder as a claim that decoration was unwanted; it is a response to the structural and urban conditions of an elevated medium-capacity railway. The same design record identifies the Muzha-section station forms as either cantilevered stations supported by one column or ordinary beam-and-column structures, depending on the site conditions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - 'heading "Neihu: three architectural dialects" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The Neihu section extends the Muzha system, but its design brief starts with the character of the places it crosses. DORTS divides its station language into three vocabularies:"
      - strong: 住宅城鄉風貌
      - text: ", a residential and urban-rural character;"
      - strong: 商業休閒環境
      - text: ", a commercial and leisure environment; and"
      - strong: 工業科技景觀
      - text: ", an industrial and technological landscape."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The viaduct is then used to connect those different settings into a single idea,
      - strong: 空中之河
      - text: ", or “river in the sky”, under the overall theme"
      - strong: 湖城故事
      - text: ", “Lake City Story”."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The result is not a claim that every station is unique.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: DORTS says the Neihu stations begin from a common architectural vocabulary and element set, then adjust them to the surrounding conditions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Public-art thinking supplies station subthemes and colour plans, while simple geometric forms are intended to ease maintenance and preserve the image of rapid transport.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The source specifically names Jiannan Road,
      - link "Dahu Park":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br20/
      - text: and Nangang Exhibition Center as stations given forms distinct from the standard station type because of their local character.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The materials make the same argument physically. DORTS describes bright, simple steel structures with painted coloured metal panels, enamelled steel panels and large areas of glass, chosen to make the station volumes feel light and visually permeable.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The technical-book account adds that architecture, landscape and public art were considered together, including colour changes in ceilings and columns, wall materials and patterns, and paving used for orientation and information.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - heading "The bridge and the space beneath it" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The official design record says approximately ten kilometres of this section's viaduct are mostly above the central islands of roads and use prestressed concrete U-girders.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Sound-control walls vary in height with the conditions along the route, to reduce disturbance to nearby residents while responding to the surrounding environment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The underside received its own landscape treatment. DORTS says the space below the stations gets too little sun for good plant growth, so the design uses a dry-landscape interpretation with rocks and pebbles of different sizes and colours, together with added lighting for a night-time urban effect.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: "The “river in the sky” therefore refers to more than the train's elevated path: the official concept joins the viaduct, station envelope, landscape and public art into one line-wide reading."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - heading "Which stations are underground?" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS's route record gives the Neihu section as 14.8 km, with 3.9 km of underground running and two underground stations.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: Its station architecture record names
      - link "Dazhi":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br14/
      - text: as underground and counts ten other Neihu stations as elevated; read with the route record's station list and its two station total, that identifies BR13
      - link "Songshan Airport":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br13/
      - text: and BR14 Dazhi as the line's underground pair.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The official pages do not provide a station-by-station list of every subtheme, the architect of each station, or a current survey of alterations to the original materials.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: This article therefore describes the builder's line-level design logic and leaves those more granular questions TBC.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - region "Specifications":
      - heading "Specifications" [level=2]
      - table:
        - rowgroup:
          - row "Neihu section 14.8 km[2]":
            - rowheader "Neihu section"
            - cell "14.8"
            - cell "km[2]":
              - text: km
              - superscript:
                - link "[2]":
                  - /url: "#ref-2"
          - row "Neihu underground running 3.9 km[2]":
            - rowheader "Neihu underground running"
            - cell "3.9"
            - cell "km[2]":
              - text: km
              - superscript:
                - link "[2]":
                  - /url: "#ref-2"
          - row "Neihu underground stations 2 [2]":
            - rowheader "Neihu underground stations"
            - cell "2"
            - cell "[2]":
              - superscript:
                - link "[2]":
                  - /url: "#ref-2"
          - row "Neihu elevated bridge described in the design record approximately 10 km[1]":
            - rowheader "Neihu elevated bridge described in the design record"
            - cell "approximately 10"
            - cell "km[1]":
              - text: km
              - superscript:
                - link "[1]":
                  - /url: "#ref-1"
    - region "References":
      - heading "References" [level=2]
      - paragraph: 3 of 3 sources on this page are primary — published by the operator, the builder or government.
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Station architectural design — Wenhu Line":

It explains the Muzha section's steel-and-glass, simple-form response to urban-road and single-column constraints; the Neihu section's three design vocabularies and Lake City Story theme; and the materials, bridge, sound-wall, underside-landscape and lighting choices.
        - listitem:
          - link "Wenshan–Neihu Line route description":

          - text: 文山內湖線路線說明 primary Taipei City Government, Department of Rapid Transit Systems ( 臺北市政府捷運工程局 ) accessed 2026-08-27 DORTS's full route record gives the Muzha and Neihu section lengths, station counts, Neihu's 3.9 km underground section and two underground stations, and the station list used to identify BR13 Songshan Airport and BR14 Dazhi.

    - paragraph:
      - text: Taiwan High Speed Rail is a 350 km railway with twelve stations, according to the Railway Bureau’s current project record.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The operator’s own business page names the same twelve-station chain from Nangang to
      - link "Zuoying":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/zuoying/
      - text: and describes station-area commerce and transport operation as part of its business scope.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: TDX independently returned twelve current Station records and one Shape record on 24 August 2026; the checked Route and StationOfRoute endpoints returned 404, so this page does not claim that TDX supplied a route sequence.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
    - heading "Construction and opening stages" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The opening chronology is four-stage in practical terms. Banqiao,
      - link "Taoyuan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taoyuan/
      - text: ","
      - link "Hsinchu":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/hsinchu/
      - text: ","
      - link "Taichung":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taichung/
      - text: ","
      - link "Chiayi":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/chiayi/
      - text: ","
      - link "Tainan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/tainan/
      - text: and Zuoying entered service on 5 January 2007.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: followed on 2 March 2007.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The later stations
      - link "Miaoli":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/miaoli/
      - text: ","
      - link "Changhua":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/changhua/
      - text: and
      - link "Yunlin":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/yunlin/
      - text: opened on 1 December 2015, and Nangang opened on 1 July 2016.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The dates matter because a station page about a later addition is not evidence that the original railway had twelve operating stations on its first day.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The route’s physical form reflects the west-coast corridor rather than a single tunnelled urban railway. The Railway Bureau reports approximately 73% bridges and viaducts, 18% tunnels and 9% embankment or cut sections.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: It identifies vehicle bases at
      - link "Wuri":
        - /url: /rail/tmrt/stations/g16/
      - text: and Zuoying, a northern Hsizhi base not yet established in the page’s account, a main workshop at Yanchao and five engineering-and-electrical bases.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: These are system-level facilities; the guide does not convert them into a guessed “depot for every station” field.
    - heading "BOT contract and financial disputes" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Railway Bureau describes the project as Taiwan’s first major national infrastructure project promoted through private investment participation.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: It records the 23 July 1998 signing of a 35-year construction-and-operation concession and a separate 50-year station-area development concession.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The stated project cost was approximately NT$513.3 billion, with the government responsible for land, the Taipei underground co-construction section, supervision and management, while the concession company funded civil works, stations, core electromechanical systems, operation and maintenance.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The original financial model did not remain unchanged. The Railway Bureau says a 27 July 2015 amendment extended the concession to 70 years, cancelled the station-area development contract, returned development land, reduced capital to clear accumulated losses and added NT$30 billion of government investment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The Control Yuan’s official record names an investigation into whether direct and indirect public investment violated BOT principles.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: In a related statement, the Control Yuan says public and state-enterprise entities supplied 37.42% and describes that as a serious departure from the government-zero-investment commitment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: Those are the source’s figures and characterization; this page does not average them into a new ownership percentage.
    - heading "Eurotrain, Shinkansen and the system boundary" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The procurement history also has an official conflict. One Control Yuan report says the winning application proposed German ICE and French TGV as its European electromechanical reference system, then records a 12 December 1999 change of the core electromechanical system—signalling, power and vehicles—to the Japanese Shinkansen system.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: That report says the change led to commercial arbitration and compensation to the German and French suppliers of US$65 million plus 5% interest.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - paragraph:
      - text: A separate Control Yuan report records the Ministry’s account that railway systems are assembled from specialist subsystems, that Siemens turnout and control equipment remained European for local requirements, and that the other equipment followed Japanese Shinkansen technology.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: "The two reports should be read together, not harmonised into a neat origin label: one foregrounds a European-to-Japanese change and its compensation, while the other explains the retained European turnout subsystem and rejects “mixed blood” as a useful description of the whole railway."
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
    - heading "Power, signalling and vehicles" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Railway Bureau identifies the Japanese Taiwan Shinkansen consortium as the 2000 core-electromechanical contractor and names the Tokaido–Sanyo Shinkansen as the reference system.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: Its published technical description gives 25,000-volt, 60-Hz AC overhead power, automatic train control and centralised traffic control.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: It describes the 700T as based on the Japanese 700 series but adjusted for Taiwan’s route and environment, with nine powered and three unpowered cars, one business car, eleven standard cars, 300 km/h maximum operating speed and a 304 m train length.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - heading "Ridership and source boundary" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The MOTC yearbook’s Table 2-9 is titled “Passenger Traffic of High-Speed Rail Stations” and publishes entry and exit values in units of 10,000 passengers.
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: The line panel uses the committed Railway Bureau open-data monthly network snapshot and keeps the exact values, source URL and retrieval date beside the chart.
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: Station-level current values, trends and rank remain TBC while the wide table is not yet safely transcribed into the station data layer with its entry/exit dimensions preserved.
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"

    - region "Quick facts":

        - listitem:

    - paragraph:
      - text: "This page has two evidence layers: an operator improvement plan and current station-information records."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The first describes a programme and targets; the second describes what the operator lists for particular stations.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:

      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - heading "What the improvement plan establishes" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The operator's two-page plan says that some stations were built long ago and that their accessibility facilities do not meet modern needs.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: It says hardware improvements must be phased because of cost, existing environmental conditions and construction difficulty, while service staff require continuing training.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The plan prioritises elevator construction at the 90 stations ranked highest by passenger entries and exits, alongside railway-construction projects.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: It states a target of elevator construction at 184 stations by ROC 110, with planned coverage of about 98.5% of the operator's passengers.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Those are targets printed in the plan, not a current audit of which stations have working lifts.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The plan describes a three-stage approach to step-free boarding.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The first stage raises platforms to 92–96 cm, the second uses new or modified rolling stock to remove vehicle steps, and the third raises platforms across the network to 115 cm.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The plan gives ROC 111 as the target year for completing that three-stage objective.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: This page does not convert those historical targets into a present-day percentage or claim that every stage was completed on schedule.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The service layer in the same plan includes staff training in accessibility service, etiquette, service technique and boarding-ramp operation.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: It also describes a revised procedure covering reservation, arrival at the station, boarding and exit, with service techniques differentiated by disability type.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The plan describes telephone assistance for wheelchair travellers and a text-message service for deaf or hard-of-hearing travellers.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: These statements describe the plan's service design; the plan is not used here as a current response-time or availability guarantee.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - heading "What current station records publish" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current station-information pages use an accessibility category and separate it from general facilities, ticketing services and other station services.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: That structure is useful because a station page can state both the facility type and its location or count when the operator provides those details.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Gushan record, station code 4380, lists a ramp at the Railway Street 20 Lane entrance, one entrance lift and two platform lifts.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: It also lists service bells at the ramp and lifts, a breastfeeding room, and escalators for entry and exit.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: Its general-facility section lists iTaiwan Wi-Fi, temporary charging, a delay-certificate machine, stairs and platforms.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Yongle record, station code 7110, lists a ramp, a service bell and a platform lift under accessibility facilities.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: Its general-facility section lists iTaiwan Wi-Fi, temporary charging, stairs and platforms, while its ticketing section lists the multi-card electronic ticket system and both student and general TR-PASS products.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Xike record, station code 0970, lists a ramp at the Xike North Station forecourt, a lift in the centre of the platform for changing platforms, and a service bell.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: Its general-facility section lists iTaiwan Wi-Fi, a delay-certificate machine, stairs and platforms, and its other sections list multi-card ticketing and a book-crossing activity.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Kaohsiung Museum of Fine Arts record, station code 4370, lists a ramp at the Cuihua Road entrance, one lift at that entrance and one at each of platforms 1 and 2.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: It also lists an accessible ticket window, service bells, a breastfeeding room, entry and exit escalators, and a two-platform island platform in the general-facility section.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: These records show why a station-specific facility list cannot be replaced by a single network-wide label.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: The operator's records differ in the facility types displayed and in whether a location or count is supplied.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - heading "Boundary of this record" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The sources used here do not provide a current, machine-readable completion register for every TRA station, a dated equipment-outage register, a continuous step-free path from every entrance to every platform, or a platform-to-vehicle gap measurement.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: They also do not establish that a listed lift or ramp is operating at the exact time a passenger travels.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Current network-wide accessibility coverage, station-by-station equipment status, tactile-way continuity, accessible toilet inventory, platform gap and live outage status remain TBC here.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: A current operator export with facility identifiers, maintenance status and an accessible-route graph would settle those gaps.
      - superscript:

      - superscript:

    - paragraph:
      - text: Beitun Main Station is stop 1 of 18 on the Green Line, and the committed TDX record pairs the code G0 with the Traditional Chinese name 北屯總站.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: TDX places it in 北屯區 at 臺中市北屯區敦富東街100號, with a published route chainage of 0.00 km in the selected direction.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The address is the source-backed siting description used here; no extra catchment boundary is inferred from it.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The station belongs to the CJ910 civil package.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: That package covers G0 , the Beitun depot and the northern track system, so the station is part of the line’s depot-end civil works rather than an isolated stop. The separate CJ900/CJ907 contract covers system equipment, including power, communications, automatic fare collection, depot equipment and trains.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The operator describes the Green Line as a steel-wheel, medium-capacity, fully driverless system using two-car trains.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":

      - text: It identifies G0 as one of the two ground-level stations; the other 16 stations are elevated.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: That system-level engineering fact is kept separate from the station address because TDX publishes the latter but not the former.
      - superscript:

      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":

    - paragraph:
      - text: The operator's current public-art roster assigns “Floating Island” (漂浮島) to this station.

          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: "That attribution is kept separate from the station's structural description: a work title is evidence of the operator's art programme, not evidence that the station is underground, elevated or interchange-built."
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The operator's major-events chronology places the 2015 construction beam accident at the G4 / G5 site and separately dates the 2020 joint-shaft fracture during test operation.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: The entry is therefore part of a documented line history, but neither event should be assigned to this station unless the source does so explicitly.

      - text: The separate Green Line system-equipment package covers power, signalling, communications, fare collection, depot equipment and trains across the route.

      - text: Keeping those contracts separate avoids treating the civil package code as a station-specific equipment list.

  - article:
    - heading "Rail vehicle model Taiwan Railways heritage rolling stock and the National Railway Museum" [level=1]:
      - img "Rail vehicle model"
      - text: Taiwan Railways heritage rolling stock and the National Railway Museum
    - paragraph: Five steam locomotives TRA still formally manages and rents out by tier, a museum that opened its first phase in 2025, and three more locomotives whose custody this page could not confirm.
    - region "Quick facts":
      - text: Taiwan Railways heritage rolling stock and the National Railway Museum
      - term: Steam locomotives formally managed by TRA
      - definition:
        - text: CT273, CK124, DT668, CK101, LDK59
        - superscript:

      - term: Locomotives restricted from Pingxi, Shen'ao and Jiji lines
      - definition:

        - superscript:
          - link "[1]":
            - /url: "#ref-1"
      - term: National Railway Museum Phase 1 opened
      - definition:
        - text: 31 July 2025
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":

      - term: Museum Phase 1 buildings
      - definition:
        - text: "6"
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":

      - term: Heritage vehicles displayed at Phase 1
      - definition:
        - text: "24"
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":

    - navigation "On this page":
      - paragraph: On this page
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "Five locomotives, still formally managed":
            - /url: "#five-locomotives-still-formally-managed"
        - listitem:
          - link "A museum, open since 2025":
            - /url: "#a-museum-open-since-2025"
        - listitem:
          - link "Custody this page could not confirm":
            - /url: "#custody-this-page-could-not-confirm"
        - listitem:

        - listitem:
          - link "Specifications":
            - /url: "#specifications"
        - listitem:
          - link "References":
            - /url: "#references"
    - heading "Five locomotives, still formally managed" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "TRA's own internal regulation still actively manages five steam locomotives as a tiered rental asset class: CT273 and CK124 in the top \"special-A\" tier, DT668 and CK101 in the \"A\" tier, and the narrow-gauge LDK59 in the \"B\" tier, each with a stated rate for a dynamic (running) rental."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The same regulation bars CT273 and DT668 from the Pingxi, Shen'ao and Jiji lines entirely, and restricts CK101 to static or motionless display on major festival days only, because its original manufacturer has closed and parts and wheels can no longer be sourced.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: CT273, a 1943 Kawasaki-built CT270-class locomotive based on the Japan Railways C57 design, was TRA's last steam locomotive withdrawn from regular service, in 1984, and was restored to operation in 2014; a 2025 news report, read via search synthesis rather than a full fetch and flagged accordingly for confidence, describes it hauling a summer tourist train between Yuli and Taitung, based at Hualien.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: DT668, a 1941 Kawasaki-built DT650-class locomotive and TRA's heaviest steam class, was withdrawn March 1984 and restored to run on the Neiwan Branch Line in November 2011. CK124 was restored to operation in 2001, and LDK59, TRA's preserved narrow-gauge locomotive, in 2011 — both dates from a secondary lead index, not independently verified against a primary source.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: "This page does not state where each is currently based with confidence: sources disagree between"
      - link "Changhua":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/changhua/
      - text: Roundhouse and TRA's Fugang depot for both CK101 and DT668, and this page publishes both locations rather than choosing one.
    - heading "A museum, open since 2025" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The National Railway Museum's first phase opened 31 July 2025 at the former
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: Railway Workshop site, comprising six restored heritage buildings — the Diesel-Electric Workshop, General Administration Building, Technical Training Institute, Materials Testing Lab, Grand Hall and Bathhouse — eight exhibitions, a weekend heritage-train ride over roughly 650 m using restored diesel railcars, and 24 displayed heritage vehicles.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: The museum's own current page confirms it remains open in 2026 on the same footprint, Tuesday through Sunday; no source read for this page states a Phase 2 opening date or scope.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: The site itself, Taipei Railway Workshop, was designated a national historic monument in 2015; sources disagree on the exact date.
    - heading "Custody this page could not confirm" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Three further CT270-class locomotives — CT271, CT278 and CT284 — are reported by secondary sources as statically preserved outside TRA custody, at parks in Keelung, Ershui and Yilan respectively. None of the three appears in TRA's own steam-locomotive rental regulation, which is consistent with their having passed out of TRA's direct management, but that inference is not confirmed by any primary source this page could read.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: A direct attempt to fetch the Yilan county park's own page describing CT284 failed to connect.
    - heading "Remaining gaps" [level=2]
    - paragraph: No individual locomotive was confirmed to hold its own cultural-asset designation in the national heritage database — only the Taipei Railway Workshop site itself is confirmed to hold monument status, and the database's own search tool could not be read by this page's sourcing process. An itemised list of the museum's 24 displayed vehicles, CT284's exact ownership status, and whether a museum Phase 2 has been announced are all TBC. Which heritage locomotives remain operable as of 2026 is not established by any source dated later than mid-2025 that this page found.

    - heading "Green Line in the current project record" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The
      - link "Taoyuan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taoyuan/
      - text: engineering bureau describes the Green Line as a 27.8-kilometre, 21-station project with 10 underground and 11 elevated stations.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: Its route begins at G01 in Bade, crosses Taoyuan and Luzhu, and divides toward Airport MRT A11 and A16 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The same page records an estimated cost of NT$982.64 billion, central government support of NT$397.44 billion and a 41.77% self-financing rate.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The station table names G01 – G15 , G15a , G15b and G16 – G19 . G02 remains provisional because the road in front of the station has not yet been named, while G16 – G19 are still unnamed in the checked project record.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: This is why the content keeps those codes visible and does not manufacture English or Chinese station names for them.
    - heading "Route and interchanges" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The bureau’s route description puts the eastern section through Bade’s Jieshou Road corridor, Taoyuan’s Jianguo and Yanping roads, the TRA Taoyuan station area, Zhongzheng Road and Luzhu’s Zhongzheng North Road. The branch toward G15a and G15b reaches the Airport MRT at A11 ; the western Aviation City branch continues through G16 – G19 to Airport MRT A16 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The project page identifies future connections with the underground TRA Taoyuan station, the
      - link "Sanying Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/sanying-line/
      - text: extension at G04 , the Nankan transfer hub and Airport MRT A11 / A16 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - heading "Construction approvals and progress" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The feasibility study was approved by the Executive Yuan on 26 August 2011, the environmental assessment on 9 September 2014 and the comprehensive planning report on 20 April 2016.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The bureau records the GM01 systems package award in 2018, GC01’s elevated civil package in 2018, GC02 and GC03 underground packages in 2019, and the GC05 lifts-and-escalators package in 2022.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: It separately records GD04A detailed design and GC04B’s later elevated civil package, with the package progress values dated to June 2026.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current construction overview lists the Green Line as being in the construction stage at 72.19% overall progress.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: "That programme figure is not silently substituted for any package figure: the line page records both the overview value and the bureau’s individual GM01, GC01, GC02, GC03, GC05 and GC04B values as different measurements with different dates."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
    - heading "Package progress, station renumbering and two extensions" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "A later engineering-bureau progress page, dated 31 July 2026, gives per-package figures more granular than the 72.19% overview: GC01 (the elevated package covering G01 , G02 , G13 , G14 , G15 , G15a and G15b ) at 94.57%; GC03 (underground, covering G08 – G12 ) at 76.222%; GM01 (systems) at 56.801%; GC02 (underground, covering G03 – G06 ) at 53.95%; GC05 (lifts and escalators) at 29.70%; and GC04B (the elevated Airport City branch package, covering G14 to G18 ) at only 7.94%, reflecting its later award and a domestic construction-labour and materials shortage the bureau cites as the reason for a formal cross-agency \"Integrity Platform\" oversight mechanism set up around that package's procurement."
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: "Four stations were renumbered during design: today's G14 , G15 , G15a and G15b were previously coded G13 a, G14 , G31 and G32 respectively — a rename, not an error, worth noting since earlier news coverage still uses the old codes."
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: In July 2026 the bureau ran a fully-automatic driverless demonstration from G11 to G15 using Siemens Trainguard-based signalling, with Siemens' global transportation head attending; the engineering bureau head separately confirmed fire inspections passed at all priority-section stations and accessibility remediation completed at G13 / G14 / G15 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Two further extensions are in planning, not yet under construction. A roughly 7.2 km, five-station extension to Zhongli (中壢) — interchanging with TRA and the Airport MRT at G25 — cleared its environmental assessment in February 2023 and its comprehensive plan in December 2023, targeting a December 2031 opening; a depot contract for it was awarded in June 2026.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: A roughly 7.83 km, five-station, fully-elevated extension to Daxi (大溪) remains at the feasibility-study stage, with station positions explicitly not yet finalised.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - heading "Data boundary and future work" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A live TDX probe on 24 August 2026 returned one
      - link "TYMC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/tymc/
      - text: Line record for the Airport MRT and no Green Line record; the corresponding station, route, shape, transfer and first/last-timetable families likewise exposed the operating Airport MRT data rather than a G project dataset.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The site therefore uses the DORTS project table as the Green Line station registry and leaves coordinates, geometry, ridership, fleet allocation, depot assignment, signalling, power, headways, fares, accessibility and opening dates TBC.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The engineering bureau’s current Green Line page estimates main-line opening in 2030.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: That is a project target, not an operating timetable or a guarantee that every station will enter service on the same day. The approved planning-report record remains linked as the deeper source family for construction, finance and design questions that the concise project page does not resolve.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - heading "Source boundary" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The primary record is intentionally layered: DORTS establishes the planned alignment, station table, approvals and progress; the construction overview supplies the programme-level percentage; the planning-report record points to the approved volumes; and TDX establishes the current absence of a Green Line operating dataset."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - region "Ridership":
      - heading "Ridership" [level=2]
      - paragraph:
        - strong: TBC.
        - text: The checked operator source does not publish a line total for this code in the retrieved period range.
      - paragraph:
