    - paragraph:
      - text: The Airport MRT is
      - link "Taoyuan Metro Corporation":
        - /url: /rail/operators/tymc/
      - text: "'s one currently operating line, connecting"
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: Main Station to
      - link "Taoyuan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taoyuan/
      - text: International Airport and on to Zhongli via 22 stations.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: "TYMC itself is not Taoyuan City's own corporation: it was jointly founded on 6 July 2010 by the Taoyuan, New Taipei and Taipei city governments in proportion to each city's share of the route, with capital of NT$3 billion, and the Ministry of Transportation and Communications designated Taoyuan City to operate it."
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: The ownership split is Taoyuan 64.01%, New Taipei 29.32% and Taipei 6.67%.
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
    - 'heading "Route length: three figures, none silently picked" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: This site's own committed TDX data gives route A-1's length as 51.76 km, the sum of surveyed inter-station chainage to the current terminus at A22 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: New Taipei City's own project record and an Executive Yuan background page instead independently agree on 51.03 km, split as roughly 10.92 km underground and 40.11 km elevated across 7 underground and 15 elevated stations, with two maintenance depots.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: zh.wikipedia's infobox gives a third figure, 51.95 km, not traced to any source cited within the article itself.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: Nothing read for this page explains what the three figures each measure differently; all three are published rather than averaged or one chosen as authoritative.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The same New Taipei project record gives the initial line's construction cost as 「工程建設總經費約1,138.5億元」— 1,138.5億元, which converts to NT$113.85 billion, not the ten-times-larger NT$1,138.5 billion a literal digit-for-digit misreading of the Chinese unit could produce.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - heading "From a failed BOT to a government-built line" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Planning has at least three defensible starting points, and different sources plainly mean different things by it: an October 1989 feasibility study is the earliest date found, though only at secondary strength; in October 1996 the central government decided to build the line under a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) model; and Long Life International Development Co. (長生國際開發) won the BOT bid in 1998."
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: The BOT arrangement collapsed on 31 December 2002, when Long Life and the then High Speed Rail Bureau agreed to terminate the contract.
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: "The government took direct responsibility afterward: MOTC designated the High Speed Rail Bureau as the project's construction body on 28 October 2003, and the central government approved the construction plan on 9 March 2004."
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Construction start likewise has more than one dated event rather than one clean answer: New Taipei's project record gives 27 February 2006 for the formal start of the Sanchong–Airport–Zhongli section and its E&M systems, while TYMC's own company history instead records a ceremonial groundbreaking on 26 June 2006, presided over by the Premier."
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: The line opened on 2 March 2017 for stations A1 through A21 , after the originally announced January 2009 target had been publicly revised six times — the specific dates and reasons for each of the six changes are not established by any source read for this page and stay TBC.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
    - 'heading "The Marubeni dispute: two confirmed figures, one unconfirmed total" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: Around the 2017 opening, contemporaneous wire reporting recorded the then High Speed Rail Bureau imposing a NT$2.5 billion delay-penalty cap on contractor Marubeni Corporation (丸紅), the contractual maximum, plus a separate NT$1.9 billion performance bond withheld over Marubeni's unauthorised subcontracting of the signalling system to a British firm — its contract required Marubeni to design that system itself.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: Marubeni separately counter-claimed NT$12.9 billion against the Ministry, on the grounds of repeated Bureau-directed design changes.
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: "No source read for this page states a combined total for the dispute of any kind: NT$2.5 billion plus NT$1.9 billion is NT$4.4 billion, not any commonly-circulated larger figure, and the individual component figures are published here on that basis rather than an unconfirmed total."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "A separate, later dispute in 2021 concerned in-service performance rather than construction delay: the Public Construction Commission recommended withholding NT$726,926,496 from Marubeni for missing three contractual operating standards — express journey time, average speed and train headway."
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
    - 'heading "Rolling stock: two fleets, two manufacturing arrangements" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The express (直達車) fleet is the purple 2000-series, built entirely by Kawasaki Heavy Industries: 11 five-car sets (201–211), 55 cars, running on third-rail DC 750V power at 1,435 mm standard gauge, with a 100 km/h operating speed."
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: "The commuter (普通車) fleet is the blue 1000-series, built under a split arrangement: Kawasaki built the prototype and sets 101 and 118–120, while the remaining sets 102–117 were assembled domestically by Taiwan Rolling Stock Co. (台灣車輛) under an industrial-cooperation programme."
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: Twenty four-car 1000-series sets, 80 cars, are in current service, each carrying 188 seats.
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: Both fleets are maintained across two depots, Qingpu and Luzhu, though no source read for this page allocates specific trains to one depot over the other.
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
    - heading "Express, commuter and journey times" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: TYMC's own current route page fixes the express (直達車) stop pattern at five stations — A1 , A3 , A8 , A12 and A13 — with a peak-hour "Huanbei Express" (環北直達車) pattern adding A18 and A21 ; the commuter (普通車) service calls at every station, A1 through A22 .
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: A Taoyuan City tourism page gives express journey times of 35 minutes from Taipei Main Station to Airport Terminal 1 and 39 minutes to Terminal 2, and commuter times of 82 minutes from Taipei Main Station to Huanbei and 19 minutes from
      - link "Taoyuan HSR Station":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/a18/
      - text: to Terminal 1.
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
    - heading "Fares and the financial turnaround" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: TYMC's own ticketing page states combination-ticket prices — an airport-line return plus a
      - link "Taipei Metro":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: 48-hour pass for NT$520, or a 72-hour pass for NT$600 — without itself restating the base single fare in the section read for this page.
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
      - text: A NT$10 single-fare discount was withdrawn from 2 January 2025, attributed by the company's chairman to rising electricity costs.
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: Whether express and commuter fares differ for the same journey is not established by any primary source read for this page and stays TBC rather than repeated from secondary aggregation.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The line's finances turned around after years of loss: a 2022 negative net worth of NT$706 million forced a NT$1.067 billion bank loan; 2023 was the first profitable year, though no source read for this page gives a specific NT$ figure for that year; 2024 profit is reported at \"over NT$400 million\" by one February 2026 retrospective and at NT$500 million by an earlier estimate published nine days before that year's end — both published rather than reconciled, since the second may be a projection rather than a final result."
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: The 2025 surplus reached a record NT$679 million, with nearly NT$1.1 billion of debt fully repaid by April 2025 and annual ridership over 46 million, up 12% on 2024.
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
    - heading "The 2023 extension, and what comes next" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A22
      - link "Laojie River Station":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/a22/
      - text: opened 31 July 2023, extending the line about 2.06 km underground beyond the former terminus at Huanbei.
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: "The Railway Bureau's own opening announcement gives three delay causes together, not one: COVID-19-era disruption to foreign electrical-and-mechanical suppliers between 2020 and 2022, the technical difficulty of integrating the extension's newer signalling generation with the existing line, and design changes needed to coordinate with a separately-planned Taoyuan railway-undergrounding project."
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: The extension's total cost rose from an original approved NT$13.801 billion, through a first revision of NT$13.8 billion, to a final NT$17.302 billion.
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
    - paragraph:
      - text: A further extension to Zhongli (
      - code: A23
      - text: ) was under construction as of the sources read for this page, planned to connect with the future Taoyuan Metro Green Line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[24]":
          - /url: "#ref-24"
      - text: Taoyuan City's own current station table gives two different target years for
      - code: A23
      - text: within different sections of the same page — 117年 (2028) and 118年 (2029) — an internal inconsistency this page reports rather than resolves.
      - superscript:
        - link "[24]":
          - /url: "#ref-24"

        - text: 2; south and north sides of the Wenhua 1st Road–Qingshan Road intersection
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: National Taiwan Sport University is named for the university it serves and is the first underground station heading south from
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: ; the Railway Bureau's own architecture report and
      - link "TYMC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/tymc/
      - text: "'s station siting both place the reason for going underground here as avoiding an excessive grade change on the approach, since the line runs elevated directly above Wenhua 1st Road through Guishan District on either side of it."
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The underground station and its 940 m cut-and-cover section plus a 170 m excavation section were built under civil package CU01, recorded as 99.58% complete at the end of the reporting year in a Railway Bureau annual report.
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
    - paragraph:
      - text: No rail interchange is established at this station by any source read for this page. TYMC's own timetable page does not list A7 among the express (直達車) stops; only the commuter (普通車) service, calling at every station, serves this stop.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - paragraph:
      - text: TYMC's own station page gives the address as Wenhua 1st Road No. 688 in Guishan District, with two exits on the south and north sides of the Wenhua 1st Road–Qingshan Road intersection.
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: The Railway Bureau's architecture report groups this station with the two airport terminal stations, the not-yet-open Terminal 3 station, Airport Hotel and Huanbei under a single underground design contract, DU01, covering six stations rather than treating each as a separate design commission.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: National Taiwan Sport University opened with the rest of the initial line on 2 March 2017.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: It sits within Guishan District,
      - link "Taoyuan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taoyuan/
      - text: ", alongside Chang Gung Memorial Hospital — the only two current Airport MRT stations in that district."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
    - paragraph:
      - text: TDX's own committed route data places A7 17.403 km along route A-1 from Taipei Main Station by cumulative surveyed distance, the same measure this project uses for every station on the line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"

- main:

  - article:
    - heading "Ticketing and fares How bus fare stages (段) actually work" [level=1]:
      - img "Ticketing and fares"
      - text: How bus fare stages (段) actually work
    - paragraph: Taipei and New Taipei buses do not charge one flat fare. They charge by the number of fare "segments" (段) a trip crosses, and where those segment points fall is not published as one complete list anywhere — only two examples are ever officially named.
    - region "Quick facts":
      - text: How bus fare stages (段) actually work
      - term: Legal basis
      - definition:
        - text: 臺北市公共汽車客運業營運管理自治條例, Article 11
        - superscript:
          - link "[2]":
            - /url: "#ref-2"
      - term: Full fare
      - definition:
        - text: NT$15 per segment
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - term: Student fare (EasyCard)
      - definition:
        - text: NT$12 per segment
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - term: Concessionary fare
      - definition:
        - text: NT$8 per segment
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - term: On-board ticket sales
      - definition:
        - text: None — cash or e-ticket only, no change given
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
    - navigation "On this page":
      - paragraph: On this page
      - list:
        - listitem:
          - link "The rule, and its legal basis":
            - /url: "#the-rule-and-its-legal-basis"
        - listitem:
          - link "What a segment actually costs":
            - /url: "#what-a-segment-actually-costs"
        - listitem:
          - link "Where the segment points actually are":
            - /url: "#where-the-segment-points-actually-are"
        - listitem:
          - link "How crossing multiple segments is counted":
            - /url: "#how-crossing-multiple-segments-is-counted"
        - listitem:
          - link "How many segments does a route actually have?":
            - /url: "#how-many-segments-does-a-route-actually-have"
        - listitem:
          - link "How this interacts with transfers and the regional pass":
            - /url: "#how-this-interacts-with-transfers-and-the-regional-pass"
        - listitem:
          - link "Specifications":
            - /url: "#specifications"
        - listitem:
          - link "References":
            - /url: "#references"
    - paragraph:
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: and New Taipei's joint-operation buses do not charge a flat fare. They charge by
      - strong: 段 (段次)
      - text: — fare segments — and a rider who does not know where the segment points fall on their own route has no reliable way to predict whether a trip costs one fare or two before boarding.
    - heading "The rule, and its legal basis" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Under 臺北市公共汽車客運業營運管理自治條例 (the Taipei City ordinance governing bus operations), Article 11 sets the underlying principle: a bus operator's fare should be uniform in principle, but a route with a longer run may instead be charged by segment or by distance"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . Article 9 of the same ordinance requires that the fare segment point (or buffer zone) be posted on the physical stop sign itself, alongside the terminus name, first/last bus times and headway
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: — the segment structure is not meant to be a surprise at tap-out, at least not by design.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Taipei's Public Transport Office states the practical version of the rule plainly: 「本市聯營公車依據「臺北市公共汽車客運業營運管理自治條例」第11條規 定採分段收費制，同時參採橋樑、河流等自然分界及重要轉運點（如華中橋、臺北車 站等）訂定，並無長度及站數之強制要求，跨越分段點即加收1段票」"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: ". In English: segment points are sited using natural boundaries — bridges, rivers — and major transfer hubs, with"
      - strong: no fixed rule for how long a segment has to be or how many stops it must cover
      - text: . Crossing a segment point (or its buffer zone) simply adds one segment's fare.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "New Taipei's own city buses run on the identical mechanic. The joint Taipei/New Taipei bus portal states it for both cities in one sentence: 「雙北市區公車係依路段分段收費，搭乘2段票(含)以上路線之車輛，若跨越分段點 (或分段緩衝區)，應加收1段票」"
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: .
    - heading "What a segment actually costs" [level=2]
    - table:
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Fare class Cash EasyCard/e-ticket":
          - columnheader "Fare class"
          - columnheader "Cash"
          - columnheader "EasyCard/e-ticket":
            - link "EasyCard":
              - /url: /ticketing/guides/cards-passes-and-fares/
            - text: /e-ticket
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Full fare NT$15 NT$15[3]":
          - cell "Full fare"
          - cell "NT$15"
          - cell "NT$15[3]":
            - text: NT$15
            - superscript:
              - link "[3]":
                - /url: "#ref-3"
        - row "Student NT$15 NT$12 (an 8-fold/20%-off card rate)[3]":
          - cell "Student"
          - cell "NT$15"
          - cell "NT$12 (an 8-fold/20%-off card rate)[3]":
            - text: NT$12 (an 8-fold/20%-off card rate)
            - superscript:
              - link "[3]":
                - /url: "#ref-3"
        - row "Concessionary (elderly, disabled/companion, eligible children) NT$8 NT$8[3]":
          - cell "Concessionary (elderly, disabled/companion, eligible children)"
          - cell "NT$8"
          - cell "NT$8[3]":
            - text: NT$8
            - superscript:
              - link "[3]":
                - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "That per-segment rate is confirmed twice, independently: once by the joint government fare portal, and once by the operators' own trade association, which publishes the identical NT$15/12/8 structure on its own site"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . Buses do not sell tickets on board and do not give change — the fare portal is explicit that payment is cash
      - emphasis: or
      - text: stored-value card, with no other option, and no change is made for cash overpayment
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . Children under 115cm ride free outright; children 115cm or taller but under 6 with an identity document also ride free; one fare-paying adult may bring up to four such children at no charge
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: .
    - heading "Where the segment points actually are" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Officially, not many are named at all. Taipei's Public Transport Office's own FAQ gives exactly two worked examples: 華中橋 (Huazhong Bridge) and 臺北車站 (Taipei Main Station)"
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . No government source fetched for this page publishes a complete list of every segment point on the network — Article 9 requires each one to be posted at its own stop, but that is necessarily a stop-by-stop disclosure, not a single published index.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Chinese Wikipedia's own article on Taipei's city buses offers a longer, nine-location list of what it calls "common" segment points —
      - link "Shilin":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r16/
      - text: (士林),
      - link "Dazhi":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br14/
      - text: (大直),
      - link "Taipei Bridge":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/o13/
      - text: (臺北橋), Taipei Main Station, the Zhonghua Road north/south stops, Wanhua (萬華), the wholesale produce market (果菜市場),
      - link "Gongguan":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g07/
      - text: (公館), and
      - link "Songshan":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g19/
      - text: (松山) — mostly major transfer hubs or bridgeheads at the old Taipei City/County boundary
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . That list is not attached to any citation on the Wikipedia page itself, and it notably does
      - strong: not
      - text: include Huazhong Bridge, which is one of only two locations the regulator names directly
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . Both lists are published here as what they are — one official but minimal, one fuller but unverified — rather than merged into a single confident list.
    - heading "How crossing multiple segments is counted" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Chinese Wikipedia's article on New Taipei's own city buses gives a worked example of the counting logic. For a corridor running through zones A, B and C, with B as the segment point: riding within one zone, or from A to B, or from B to C, is one segment; riding all the way from A to C is two segments (the single-segment fare, doubled)"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . On a longer corridor with two segment points, A–B–C–D–E, both B and D count as crossing points
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . This is an illustrative example rather than a government fare rule in itself, but it does not contradict, and directly illustrates, the primary rule already confirmed above.
    - heading "How many segments does a route actually have?" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "There is no fixed one-to-four-segment ceiling. Counting directly over this project's own already-committed New Taipei route-service data — 562 routes with a published fare row — segment counts run from 1 to 8: 128 routes are 1-segment, 77 are 2-segment, 37 are 3-segment, 13 are 4-segment, 8 are 5-segment, 3 are 6-segment, and 3 reach 8 segments, alongside a handful of free routes"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . Taipei-proper's committed bus dataset has no comparable segment-count field, so its distribution remains TBC.
    - heading "How this interacts with transfers and the regional pass" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The bidirectional MRT–bus transfer discount — NT$8 for an ordinary card, NT$6 for a student card, NT$4 for a welfare card, within a 60-minute window — applies against a segment fare the same way it applies against any bus fare
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: . That same FAQ's own title is explicit that the discount excludes "distance-charged buses" (里程收費公車) — a separate, named fare category outside the segmented system described above; its own fare mechanics remain TBC.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The TPASS 基北北桃1200都會通 regional pass sidesteps the segment system entirely for a pass holder: its own operating notice confirms unlimited rides at unlimited distance on both Taipei's joint-operation network and New Taipei's city buses"
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: . A pass holder does not pay per segment at all — there is no separate multi-segment surcharge or cap to interact with.

      - paragraph: 7 of 9 sources on this page are primary — published by the operator, the builder or government.

          - text: "公車之分段點決定之依據為何? primary Taipei Public Transport Office ( 臺北市公共運輸處 ) accessed 2026-08-20 The regulator's own FAQ, fetched and quoted in full.     - paragraph:
      - text: Two different companies issue the two cards that work almost everywhere in Taiwan, and neither is a government agency. EasyCard came out of
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: "'s own metro company; iPass began life as Kaohsiung Metro's own card. The regional commuter pass that sits on top of them is younger still, run by"
      - link "Taipei Metro":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: on behalf of four separate city governments, and it is one of the few transit policy changes anywhere that made the product both cheaper and broader at the same time
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: .
    - heading "EasyCard — a metro operator that founded a payments company" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: EasyCard Corporation (悠遊卡股份有限公司) has NT$700 million in registered capital and was established in March 2000
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: . Its predecessor, 台北智慧卡票證股份有限公司 (Taipei Smart Card Corporation), was set up on 25 February 2000 by Taipei Metro itself, together with the Taipei City Government's parking authority, Greater Taipei's bus operators, and a vendor consortium — 神通 (Mitac), 台新 (Taishin), 國泰世華 (Cathay United), 中信銀 (CTBC), 富邦 (Fubon), 三商行 and 所羅門科技 (Solomon Technology)
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . A metro operator founding the region's dominant payments company is an unusual origin story, and it explains why TRTC is still a named shareholder today, alongside the Taipei City Government, twelve Taipei-area bus operators and a roster of banks
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The card reached Taipei Metro in June 2002 — at ten stations initially — and went live system-wide across Greater Taipei's buses and the metro on 30 September 2002
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - text: . One million cards had been issued by that December
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: .
      - strong: The two Chinese Wikipedia articles about this launch do not agree with each other
      - text: ": one describes June as ten metro stations only, with September as the full system going live; the other describes June as the"
      - emphasis: entire
      - text: metro line already running, plus one bus route and fifteen car parks, with September described instead as the card going on general retail sale (「悠遊卡全面上市」)
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: . Both are read here in full and neither cites the other; this page carries the more specific account without treating that as resolving the disagreement.
    - paragraph:
      - text: By the company's own account, as of end-October 2022 it had
      - strong: 98.32 million cards in circulation
      - text: ", more than 9 million of them active, with NT$42.13 billion spent January–October that year and a 73.7% share of the stored-value market"
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . That is the most recent figure this page can source to the company directly; it listed on Taiwan's emerging stock market on 3 January 2023, under code 6035
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: . The card now reaches well beyond transport — convenience stores, supermarkets, dining, scenic-site admission, hospitals and clinics, government fee payment and library book loans, on top of High Speed Rail, TRA, intercity coaches,
      - link "YouBike":
        - /url: /bike/history/youbike/
      - text: and the
      - link "Blue Highway":
        - /url: /ferry/routes/blue-highway/
      - text: ferries
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - heading "iPass — Kaohsiung's card, not a Taipei one" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: iPass (一卡通) is not a Taipei product at all. It began as an electronic ticket issued directly by Kaohsiung Rapid Transit Corporation, first issued in December 2007 and activated with the opening of the Kaohsiung MRT Red Line on 9 March 2008
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: . A dedicated card company — 一卡通票證股份有限公司 — was approved by the Financial Supervisory Commission on 6 December 2013 and took over the ticketing business on 13 February 2014
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - superscript:
        - link "[6]":
          - /url: "#ref-6"
      - text: ", with shareholders including the Executive Yuan's National Development Fund, the Kaohsiung City Government, Union Bank of Taiwan and Kaohsiung Rapid Transit Corporation itself"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . It gained its own electronic-payment business licence in July 2017
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: . Today Taipei's own Public Transport Office names iPass, alongside EasyCard and icash (愛金卡), as one of the electronic tickets approved on the joint-operation bus network
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: — two cards from two different cities' metro operators, both now interchangeable across the same buses and trains.
    - 'heading "The regional pass: 基北北桃1200都會通" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current commuter pass is issued by Taipei Metro on behalf of four city governments — Keelung, Taipei, New Taipei and
      - link "Taoyuan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taoyuan/
      - text: — under the Executive Yuan's public-transport promotion programme
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . It costs
      - strong: NT$1,200 for 30 days
      - text: ", unlimited rides, unlimited distance, within that zone"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . It replaced a Taipei/New Taipei-only pass that had cost
      - strong: NT$1,280
      - text: and covered less
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: — a rare case of a public transport product getting both cheaper and broader in the same change.
    - heading "What it actually covers" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The operating notice is specific, and worth quoting rather than summarising
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: ":"
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: Metro and light rail
        - text: ": every"
        - link "New Taipei Metro":
          - /url: /rail/operators/ntmc/
        - text: and Taipei Metro line, plus the
        - link "Taoyuan Airport MRT":
          - /url: /rail/metro/lines/airport-mrt/
        - text: .
      - listitem:
        - strong: City buses
        - text: ": Keelung, New Taipei and Taoyuan city bus routes, and Taipei's joint-operation network."
      - listitem:
        - strong: TRA
        - text: ", but only between named stations — the main line from Keelung to Taoyuan's Xinfu station, the Yilan Line between Badu and Fulong, and the Shen'ao and Pingxi branch lines — and"
        - strong: not
        - text: "on reserved-seat-only services that sell no standing tickets, which the notice names explicitly: 觀光 (sightseeing), 團體 (group), 太魯閣, 普悠瑪 and EMU3000 trains."
      - listitem:
        - strong: Highway and intercity coaches
        - text: ", on a named list of more than ninety route codes across roughly a dozen operators, from 國光客運 to 基隆客運 to 葛瑪蘭客運."
      - listitem:
        - strong: YouBike
        - text: ", with the first 30 minutes free at Taipei and New Taipei docks, and the first 60 minutes free at Taoyuan docks"
        - superscript:
          - link "[7]":
            - /url: "#ref-7"
        - text: .
    - heading "One card, one pass at a time" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: A single EasyCard can carry only one active monthly pass — the notice's own words are that a card can be set to one product 「僅能設定一種定期票」, and a rider has to wait for the current pass to expire before setting up a different one
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: ". That rule is why the transition from the old 1,280 pass required a genuine choice rather than simply layering the new pass on top: a card already carrying an active 1,280 pass had to have it cancelled and refunded before the 1,200 pass could be set on the same card"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: .
    - heading "You do not need a special \"TPASS card\"" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The pass is not tied to any particular physical card. The operating notice lists the whole family of EasyCard products it can be loaded onto: ordinary cards, co-branded bank cards, EasyCard Debit cards, Samsung Wallet EasyCards, SuperCard, telecom-issued EasyCards, student cards, and digital student IDs"
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: . Co-branded and Debit cards need at least 60 days of remaining validity to qualify, but nothing requires buying a distinct "TPASS" card to use the pass
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: .
      - strong: SuperCard specifically
      - text: is EasyCard's name for a newer card generation the company describes as 「新一代悠遊卡，手機就是你的加值機」 — a card that can be topped up from a phone rather than only at a machine
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
      - text: — and it is one option among the family above, not a requirement.
    - paragraph:
      - text: What
      - emphasis: is
      - text: "sold separately is a commemorative TPASS-branded EasyCard, issued by the central government's Directorate General of Highways: it costs NT$100 to buy, and that NT$100 is refunded as an account top-up once the buyer completes real-name registration and taps the card at a convenience store"
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
      - text: . That refund is the source of the "the card is effectively free" claim that circulates about the pass — it is correct, but it describes a specific commemorative card, not a requirement to use the pass at all.
    - heading "The launch, dated" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Presale for the TPASS EasyCard opened at four convenience-store chains on 18 May 2023; card collection and 1,200-pass presale at MRT stations began 15 June 2023; the predecessor 1,280 pass was withdrawn from sale on 30 June 2023; and the new pass, with its expanded coverage, went live on 1 July 2023
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: ". On launch day TRTC put its own scale in numbers: 1,360 fare gates and 645 ticket machines across the system configured to sell and refund the new pass"
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: .
    - heading "The 1,280 pass's refund rule was not as simple as it sounds" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: New Taipei City's own operating document for the old 1,280 pass gives its general, voluntary refund formula as the pass price
      - strong: minus a front-loaded daily deduction — NT$180 for the first day, NT$130 for every day after — minus a NT$20 handling fee
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: ". That is not a flat pro-rata split, and it is not fee-free: cancelling early cost proportionally more than cancelling late. A separate clause in the same document, covering only a card that has"
      - emphasis: physically failed
      - text: through no fault of the holder, does use a simple pro-rata formula with no stated fee — pass price minus (pass price × elapsed days ÷ 30)
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: . The two are easy to conflate, and this page keeps them separate rather than publishing the more generous one as the general rule.
    - heading "Taipei Metro's own fare structure" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Underneath any card or pass sits Taipei Metro's base fare system, which is banded by distance rather than by zone or station count. The system's own fare table gives ten tiers, each five dollars apart, running from the minimum to the maximum single fare

    - paragraph:
      - text: That is the full/adult fare. Two discounts apply at a flat
      - strong: 40% of the full fare per ride
      - text: ": the children's fare, for ages 6–11 with a digital student ID or a recognised children's card"
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: ", and the concessionary fare on 社福卡 — 敬老卡 (senior), 愛心卡 (disability) and 愛心陪伴卡 (companion) cards. Below age 6, or below 115cm regardless of age, a child rides free alongside a fare-paying passenger, and one adult can bring up to four such children"
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Taipei-registered 敬老卡/愛心卡 holders get a separate, richer benefit on top of the 40% floor:"
      - strong: 600 points a month
      - text: ", one point worth NT$1, usable across TRTC, New Taipei's light rail and"
      - link "Circular Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/circular-line/
      - text: ","
      - link "Maokong Gondola":
        - /url: /rail/cable/lines/maokong-gondola/
      - text: ", Taipei's joint-operation buses, and YouBike rental within Taipei City"
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: . Points do not carry over to the next month, and once they run out the fare reverts to 40% off on rail and 50% off on bus
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: . A 愛心陪伴卡 used on its own, without the primary card tapping immediately before it, earns no points of its own
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: .
    - heading "Transferring between MRT and bus" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "A bidirectional transfer between Taipei Metro and a Taipei or New Taipei joint-operation bus, completed within 60 minutes, discounts the second leg:"
      - strong: NT$8 for an ordinary card, NT$6 for a student card, NT$4 for a social-welfare card
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: . Taipei's Public Transport Office states the same NT$8/NT$6 figures independently on its own FAQ page
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: — agreement between the regulator and the operator, not one source repeating itself. The discount does not extend to distance-charged buses, or to any other mode — YouBike, the Danhai and Ankeng light rail lines, TRA, Maokong Gondola, intercity coaches, High Speed Rail or taxis are all outside it
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: .
    - 'heading "A new scheme: cashback for frequent riders" [level=3]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: Separately from any pass, TRTC introduced a frequent-rider cashback scheme on 3 January 2026, for full-fare stored-value or QR-code riders only — 社福卡 and other already-discounted card types do not qualify
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: . It is based on the
      - emphasis: previous
      - text: "calendar month's ride count:"
      - strong: 11–20 rides earns 5% cashback, 21–40 earns 10%, 41 or more earns 15%
      - text: ", calculated against that month's total fare spend and credited automatically to the same card's e-wallet on the first tap of the following month, valid for one year from the 1st of the crediting month"
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: .
    - 'heading "EasyCard, iPASS and icash: the overlap has edges" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current Taipei Metro payment table, fetched on 23 August 2026, lists EasyCard, iPASS and icash as stored-value cards, but marks the NT$1,200 TPASS as an EasyCard product rather than a pass available on all three cards
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: iPASS's own current acceptance directory lists Taipei, New Taipei, Taoyuan,
      - link "Taichung":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taichung/
      - text: and Kaohsiung rail and bus systems, TRA, and YouBike, while warning that acceptance can still vary by named operator or route
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: TRA's current electronic-ticket rules accept EasyCard, iPASS and icash on the listed island and branch-line services, but exclude sightseeing, group, Taroko, Puyuma, EMU3000 and other trains for which the rule says electronic tickets are not valid
      - superscript:
        - link "[24]":
          - /url: "#ref-24"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The three cards therefore overlap on Taipei Metro and much of the ordinary regional network without being interchangeable products: the TPASS container is EasyCard-only, and iPASS publishes a wider national acceptance directory than any single Taipei operator's fare table"
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: EasyCard's own company page lists non-transit uses including convenience stores, supermarkets, dining, attractions, hospitals, government fees and libraries
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: iPASS's current directory separately lists non-transit categories including convenience stores, supermarkets, shopping, dining, attractions, cinemas, hotels, libraries, government fees, school services, medical services, donations and sports centres
      - superscript:
        - link "[21]":
          - /url: "#ref-21"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current icash transport PDF establishes selected bus acceptance, but it is not a complete current Taipei-region acceptance or refund catalogue, so this guide does not infer broader icash non-transit coverage from it
      - superscript:
        - link "[31]":
          - /url: "#ref-31"
      - text: .
    - 'heading "Concessions: the identity document matters" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Taipei Metro ticket page retrieved on 23 August 2026 defines concessionary eligibility for nationals aged 65 or over, a disability certificate holder and one companion, and Taipei or New Taipei Indigenous residents aged 55 or over with the required household documentation
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The same page defines the Taipei/New Taipei child ticket for a locally registered child aged 6 to under 12 with household-registration proof, while the existing metro fare guidance records the separate free-travel threshold for a child under 6 or under 115 cm accompanied by a fare-paying passenger
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "TRA's current rules use a different national definition: senior nationals are 65 or over, children are 6 to under 12, and a disability certificate holder may travel with the necessary companion at the concessionary rate"
      - superscript:
        - link "[24]":
          - /url: "#ref-24"
      - text: .
    - heading "Single-journey tokens and refunds" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Taipei Metro single-journey fare retrieved on 23 August 2026 is NT$20–65, valid on the day of issue, and sold by station vending machines and station information counters, with a QR single ticket also available through Taipei Metro Go
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The token is a contactless ticket: the gate reads it at entry and recovers it at the exit gate, so it is not a souvenir to carry through the journey"
      - superscript:
        - link "[27]":
          - /url: "#ref-27"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: An unused single ticket can be refunded only on its purchase day, while a used ticket or one left after a midway exit is not refundable under the passenger regulations retrieved on 23 August 2026
      - superscript:
        - link "[28]":
          - /url: "#ref-28"
      - text: .
    - heading "Deposits and stored-value refunds" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: EasyCard's current refund FAQ requires the card to be locked before a termination refund, charges NT$20 unless the card has been used at least five times and held for at least three months, and gives no balance refund for an anonymous lost card
      - superscript:
        - link "[25]":
          - /url: "#ref-25"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: For an EasyCard deposit product, the current formula is refundable deposit plus usable balance minus the refund fee, with the card cost also deducted when the card is damaged
      - superscript:
        - link "[26]":
          - /url: "#ref-26"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "iPASS has no rental or deposit system: its current product page says only the stored balance is refundable, not the product purchase price, and its return process can charge NT$20 when the card has not met the five-use or three-month threshold"
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: iPASS's current return process requires the physical card to be sent by registered mail, and an anonymous lost card is not a recoverable balance under the product rules
      - superscript:
        - link "[23]":
          - /url: "#ref-23"
      - superscript:
        - link "[22]":
          - /url: "#ref-22"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The fetched icash transport document does not establish a current complete icash refund rule, so that figure and procedure remain TBC rather than being borrowed from EasyCard or iPASS
      - superscript:
        - link "[31]":
          - /url: "#ref-31"
      - text: .
    - 'heading "The NT$1,200 TPASS: coverage, purchase and take-up" [level=2]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: The TPASS operating notice prices the 基北北桃 pass at NT$1,200 for 30 days of unlimited use on the named MRT and light-rail systems, municipal buses, the specified TRA segment, listed intercity-coach routes and YouBike coverage; the TRA and coach clauses contain their own route and train exclusions
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The notice does not list Blue Highway ferries among those named coverage categories, so this guide does not assume that a ferry fare is included in the pass without a separate operator or government confirmation
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current Taipei Metro purchase instructions say to select TPASS/1200 at the station process, and explain how an active 1280 pass on the same EasyCard is handled when the 1200 pass is purchased
      - superscript:
        - link "[29]":
          - /url: "#ref-29"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The latest take-up figure found in a full official page is dated 19 February 2025: Taipei City reported cumulative issuance above nine million passes and more than 700 million uses, with the page updated on 13 March 2025"
      - superscript:
        - link "[30]":
          - /url: "#ref-30"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Those are dated cumulative totals, not a 2026 monthly sales rate, so no newer growth figure is inferred here
      - superscript:
        - link "[30]":
          - /url: "#ref-30"
      - text: .

            - /url: https://www.traffic.ntpc.gov.tw/userfiles/1130901/files/%E5%85%AC%E5%85%B1%E9%81%8B%E8%BC%B8%E5%AE%9A%E6%9C%9F%E7%A5%A8%E8%A9%B3%E7%B4%B0%E8%AA%AA%E6%98%8E(1).pdf
          - text: "公共運輸定期票詳細說明 primary 新北市政府交通局 (New Taipei City Department of Transportation) accessed 2026-08-12 The predecessor 1,280 pass's own operating rules, read in full as a PDF. Source for its NT$1,280 price and coverage, and — the finding that corrects an unsourced claim in this project's own lead notes — its general refund formula: pass price minus a front-loaded daily deduction (NT$180 day one, NT$130 each day after) minus a NT$20 handling fee. A separate clause, for a physically failed card only, uses a simple pro-rata formula with no fee."
        - listitem:
          - link "Taipei Metro system fare table":
            - /url: https://www-ws.gov.taipei/Download.ashx?u=LzAwMS9VcGxvYWQvNDA1L3JlbGZpbGUvMTgyODgvNzYxOC8xMWEzNWM2Mi1jZmQ2LTQzYjctOGVmMi1mMjFjOTE2MjU4OGMucGRm&n=56Wo5YO56KGoKHBkZuaqlCkucGRm&icon=..pdf
          - text: 臺北捷運系統票價表 primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-12 The full station-to-station fare grid, linked from TRTC's own fare page, read directly rather than summarised. Its own printed key gives the ten distance bands this page uses (「小（等）於5公里 20元」 through 「大於31公里 65元」). The document's own print date reads 2020/1/6; carried as the current table because it is the one TRTC's live fare page still links to.
        - listitem:
          - link "How are the point deductions/charges calculated for senior, disability and companion cards on Taipei Metro, New Taipei light rail and joint-operation buses?":
            - /url: https://www.metro.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=566DA580861CEE77&s=41B78C4788395C41
          - text: "臺北市及新北市之敬老卡、愛心卡、愛心陪伴卡搭乘臺北捷運、新北輕軌(淡海輕軌及安坑輕軌)及臺北地區聯營公車等運具之扣點/扣款方式為何？ primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-12 Fetched in full twice to settle a conflict against a search-engine-generated summary of the same page, which had stated 480 points. Both direct fetches returned 600 points verbatim: 「設籍臺北市：敬老卡及愛心卡：每月享有600點(每點折算1元)」."
        - listitem:
          - link "How do Taipei/New Taipei children aged 6 and above but under 12 get a fare discount on Taipei Metro?":
            - /url: https://www.metro.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=566DA580861CEE77&sms=87415A8B9CE81B16&s=00695D3417F06354
          - text: 臺北市/新北市6 歲以上未滿 12 歲兒童搭乘臺北捷運如何享有票價優惠? primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-12 Source for the 40% (4折) child fare with a digital student ID, children's discount card or New Taipei children's card, and for children from other counties paying the full adult fare. Confirmed on a direct, targeted fetch that this page does not itself state the under-6/under-115cm free-ride rule — that is on a separate FAQ page, cited next.
        - listitem:
          - link "What are the eligibility requirements for free travel on Taipei Metro?":
            - /url: https://www.metro.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=566DA580861CEE77&sms=87415A8B9CE81B16&s=659D91B390310152
          - text: 搭乘捷運免票資格為何？ primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-12 Source for children under 6, or under 115cm regardless of age, riding free when accompanied by a fare-paying passenger, one adult covering up to four such children, and the 115cm/ID threshold above which a child must show identification.
        - listitem:
          - link "What is the two-way transfer discount between MRT and bus (excluding distance-charged buses)? How is it deducted for each stored-value card type?":
            - /url: https://www.metro.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=566DA580861CEE77&sms=87415A8B9CE81B16&s=1CDFC00134A98701
          - text: 何謂捷運與公車（不含里程收費公車）間雙向轉乘優惠？儲值卡各票種雙向轉乘優惠如何扣款？ primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-12 Source for the NT$8/NT$6/NT$4 transfer discount by card type, the 60-minute window, and the list of modes the discount does not extend to (YouBike, Danhai/Ankeng light rail, TRA, Maokong Gondola, intercity coaches, THSR, taxis).
        - listitem:
          - link "Which electronic tickets are approved for Taipei's joint-operation buses, and what are their discounts?":
            - /url: https://pto.gov.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=6B4D38874E971F4B&s=368ADCCC65AB0818
          - text: 臺北市聯營公車所核備之電子票證及其優惠各為何? primary 臺北市公共運輸處 (Taipei Public Transport Office) accessed 2026-08-12 Names EasyCard, iPass and icash (愛金卡) as the approved cards, and independently states the same NT$8/NT$6 MRT–bus transfer amounts as TRTC's own FAQ — agreement between the regulator and the operator, not a single source repeated.
        - listitem:
          - link "SuperCard":
            - /url: https://www.easycard.com.tw/easycards?cls=1662119407
          - text: SuperCard 超級悠遊卡 primary EasyCard Corporation ( 悠遊卡股份有限公司 ) accessed 2026-08-12 EasyCard's own product page for SuperCard, source for the company's description of it as a newer card generation toppable from a phone (「新一代悠遊卡，手機就是你的加值機」). It is one option among the card family the megacity-notice PDF lists as eligible to carry the pass, not a synonym for it.
        - listitem:
          - link "Frequent-rider discount scheme":
            - /url: https://www.metro.taipei/cp.aspx?n=AB56163F79ECB2C2
          - text: 常客優惠方案 primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-12 Source for the scheme's 3 January 2026 start date, the 5%/10%/15% cashback tiers at 11–20/21–40/41+ rides in the prior month, the exclusion of welfare and already-discounted cards, and the one-year validity of the credited cashback.
        - listitem:
          - link "Taipei Metro multiple payment methods and discounts":
            - /url: https://web.metro.taipei/QRCode/multipayment/Discount/directions.html
          - text: 臺北捷運多元支付方式及優惠 primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The live payment comparison table. It lists EasyCard, iPASS and icash as stored-value cards for Taipei Metro and shows that the NT$1,200 pass is available only on EasyCard.
        - listitem:
          - link "Where can I use iPASS?":
            - /url: https://www.i-pass.com.tw/Range/Index/0?type=1
          - text: 一卡通使用範圍 primary 一卡通票證股份有限公司 (iPASS Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The current iPASS acceptance directory. It lists Taipei/New Taipei/Taoyuan/Taichung/Kaohsiung rail and bus systems, TRA, YouBike and the non-transit acceptance categories, with operator-specific caveats.
        - listitem:
          - link "Adult iPASS card":
            - /url: https://web.i-pass.com.tw/Page/Adult
          - text: 普通卡 primary 一卡通票證股份有限公司 (iPASS Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The current product page. It says the stored-value card has no rental or deposit system, starts with a zero balance, and refunds stored value rather than the product purchase price.
        - listitem:
          - link "iPASS card return process":
            - /url: https://www.i-pass.com.tw/Page/CardReturnProcess
          - text: 一卡通票證退卡流程 primary 一卡通票證股份有限公司 (iPASS Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The current return procedure. It requires the physical card by registered post and sets the NT$20 charge when the card has not been used at least five times or held for at least three months.
        - listitem:
          - link "Regulations for travel with electronic tickets":
            - /url: https://www.railway.gov.tw/tra-tip-web/tip/tip00C/tipC21/view?lang=zh_TW&proCode=8ae4cac3756b7b41017572e76e08178d&subCode=8ae4cac290f06c930190f390e6930537
          - text: 多卡通電子票證乘車營運規定 primary 臺灣鐵路股份有限公司 (Taiwan Railways Administration) accessed 2026-08-23 The live TRA rules, effective for travel from 23 June 2025. It covers EasyCard, iPASS and icash acceptance, train exclusions, no-seat-reservation operation, and the senior, child and disability concession categories.
        - listitem:
          - link "EasyCard refund FAQ":
            - /url: https://www.easycard.com.tw/faq?page=8
          - text: 悠遊卡退卡退費 primary 悠遊卡股份有限公司 (EasyCard Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The current card-termination rules. It requires card locking, charges NT$20 unless the five-use and three-month conditions are met, and gives no balance refund for an anonymous lost card.
        - listitem:
          - link "EasyCard deposit-card refund FAQ":
            - /url: https://www.easycard.com.tw/faq?page=11
          - text: "悠遊卡押金卡退費 primary 悠遊卡股份有限公司 (EasyCard Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The current deposit-card formulas: refundable deposit plus usable balance minus the refund fee, with the card cost also deducted for a damaged card."
        - listitem:
          - link "Taipei Metro ticket types":
            - /url: https://www.metro.taipei/cp.aspx?n=CEF54168B23F73B4&s=AD70DC4F6A708EA7
          - text: 臺北捷運票種說明 primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The current ticket page. It gives the NT$20–65 single-journey range, ticket validity, sales points, QR purchase option, and eligibility for child and concession tickets.
        - listitem:
          - link "Regulations for use of the Taipei Metro system":
            - /url: https://web.metro.taipei/QRCode/Regulations%20for%20Use%20of%20the%20Taipei%20Metro%20System-Chinese.pdf?date=20250924
          - text: 臺北捷運系統旅客須知 primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The current passenger-regulations PDF. It says an unused single ticket can be refunded only on its purchase day and that a used ticket or a ticket after a midway exit is not refundable.
        - listitem:
          - link "TPASS 1200 purchase instructions":
            - /url: https://web.metro.taipei/event/1200/Ticket1200.aspx?type=2
          - text: 基北北桃1200都會通購票說明 primary 臺北大眾捷運股份有限公司 (Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The current TRTC purchase instructions. They explain selecting TPASS/1200 and the automatic handling of an active 1280 pass on the same EasyCard.
        - listitem:
          - link "TPASS use reaches nine million cards":
            - /url: https://sec.gov.taipei/News_Content.aspx?n=49B4C3242CB7658C&s=30B81710E7FD062D&sms=72544237BBE4C5F6
          - text: 基北北桃1200都會通發行量突破900萬張 primary 臺北市政府 (Taipei City Government) accessed 2026-08-23 The city government's 19 February 2025 release, updated 13 March 2025. It reports cumulative issuance above nine million and total uses above 700 million at that date.
        - listitem:
          - link "icash transport acceptance list":
            - /url: https://www.icash.com.tw/pdf/icash_trans.pdf
          - text: 愛金卡交通運輸使用範圍 primary 愛金卡股份有限公司 (icash Corporation) accessed 2026-08-23 The current transport PDF fetched from icash. It lists selected bus operators and does not establish a complete current Taipei-region non-transit or refund catalogue; the guide preserves that limitation.
    - paragraph: "Last updated: 2026-08-23"

    - paragraph:
      - link "Taipei Metro":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: ’s first published fares were NT$20, NT$25, NT$30 and NT$35 when the
      - link "Muzha Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/wenhu-line/
      - text: opened on 28 March 1996.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - text: The current TRTC data set is a station-to-station record in the NT$20–65 range and identifies the
      - link "Circular Line":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/circular-line/
      - text: Phase 1 charge from 1 March 2020 as the basis of the current published data.
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
    - heading "Taipei Metro fares" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The opening fare is the anchor: four bands, not the ten bands in the current fare table."
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
      - text: The official fare-setting paper says the distance-banded price had remained unchanged for more than ten years when written, but it does not provide a gazette-by-gazette list of every later adjustment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[2]":
          - /url: "#ref-2"
    - table:
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Date Fare event Evidence boundary":
          - columnheader "Date"
          - columnheader "Fare event"
          - columnheader "Evidence boundary"
      - rowgroup:
        - 'row "28 Mar 1996 Muzha Line opened with NT$20, NT$25, NT$30 and NT$35 fares.[1] Opening gazette itself: TBC."':
          - cell "28 Mar 1996"
          - cell "Muzha Line opened with NT$20, NT$25, NT$30 and NT$35 fares.[1]":
            - text: Muzha Line opened with NT$20, NT$25, NT$30 and NT$35 fares.
            - superscript:
              - link "[1]":
                - /url: "#ref-1"
          - 'cell "Opening gazette itself: TBC."'
        - 'row "1 Mar 2020 Circular Phase 1: NT$20 to 5 km, then published distance increments, up to NT$65 above 31 km.[6] Official fare notice, distinct from the open-data mirror.[5]"':
          - cell "1 Mar 2020"
          - 'cell "Circular Phase 1: NT$20 to 5 km, then published distance increments, up to NT$65 above 31 km.[6]"':
            - text: "Circular Phase 1: NT$20 to 5 km, then published distance increments, up to NT$65 above 31 km."
            - superscript:
              - link "[6]":
                - /url: "#ref-6"
          - cell "Official fare notice, distinct from the open-data mirror.[5]":
            - text: Official fare notice, distinct from the open-data mirror.
            - superscript:
              - link "[5]":
                - /url: "#ref-5"
        - row "Current dataset TRTC publishes the current station-to-station grid through 31 Mar 2026.[5] Current publication, not a dated change gazette.":
          - cell "Current dataset"
          - cell "TRTC publishes the current station-to-station grid through 31 Mar 2026.[5]":
            - text: TRTC publishes the current station-to-station grid through 31 Mar 2026.
            - superscript:
              - link "[5]":
                - /url: "#ref-5"
          - cell "Current publication, not a dated change gazette."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The 1996 and 2020 rows measure different scopes: opening"
      - link "Muzha":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br02/
      - text: service versus the later integrated network.
      - superscript:
        - link "[1]":
          - /url: "#ref-1"
      - superscript:
        - link "[5]":
          - /url: "#ref-5"
      - text: Both values are published; neither is averaged away.
    - heading "Transfer discounts and concessions" [level=2]
    - paragraph: "The official report supplies the strongest dated sequence found:"
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - strong: "25 November 1996:"
        - text: transfer vouchers began, with an initial NT$4 discount.
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - listitem:
        - strong: "1 July 1999:"
        - text: stored-value tickets replaced vouchers, allowing a one-way free transfer within two hours.
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - listitem:
        - strong: "1 November 2003:"
        - text: the first two-way
        - link "EasyCard":
          - /url: /ticketing/guides/cards-passes-and-fares/
        - text: stage gave NT$8 to a full fare and NT$6 to a student card.
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - listitem:
        - strong: "27 December 2003:"
        - text: the second stage added a NT$4 welfare-card discount.
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
      - listitem:
        - strong: "1 April 2005:"
        - text: the window became one hour while the discount stayed unchanged.
        - superscript:
          - link "[3]":
            - /url: "#ref-3"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current bus portal publishes NT$15 per segment, NT$12 for a student EasyCard segment and NT$8 for concessions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: TRTC’s current FAQ gives MRT–bus discounts of NT$8, NT$6 and NT$4 within 60 minutes.
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - text: The old report’s one hour and the current FAQ’s 60 minutes are the same duration, retained without inventing a separate change.
    - heading "Bus fares" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - link "Taipei":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/taipei/
      - text: and New Taipei buses use segment fares, not one flat price for every journey.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: The current passenger table is NT$15 full fare per segment, NT$12 for a student EasyCard segment and NT$8 for elderly, disabled/companion and eligible-child concessions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[7]":
          - /url: "#ref-7"
      - text: Taipei PTO records the latest joint-operation bus operating-rate approval as 1 July 2020 while passenger fares stayed at 15/12/8 and the city subsidised the difference.
      - superscript:
        - link "[8]":
          - /url: "#ref-8"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "This is a measurement conflict, not a price contradiction: operating rate is the regulated cost/revenue figure, while passenger fare is what the rider pays. The historical report records a 1997 bus-rate-related transfer-discount change, but a complete gazette-backed chronology of every passenger-fare adjustment remains TBC."
      - superscript:
        - link "[3]":
          - /url: "#ref-3"
    - heading "New Taipei Metro and the trial line" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current linked
      - link "NTMC":
        - /url: /rail/operators/ntmc/
      - text: tables publish Danhai station-pair fares of NT$20–30, Ankeng fares of NT$20–25 and Circular Line fares of NT$20–40.
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: These are current station-pair tables, not a claim that each line has held one fare since opening.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The
      - link "Sanying":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/sanying-line/
      - text: page says electronic-ticket users ride free from 16–31 August during trial operation while other passengers buy a single ticket.
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: Its fetched HTML does not publish a normal post-trial station-pair table, so that value is TBC rather than an inference from another line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
    - heading "Passes and recent rebates" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: TRTC’s chronology records the NT$1,280 30-day unlimited pass from 16 April 2018.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
      - text: The Highway Bureau records the NT$1,200 TPASS launch on 1 July 2023 and its named MRT, light-rail, bus, TRA, coach and
      - link "YouBike":
        - /url: /bike/history/youbike/
      - text: coverage.
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: The predecessor ended sales on 30 June 2023.
      - superscript:
        - link "[4]":
          - /url: "#ref-4"
    - paragraph:
      - text: TPASS 2.0 is a 2025 frequent-user rebate programme, while TRTC separately publishes its own ride-count cashback scheme beginning 3 January 2026.
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: Neither is rewritten as a change to the underlying station-to-station fare.
    - heading "Accessibility" [level=2]
    - paragraph:
      - text: TRTC’s fetched station API covers all 121 records returned by its station-label endpoint and preserves station-specific lift/ramp, accessible-toilet, tactile-paving and stair anti-slip fields.
      - superscript:

    - heading "Export, not domestic VSCC qualification" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The first export shipment — 20 buses to Guatemala — cleared customs 8 February 2023 and shipped two days later, arriving after a 42-day voyage on 30 March, deployed by operating partners Innovate Group and Luka Electric Group in Antigua and Mixco
      - superscript:
        - link "[9]":
          - /url: "#ref-9"
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: . A magazine account reports unverified order commitments of 100 buses/year from Guatemala and 200 buses/year from Paraguay, at a cited unit price of USD 450,000 — figures not checked against any contract document
      - superscript:
        - link "[10]":
          - /url: "#ref-10"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong: 唐榮車輛科技 does not appear on any VSCC electric-bus qualified-model register checked for this site
      - text: — current, lapsed-certificate, or the earlier demonstration-programme list — see the
      - link "VSCC qualified-model registry":
        - /url: /bus/models/vscc-qualified-registry/
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - text: . This directly contradicts a 2021-era secondary claim that Tang Eng was "among the first companies to pass the electric bus demonstration programme vehicle qualification review"
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: . Whether Tang Eng never qualified domestically, or qualified and was later dropped from the register entirely — rather than moved to the lapsed-certificate section where other manufacturers' expired models do appear — is not explained by any source found
      - superscript:
        - link "[11]":
          - /url: "#ref-11"
      - superscript:
        - link "[12]":
          - /url: "#ref-12"
      - text: .

    - heading "What the primary sources establish, and what they do not" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Control Yuan independently corroborates four qualified manufacturers as of 29 November 2024 — 成運, 華德, 創奕 and 鴻華 — with combined planned capacity of 5,960 vehicles by the end of 2025
      - superscript:
        - link "[13]":
          - /url: "#ref-13"
      - text: . 唐榮車輛科技 (Tang Eng) does not appear on any of the four register snapshots checked for this page, current or lapsed — see
      - link "its own page":
        - /url: /bus/models/tang-eng-alighter/
      - text: for the secondary source this contradicts.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The regulation governing the process, 車輛型式安全審驗管理辦法, is issued under 公路法第63條第5項 and requires domestic bus body-builders to submit chassis construction specifications, and requires Class A/B buses to submit durability-performance test verification
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - text: . Its own text defines the certifying body generically as "a domestic vehicle-professional institution entrusted by MOTC" rather than naming VSCC specifically — VSCC's own page is what identifies VSCC as that body
      - superscript:
        - link "[14]":
          - /url: "#ref-14"
      - superscript:
        - link "[15]":
          - /url: "#ref-15"
      - text: .
    - paragraph: This register gives model names, type codes, applicants and route/use classes — it does not give unit counts, fleet allocations, or vehicle-by-vehicle registrations. Taiwan publishes no equivalent census; per-model deployment figures on this site come from operator and news records, not from this registry, and are marked as such.

    - heading "Water operations recorded by public sources" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Taipei City emergency-support plan lists 好樂好 among the city's
      - link "Blue Highway":
        - /url: /ferry/routes/blue-highway/
      - text: operators, names 葉志哲 as chairman and publishes 2558-5519 and 0937-185158 as emergency contacts
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: . Its vessel table attributes 11 small vessels to the company and gives 19.93 tonnes, 12 knots and 1.2 metres in the first row
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: . The report is a dated planning record
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: ; it does not establish that 11 vessels remain in service today, and the remaining vessel rows are not reattributed here because the extracted table does not repeat the company name on each row
      - superscript:
        - link "[16]":
          - /url: "#ref-16"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: A 2004 Taipei Transportation Department announcement records a cross-city trial between Dadaocheng,
      - link "Guandu":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r25/
      - text: and Fisherman's Wharf
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: . It says 好樂好 planned to use the three passenger boats 飛魚一號, 飛魚五號 and 飛魚六號, with two weekday and six holiday departures, and publishes route-by-route fares and approximate journey times
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: . This is historical operating evidence, not a current timetable
      - superscript:
        - link "[17]":
          - /url: "#ref-17"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The 2020 official timetable records 好樂好 Dadaocheng–Tamsui sailings at NT$300 full fare and NT$150 half fare, plus Dadaocheng river cruises at NT$200 and NT$100, with operating days and departure times listed separately
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
      - text: . That timetable also says
      - link "EasyCard":
        - /url: /ticketing/guides/cards-passes-and-fares/
      - text: was accepted by 好樂好, while noting that operators' hours could change and passengers should confirm before travel
      - superscript:
        - link "[18]":
          - /url: "#ref-18"
      - text: . The Public Transportation Office's current FAQ says operators also offer non-fixed charters, dining and package trips, and lists a different 好樂好 service number, 02-2550-2339
      - superscript:
        - link "[19]":
          - /url: "#ref-19"
      - text: . The two published phone numbers are retained as a dated source conflict rather than silently selecting one.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The company's booking page currently advertises a regular Dadaocheng Wharf–Tamsui Wharf service of about 90 minutes that sails when reservations reach ten people, and its page lists monthly 2026 event entries
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
      - text: . That current listing is a booking condition, not a guarantee that every advertised departure will run; the page itself says the service is scheduled subject to the listed conditions
      - superscript:
        - link "[20]":
          - /url: "#ref-20"
      - text: .
