    - heading "Company history and legal identity" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Danan’s own profile says it was established in August 1969 by Yulon Motor and the Veterans Affairs Council, with early investment vehicles including Rongqiao and Xufa; it says the Veterans Affairs Council took over in February 1977 and that Danan and Shin-Shin jointly operated intercity services afterward
      - superscript:
        - link "[31]":
          - /url: "#ref-31"
      - text: ". The MOEA record gives a different date for the legal entity: 24 April 1969, unified business number 11011623, registered address 臺北市士林區承德路四段274號, representative 張捷, total capital NT$350 million and paid-in capital NT$308,652,850"
      - superscript:
        - link "[32]":
          - /url: "#ref-32"
      - text: . These are retained as separate operator-stated and statutory dates rather than collapsed into one founding claim

        - link "[31]":

      - superscript:
        - link "[32]":
          - /url: "#ref-32"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The current MOEA director table records the Veterans Affairs Council as the represented entity for three directors, alongside corporate representations for 欣湖天然氣, 欣泉投資 and 欣欣客運
      - superscript:
        - link "[32]":
          - /url: "#ref-32"
      - text: . That is evidence of the current registered board representation shown by the record; it does not by itself establish a complete parent-group or merger chronology
      - superscript:

      - text: .

    - heading "Legal identity and operating character" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Kuo-Kuang Motor Transportation is the English rendering used here for 國光汽車客運股份有限公司. The Ministry of Economic Affairs registry identifies the company by unified business number 70810572, records it as approved, and gives 15 June 2001 as its approved-establishment date
      - superscript:
        - link "[33]":
          - /url: "#ref-33"
      - text: . The same statutory record names 王雅萱 as representative, gives the registered address as 1F, No. 53, Section 4, Chongyang Road, Sanchong District, New Taipei City, and records NT$465 million in paid-in capital
      - superscript:
        - link "[33]":
          - /url: "#ref-33"
      - text: . Its registered activities cover highway passenger transport, city-bus passenger transport and sightseeing-bus passenger transport, alongside parking, vehicle repair and other ancillary activities
      - superscript:
        - link "[33]":
          - /url: "#ref-33"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The registry lists corporate representatives on the current board from construction, vehicle-manufacturing and investment companies, but it does not identify a single parent group
      - superscript:
        - link "[33]":
          - /url: "#ref-33"
      - text: . That distinction matters because a board representation list is evidence of the registered governance arrangement, not proof of a consolidated operating group
      - superscript:
        - link "[33]":
          - /url: "#ref-33"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The company’s self-authored profile gives a different date layer: it says operations began on 1 July 2001, and describes the business around safety and quality, professional efficiency and comfortable service"
      - superscript:
        - link "[34]":
          - /url: "#ref-34"
      - text: . The profile also describes national intercity service, online and voice ticketing, maintenance capability, parking management, city-bus service and a sightseeing-bus division said to have been established in 2008
      - superscript:
        - link "[34]":
          - /url: "#ref-34"
      - text: . Its more-than-860-bus and more-than-96-route figures, together with an average daily passenger figure tied explicitly to 2005, are retained as a dated historical snapshot rather than a current fleet census
      - superscript:
        - link "[34]":
          - /url: "#ref-34"
      - text: .

    - heading "Conflicts" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "台中客運's own site gives two different depot/station lists: its About page names roughly eight facilities"
      - superscript:

      - text: ", its separate Stations page names twelve, including a transfer station and a 秋紅谷 site the About page omits"
      - superscript:

      - text: . Both are the operator's own primary pages; neither explains the discrepancy, and this site publishes both rather than merging them.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The route-map dataset warns that its compiled publication can lag actual operations, while the citybus interface directs passengers to dynamic information or operator schedules for actual departures.
      - superscript:
        - link "[61]":

      - superscript:
        - link "[62]":
          - /url: "#ref-62"
      - text: These sources measure different publication layers, so the JSON retains route identity and stops but does not turn them into a frequency claim.
      - superscript:
        - link "[61]":
          - /url: "#ref-61"
      - superscript:
        - link "[63]":
          - /url: "#ref-63"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The full CSV contains 23 raw operator-label values, while the visible operator-link group on the citybus page presents 14 labels.
      - superscript:
        - link "[63]":
          - /url: "#ref-63"
      - superscript:
        - link "[62]":
          - /url: "#ref-62"
      - text: The first is a count of labels attached to route records and the second is a portal link list; neither is treated as a legal-company count.
      - superscript:
        - link "[63]":
          - /url: "#ref-63"
      - superscript:
        - link "[62]":
          - /url: "#ref-62"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The city-bus CSV has no departure-time field, while the separate 小黃公車 page describes 26 services with fixed departure times and linked image schedules.
      - superscript:
        - link "[63]":
          - /url: "#ref-63"
      - superscript:
        - link "[64]":
          - /url: "#ref-64"
      - text: The two values belong to different networks and publication formats, so the Yellow timetable is kept in its own data-layer object.

    - heading "Operators — a network that keeps changing hands" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - link "Tainan":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/tainan/
      - text: "'s city-bus operator roster has been actively reshaped by tender through the 2020s, unlike Taipei's stable joint-operation group"
      - superscript:
        - link "[65]":
          - /url: "#ref-65"
      - text: .
      - strong: 興南客運
      - text: (Shing Nan Bus) is the oldest, tracing to 台灣輕鐵株式會社 (1921) and a 1941 merger into 興南乘合自動車株式會社
      - superscript:
        - link "[66]":
          - /url: "#ref-66"
      - text: .
      - strong: 新營客運
      - text: (Xinying Bus), formally established January 1950, joined the Tainan system in a first batch of 44 transferred highway routes — sources disagree on whether that was 2011 or 2012
      - superscript:
        - link "[67]":
          - /url: "#ref-67"
      - text: .
      - strong: 府城客運
      - text: "(Fucheng Bus) is younger and structurally distinct: founded 2013 as a subsidiary spun off from"
      - strong: Kaohsiung Bus
      - text: (高雄客運, also documented on this site's
      - link "Kaohsiung page":
        - /url: /bus/regional/kaohsiung/
      - text: ) specifically to give Tainan a dedicated city-bus brand, after the original, differently-owned 台南客運 stopped running city routes in 2003
      - superscript:
        - link "[68]":
          - /url: "#ref-68"
      - text: .
      - strong: 漢程客運
      - text: (Han-Cheng Bus), founded 2013 in Kaohsiung as part of the same 台灣愛巴士 交通聯盟 alliance as 巨業交運/巨業交通, expanded into Tainan in December 2019 as its fourth operator
      - superscript:
        - link "[69]":
          - /url: "#ref-69"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Route 77 traces a small chain of hand-offs that is itself informative.
      - text: Launched 2016 as Tainan's first electric-bus route, it passed from its original operator to 府城客運 and then, from 10 April 2023, to 漢程客運 — the same 40 daily trips and alignment carried through each transfer
      - superscript:
        - link "[70]":
          - /url: "#ref-70"
      - text: . A
      - strong: 2024-08-21 network reorganisation
      - text: awarded 巨業交通 nine routes (existing and new, first batch targeted for Q4 2024) and 統聯客運 ten routes, making 統聯客運 Tainan's sixth operator from
      - strong: 3 January 2025
      - superscript:
        - link "[65]":
          - /url: "#ref-65"
      - text: — after the TDX snapshot above was retrieved, so that operator may not yet appear in the committed route/operator records.

    - heading "Gaps and conflicts" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The route and stop datasets provide current structure, but not a historical route-change log, reliability series, depot allocation, vehicle assignment or accessibility inventory.
      - superscript:
        - link "[71]":
          - /url: "#ref-71"
      - superscript:

      - superscript:
        - link "[73]":
          - /url: "#ref-73"
      - text: TDX provides route and stop update timestamps, while the ridership catalogue provides annual route totals; neither is a complete timetable history.
      - superscript:
        - link "[74]":
          - /url: "#ref-74"
      - superscript:
        - link "[75]":
          - /url: "#ref-75"
      - text: The city portal and the 小黃公車 Q&A are therefore retained as the service-information boundary, and any timetable or route change should be refreshed from those sources before publication.
      - superscript:
        - link "[76]":
          - /url: "#ref-76"
      - superscript:
        - link "[77]":
          - /url: "#ref-77"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The official sources disagree on the current 小黃公車 count. The Q&A page says 52 routes across 32 administrative districts, while the 5 August 2026 expansion notice says that adding 黃3, 黃16 and 黃23 increased the total from 46 to 49 routes across 31 districts.
      - superscript:
        - link "[77]":
          - /url: "#ref-77"
      - superscript:
        - link "[78]":
          - /url: "#ref-78"
      - text: These may be different publication snapshots or scopes, but the fetched sources do not explain the difference. The data layer preserves the Q&A table's 52 unique route names and reports the notice's 49 separately; it does not average them or choose a winner.
      - superscript:
        - link "[77]":
          - /url: "#ref-77"

    - heading "Classification and conflict" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The official catalogue places 棕20 under 捷運棕線接駁公車.
      - superscript:
        - link "[79]":
          - /url: "#ref-79"
      - text: TDX has a separate normalized record 棕20預, while the full official page describes reservation-only 美堤碼頭 detours without publishing that separate label.
      - superscript:
        - link "[80]":
          - /url: "#ref-80"
      - text: The two values are retained.
      - superscript:
        - link "[81]":
          - /url: "#ref-81"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The confirmed outbound stop sequence in this separate TDX record runs from 行善行愛路口, past 新湖行善路口/濱江國中/外雙溪(至善), ending at 故宮博物院(正館); the return working ends at 行善石潭路口 rather than the outbound origin.
      - superscript:
        - link "[81]":
          - /url: "#ref-81"
      - text: "One confirmed interchange is recorded in the curated stop-ID join set: Jiannan Rd. ("
      - link "BR15":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br15/
      - text: ), the same single station confirmed for plain 棕20.
      - superscript:
        - link "[81]":
          - /url: "#ref-81"
      - text: This record carries 2 subroutes under a single operator, 大南汽車, distinct from plain 棕20's own 4-subroute TDX record.
      - superscript:
        - link "[81]":
          - /url: "#ref-81"
      - text: The outbound working covers 19 stops and the return, ending at 行善石潭路口 rather than the outbound origin, also covers 19 — an asymmetric loop rather than a there-and-back working over the same stop set.
      - superscript:
        - link "[81]":
          - /url: "#ref-81"
      - text: Whether this separately filed record represents a distinct scheduled service or is simply TDX's own alternate encoding of plain 棕20's reservation-only detour was not established by any source checked for this entry.
      - superscript:
        - link "[81]":
          - /url: "#ref-81"
      - superscript:
        - link "[80]":
          - /url: "#ref-80"
      - text: Both endpoints, 行善行愛路口 and 故宮博物院(正館), match plain 棕20's own published outbound termini exactly.

      - text: The official 大臺北公車 catalogue lists 棕7綠野香坡 under 捷運棕線接駁公車.
      - superscript:
        - link "[82]":
          - /url: "#ref-82"
      - text: The TDX snapshot still identifies this record as 棕7綠野香坡.
      - superscript:
        - link "[83]":
          - /url: "#ref-83"
      - text: "The full PDA page states: 「原〖812〗路線自115年6月30日起，縮駛至『捷運橫溪站』並調整路線番號為〖三鶯2線〗」."
      - superscript:
        - link "[84]":
          - /url: "#ref-84"
      - text: Both values are retained; the identity is unresolved — the PDA statement describes route 812 being shortened and renumbered to 三鶯2線, a different identity from 棕7綠野香坡, and this search found no primary source connecting that 812 renumbering to this specific 棕7 stop-pattern record.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The confirmed outbound stop sequence in the current TDX record runs from 伴山別墅(一), past 伴山別墅(二)/碧潭橋頭, ending at 市政府(市府)/捷運市政府站.
      - superscript:
        - link "[83]":
          - /url: "#ref-83"
      - text: "Two confirmed interchanges are recorded in the curated stop-ID join set: Taipei City Hall ("
      - link "BL18":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/bl18/
      - text: ) and Muzha (
      - link "BR02":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/br02/
      - text: ), the same pair confirmed for plain 棕7.
      - superscript:
        - link "[83]":
          - /url: "#ref-83"
      - text: The route runs 2 subroutes under a single operator, 臺北客運, matching plain 棕7's own operator despite the unresolved identity conflict above.
      - superscript:
        - link "[83]":
          - /url: "#ref-83"
      - text: The outbound working covers 55 stops, longer than either plain 棕7 (47) or 棕7建業路; the return, starting from 消防局(松仁), covers 54.
      - superscript:
        - link "[83]":
          - /url: "#ref-83"
      - text: Whether that longer stop count reflects the 綠野香坡 (Green Fields) residential detour named in the identity, or the possible 812/三鶯2 renumbering above, was not established by any source checked for this entry.

    - paragraph:
      - text: The committed TDX snapshot contains a colour-red record named 紅68預, which is why this page exists.
      - superscript:
        - link "[85]":
          - /url: "#ref-85"
      - text: The full official catalogue lists 39 labels under 捷運紅線接駁公車 and omits 紅68預.
      - superscript:
        - link "[86]":
          - /url: "#ref-86"
      - text: The full official schedule page is labelled 紅68 and records appointment-only trial workings within that service; it does not name a separate 紅68預 route.
      - superscript:
        - link "[87]":
          - /url: "#ref-87"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Despite the classification conflict, the TDX-only record does carry its own confirmed stop sequence and curated interchange: from 洲美里, past 洲美街219號/洲美國小/福美站/三王宮, through 福美承平路口, and on the outbound working past 遠雄商舟大樓/中鼎第二總部大樓, ending at 捷運芝山站(福華)."
      - superscript:
        - link "[85]":
          - /url: "#ref-85"
      - text: "One confirmed interchange is recorded in the curated stop-ID join set: Zhishan ("
      - link "R17":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r17/
      - text: ), matching the route's own terminus and identical to plain 紅68's own confirmed interchange.
      - superscript:
        - link "[85]":
          - /url: "#ref-85"
      - text: The stop sequence is otherwise near-identical to plain 紅68's own, differing only in whether the 中鼎 第二總部大樓 detour is included — the same detour the schedule page's own appointment-only note describes.

    - heading "Classification and corridor" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The official catalogue lists 108 under 一般公車, as a separate routeid entry from its 108區 shuttle variant.
      - superscript:
        - link "[88]":
          - /url: "#ref-88"
      - text: Its full schedule page gives service span weekday and holiday 0700–1730, headway weekday 30–40 minutes and holiday 20–30 minutes at both peak and off-peak, a single-section fare (一段票), and 大都會客運陽明山站 as the service contact.
      - superscript:
        - link "[89]":
          - /url: "#ref-89"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The schedule page's own 起迄站名 field names the same stop, 陽明山公車總站, on both sides, which reads as a loop starting and ending at the Yangmingshan bus terminal.
      - superscript:
        - link "[89]":
          - /url: "#ref-89"
      - text: A community wiki instead describes the route as running from 陽明山 to a different terminus, 擎天崗 (起點站為陽明山，終點站為擎天崗), not as a loop.
      - superscript:
        - link "[90]":
          - /url: "#ref-90"
      - text: This is a direct conflict between a primary field and a secondary description; both values are published here and neither is picked.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The confirmed stop sequence never leaves Yangmingshan National Park: from the Yangmingshan bus terminal it calls at the park's own visitor infrastructure — the park headquarters, Yangmingshuwu (the former presidential retreat), the Xiaoyoukeng service station, Menghuan Lake and Lengshuikeng — before returning via the Qingshan recreation area."
      - superscript:
        - link "[91]":
          - /url: "#ref-91"
      - text: No stop on either direction is named for an MRT station, and the curated stop-ID join set carries no confirmed MRT connection for this route at all — a rider transfers to it at the mountain-top terminal itself, not partway along an urban corridor.
      - superscript:
        - link "[91]":
          - /url: "#ref-91"

    - heading "Operators — a genuine count conflict" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The scenic-area administration's own contact page names four ferry brands serving Green Island: Kaixuan (凱旋), Green Island Star (綠島之星), Uranus (天王星) and Golden Star/Hengxing (金星、恆星)."
      - superscript:
        - link "[95]":
          - /url: "#ref-95"
      - text: "Several other sources — including two of the operators' own sites and a booking aggregator — describe only three companies as running the actual pooled, scheduled service: Kaixuan (registered as Farnlin Shipping, 帆利航運), Green Island Star (registered as Long Hong Shipping, 龍鴻航業) and Uranus (registered as Changjie Shipping, 長杰航運, whose new vessel Tianwangxing 21 began sailing 28 March 2025)."
      - superscript:
        - link "[96]":
          - /url: "#ref-96"
      - text: No operational detail for Golden Star/Hengxing was found in any source beyond a phone number on the administration's own contact list. Both counts are published here rather than one being picked.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The administration's page separately lists two different phone numbers for Uranus across its two hosted pages (089-281617 on the general ferry page, 089-281618 on the Green Island subsite), and assigns that same 089-281618 number to Golden Star/Hengxing on the subsite while the general page gives Golden Star/Hengxing a third number, 089-281477.
      - superscript:
        - link "[95]":
          - /url: "#ref-95"
      - superscript:
        - link "[97]":
          - /url: "#ref-97"
      - text: Neither discrepancy is resolved here.

      - superscript:
        - link "[99]":

      - text: The East Coast National Scenic Area Administration's page gives "about 2-3 hours."
      - superscript:
        - link "[100]":
          - /url: "#ref-100"
      - text: A booking aggregator separately reports 150 minutes outbound and 200 minutes on the return leg when the return is routed via Green Island. For the Houbihu–Orchid Island leg, Taitung County's page gives "120-150 minutes," roughly consistent with a private portal's "about 2 hours."
      - superscript:
        - link "[98]":
          - /url: "#ref-98"
      - superscript:
        - link "[101]":
          - /url: "#ref-101"
      - text: None of these figures is treated as more authoritative than another; the range itself is the finding.

    - heading "What remains date-sensitive" [level=3]

      - superscript:

      - text: "The live page and the older ticket PDF also publish slightly different wind threshold values: the live page gives 15.6, 13.6 and 10.5 m/s for its named service groups, while the PDF’s table displays 15.5, 10, 10 and 13.5 m/s across its service columns."

      - superscript:

          - /url: "#ref-103"
      - text: The headings in the PDF’s extracted text do not expose a clean one-to-one mapping for every column, so the values are reported as a dated source conflict rather than reconciled by guesswork.

    - heading "One historical double-track record" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taiwan Railways' full construction-history table lists Changhua–Minxiong as a 71.7 km double-track segment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[104]":
          - /url: "#ref-104"
      - text: The table gives 1957 as the construction year and 1970 as the operation-start year, with Taiwan Railways Administration listed as the constructor.
      - superscript:
        - link "[104]":
          - /url: "#ref-104"
      - text: Its explanation is 添築雙線, rendered by the operator as “Extended to be double-tracked.”
      - superscript:
        - link "[104]":
          - /url: "#ref-104"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The full operator PDF repeats the same segment and values in its row 43, so the HTML table and PDF are two presentations of the same primary construction record, not two different measurements.
      - superscript:
        - link "[105]":
          - /url: "#ref-105"
      - text: This page therefore treats 71.7 km as the operator's historical construction-table scope. It does not turn the row into a separate present-day line, and it does not infer that the table's operation-start field supplies an exact commissioning date.
      - superscript:
        - link "[104]":
          - /url: "#ref-104"
      - superscript:

    - heading "What is disputed" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: BES's own statement says the damaged section was between its
      - link "Y12":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y12/
      - text: Qiaohe and
      - link "Y14":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y14/
      - text: Banxin engineering labels and that the contractor followed the approved drawings.
      - superscript:
        - link "[108]":
          - /url: "#ref-108"
      - text: BES says the upper and lower bearing arrangements both had milled-through slope plates but only the upper support failed; it therefore argues that the milling-through detail and bearing failure were not the main cause, and that the design strength and unequal seismic demand require further examination.
      - superscript:
        - link "[108]":
          - /url: "#ref-108"
    - paragraph:
      - text: That position conflicts with the Control Yuan's finding that the work did not follow the drawings and that the pin's loss of the shear interface was the failure mechanism.
      - superscript:
        - link "[109]":
          - /url: "#ref-109"
      - text: The sources on this page establish the competing positions, not a final court determination. The full court merits judgment, final settlement and current responsibility allocation remain TBC.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The repair itself added permanent unseating-prevention and uplift-restraint devices as a second line of defence, while replacing the pot-bearing facilities and restoring track, cables and other systems.
      - superscript:
        - link "[110]":
          - /url: "#ref-110"
      - text: That is the published remedy; it does not by itself decide which party's explanation of the original cause will prevail.

    - paragraph:

    - heading "Two disputes, not one" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: The delay claim, 1988–2005.
      - text: Matra sued for the cost of a contract that ran years longer than it was written for, because the civil works its equipment depended on were late — the claim arises, in 自由時報's words, 「因土木工程部分包商施工延誤，連帶造成馬特拉的工期延長，增加成本費用」
      - superscript:
        - link "[117]":
          - /url: "#ref-117"
      - text: . This is the dispute that went to arbitration in 1993 and was still before the Supreme Court in 2005
      - superscript:
        - link "[117]":
          - /url: "#ref-117"
      - text: . It is about money and contract law, and
      - strong: Matra won it
      - superscript:
        - link "[117]":
          - /url: "#ref-117"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - strong: The withdrawal, 1996–97.
      - text: After the line opened, Matra pulled its technical staff out of Taiwan and stopped maintaining the system
      - superscript:
        - link "[118]":
          - /url: "#ref-118"
      - text: . This is the dispute everybody remembers — the one that produced the most famous sentence said about the
      - link "Taipei Metro":
        - /url: /rail/operators/trtc/
      - text: ", and the one that steered the procurement that followed."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "They are connected: the withdrawal happened because the delay claim had poisoned the relationship. But they are not the same event, and the NT$1.64 billion that circulates belongs to the first, not the second"
      - superscript:
        - link "[117]":
          - /url: "#ref-117"
      - text: .

    - heading "The Pingxi Line began as a private colliery railway" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: What is now TRA's Pingxi Line began as 石底線, a private railway built to move coal out of the Shidi coalfield. In June 1918, 顏雲年, who held two of the coalfield's mining rights, joined with the Japanese trading house 藤田組 to form 臺北炭礦株式會社 and build a railway once wartime raw-material prices made the investment worthwhile; construction began in January 1919.
      - superscript:
        - link "[119]":
          - /url: "#ref-119"
      - text: 藤田組 withdrew after the post-WWI economic downturn, and Yan Yunian bought out its stake, bringing in further investors and reorganising the enlarged company as 臺陽礦業株式會社 in 1920.
      - superscript:
        - link "[119]":
          - /url: "#ref-119"
      - text: "Sources disagree by a year on when the line was finished: an encyclopedia account gives July 1921, while an independently fetched enthusiast history gives July 1922."
      - superscript:
        - link "[119]":
          - /url: "#ref-119"
      - superscript:
        - link "[120]":
          - /url: "#ref-120"
      - text: Both are published here rather than resolved. The colonial government purchased the line in 1929, relieving Taiyang Mining's cash-flow problems and renaming it 平溪線 under the Railway Bureau — the exact day and purchase price given in some secondary accounts rest on a citation this research did not independently verify.
      - superscript:
        - link "[120]":
          - /url: "#ref-120"
    - paragraph: "A separate, later, and unrelated operation also carries the Pingxi name: 新平溪煤礦 (New Pingxi Coal Mine) at Shifen, now preserved as a museum with its own narrow-gauge electric mining train. Its own 1965 opening and 1997 closure dates are unverified in this research, sourced only to a search summary rather than a fetched page. It is a different company and a different mine from the 1918-1929 石底線/臺陽礦業 story above, not established by any source found to be connected to it."

    - 'heading "Jinguashi: two railways, one popular name" [level=3]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: Japanese merchant 田中長兵衛, through 田中組, and separately 藤田組, obtained mining rights at Jinguashi for gold and copper extraction.
      - superscript:
        - link "[121]":
          - /url: "#ref-121"
      - text: 金瓜石礦山株式會社, established in 1925, built a light railway connecting Jinguashi to Ruifang, completed in 1931.
      - superscript:
        - link "[122]":
          - /url: "#ref-122"
      - text: Nippon Mining (日本礦業株式會社) purchased the Jinguashi mining rights in 1933 and expanded processing facilities, including the 十三層 ore-flotation plant.
      - superscript:
        - link "[122]":
          - /url: "#ref-122"
      - superscript:
        - link "[121]":
          - /url: "#ref-121"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The name "金瓜石線" is used by different sources for two different railways. The National Central Library's digital archive applies it to the 1931 Jinguashi-Ruifang light railway described above.
      - superscript:
        - link "[122]":
          - /url: "#ref-122"
      - text: Wikipedia's dedicated article instead applies the same name to a separate, later 762 mm industrial line running from 水湳洞 through 焿子寮 and 深澳 to the port at 八尺門, completed in 1936 and measured at 12.0 km with five stations as of a 1953 survey — a line the National Archives Administration independently corroborates under the alternate name 水八鐵路, carrying ore to the port for shipment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[123]":
          - /url: "#ref-123"
      - superscript:
        - link "[121]":
          - /url: "#ref-121"
      - text: This line's passenger service ended in August 1962 due to deteriorated track.
      - superscript:
        - link "[123]":
          - /url: "#ref-123"
      - text: Both usages of "金瓜石線" are published here without picking one as correct.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Postwar, mining continued under 臺灣金屬鑛業股份有限公司 (Taiwan Metal Mining Co.), formed in 1955.
      - superscript:
        - link "[121]":
          - /url: "#ref-121"
      - text: Sources disagree on when mining at Jinguashi finally ended — two sources agree independently on 1987, but a third gives 1985 under a differently named company (臺灣金礦公司), and this research could not determine whether that is the same entity operating under an inconsistent name or a genuinely separate closure event.

    - 'heading "Houtong: a station, then a mine, then a museum" [level=3]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: Houtong Station opened on 27 January 1920 as part of the Yilan Line.
      - superscript:
        - link "[124]":
          - /url: "#ref-124"
      - text: The Ruisan coal-preparation plant nearby was completed in March 1922, originally under Mitsui zaibatsu operation; Mitsui later abandoned the site believing reserves exhausted, and in 1934 李建興 and his brothers leased the workings, forming what was formally registered on 15 November 1954 as 瑞三鑛業股份有限公司.
      - superscript:
        - link "[125]":
          - /url: "#ref-125"
      - text: The company became Taiwan's largest single coal producer, with a cumulative 1946-1980 output of 6,741,118 tonnes — reported as 5.23% of national production over that span, a figure not directly comparable to a separate broadcaster's claim that the mine supplied "one-seventh" of Taiwan's coal at its single-year peak, since the two describe different measurement periods.
      - superscript:
        - link "[125]":
          - /url: "#ref-125"
      - text: The mine closed on 1 May 1990, following declining economics and three fatal disasters in 1984.
      - superscript:
        - link "[125]":
          - /url: "#ref-125"
      - superscript:
        - link "[126]":
          - /url: "#ref-126"
      - text: The preparation plant and coal-transport bridge were registered as historic buildings on 7 November 2005; the wider site was named and opened as 猴硐煤礦博物園區 (Houtong Coal Mine Museum Park) on 24 July 2010, and the Ruisan plant itself reopened after restoration in September 2022, with a second restoration phase that broke ground on 21 October 2024, targeted for completion in 2026.
      - superscript:
        - link "[126]":
          - /url: "#ref-126"

    - heading "Heritage status and today's rail bike" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Two of the 1938-era replacement iron bridges — 內社川鐵橋 (Neishechuan Iron Bridge) and the Yutengping replacement span — were designated
      - link "Miaoli":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/miaoli/
      - text: County monuments, approved by the county's Tangible Cultural Assets Review Committee on 10 March 2019 and announced the next day, making them the corridor's fourth and fifth protected heritage sites after Shengxing Station, Longteng Broken Bridge and Taichung's Taian Station.
      - superscript:
        - link "[127]":
          - /url: "#ref-127"
      - text: "This page does not state the designation dates for Shengxing Station or Longteng Bridge themselves as established facts: they are reported by several secondary accounts, but the Ministry of Culture's own heritage database could not be read to confirm them directly (see Remaining gaps)."
    - paragraph:
      - text: The old alignment briefly returned to scheduled service on 5 June 2010, with a steam-hauled heritage train running Sanyi to the former Taian station.
      - superscript:
        - link "[128]":
          - /url: "#ref-128"
      - text: Miaoli County Government has since redeveloped the corridor as 舊山線鐵道自行車 (Old Mountain Line Rail Bike), which the Tourism Administration describes as Taiwan's first rail-bike attraction, run under a "dynamic preservation" model rather than as a TRA passenger service.
      - superscript:
        - link "[129]":
          - /url: "#ref-129"
      - text: Sources disagree on exactly when the Rail Bike itself began operating, and this page does not pick between them.

    - 'heading "Taichung: the one port line still running, on a disputed birth date" [level=3]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taichung Port Station remains an active TRA station today, with a freight-consignment desk still listed on the operator's own current station page.
      - superscript:
        - link "[130]":
          - /url: "#ref-130"
      - text: "The line itself is 7.8 km, but its origin date is genuinely disputed between two different TRA-adjacent sources: a Wikipedia article, uncited for this specific figure, gives an opening or operator-transfer date of 31 October 1976, while a TRA construction-history PDF — read directly for a separate piece of this project's research — lists the same line as built in 1973 and put into operation in 1974, and the current TRA HTML construction-history page omits the line entirely."
      - superscript:
        - link "[131]":
          - /url: "#ref-131"
      - superscript:
        - link "[132]":
          - /url: "#ref-132"
      - text: Both dates are published here without resolving which is correct. TRA's own 2024 social-media statement puts the line's annual freight volume at 202,000 tonnes — mostly wheat moved to flour mills at Fugang and
      - link "Hsinchu":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/hsinchu/
      - text: ", at roughly three round trips per day on the port line itself — within a system-wide TRA freight total of 6.81 million tonnes that year."
      - superscript:
        - link "[133]":
          - /url: "#ref-133"
      - text: A separate, uncited claim on Wikipedia that this wheat traffic ended in June 2025 and was replaced by irregular energy-storage-container shipments from November 2025 could not be corroborated against any primary or independently written source in repeated searches, and is not published here as established.

    - heading "Six transport projects under one 1970s banner" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Premier Chiang Ching-kuo announced the Ten Major Construction Projects (十大建設) in 1973, to be completed 1974-1979, in response to the 1973 oil crisis and infrastructure bottlenecks from a decade of rapid industrialisation.
      - superscript:
        - link "[143]":
          - /url: "#ref-143"
      - text: "Six of the ten were transport projects: the Sun Yat-sen Freeway (Keelung to Kaohsiung, 373 km, completed 31 October 1978), railway electrification of the western trunk line (completed 27 June 1979), the North-Link Line connecting the eastern rail network to the western one (full operation from 1 February 1980), Taoyuan International Airport (opened 26 February 1979 as Chiang Kai-shek International Airport), Taichung Port, and Su'ao Port."
      - superscript:
        - link "[143]":
          - /url: "#ref-143"
      - text: The freeway's construction cost is reported with three different figures across the same secondary source — NT$42.9 billion, "over NT$40 billion," and NT$44.8 billion — none of which this research traced to a primary government figure, so all three are published here rather than resolved.
      - superscript:
        - link "[144]":
          - /url: "#ref-144"
      - text: "A separate full-page fetch of a popular history site, checked specifically because a search-engine summary had implied it documented a substantive motorway-versus-rail policy debate, found only a much thinner account: that Chiang overrode unspecified objections in 1970, with no named opponents and no cost comparison — an example of a search snippet outrunning what the underlying page actually supports."
      - superscript:
        - link "[145]":
          - /url: "#ref-145"
      - text: No source found in this research documents a contemporaneous, sourced debate over widening the existing rail/road corridor as an alternative to a new freeway alignment.

    - heading "Construction and opening chronology" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The government’s network history places the Red and Orange lines in the first stage of Kaohsiung’s first-period MRT development plan, approved in ROC80, and says that the two routes were completed and opened in ROC97.
      - superscript:
        - link "[153]":
          - /url: "#ref-153"
      - text: "KRTC’s company history gives a more granular institutional chronology: the city invited private participation on 1 February 1999, the China Steel-led application was selected on 10 May 2000, the company received its licence on 28 December 2000, and the construction and development agreements were signed on 12 January 2001."
      - superscript:
        - link "[154]":
          - /url: "#ref-154"
      - text: KRTC records construction beginning in October 2001 and describes the concession as 36 years from the start of construction, comprising more than six years of construction before the Red and Orange lines entered service.
      - superscript:
        - link "[154]":
          - /url: "#ref-154"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "MTBU treats the Red and Orange network as one private-participation construction and operating project: its page gives six years of construction, 30 years of operation and a 36-year concession, with a planned 42.7 km and 38 stations, three depots and a total construction cost of NT$183.963 billion."
      - superscript:
        - link "[155]":
          - /url: "#ref-155"
      - text: KRTC records the Red Line’s regular service opening on 9 March 2008 and the Orange Line’s opening on 14 September 2008; the latter date marks the full operation of the original cross-shaped network, not the first Red Line service.
      - superscript:

    - paragraph:
      - text: The historical service-indicator document is a separate design snapshot. It describes a Red Line of 28.3 km, with 19.8 km underground and 8.5 km elevated, and 23 stations at the time of that document.
      - superscript:
        - link "[157]":
          - /url: "#ref-157"
      - text: The current government page reports 28.3 km and 24 Red Line stations, while the TDX route pull reports 29.72 km and its current sequence includes
      - link "R24":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r24/
      - text: and RK1.
      - superscript:

          - /url: "#ref-155"
      - superscript:
        - link "[158]":
          - /url: "#ref-158"
      - superscript:
        - link "[159]":
          - /url: "#ref-159"
      - text: Those values are retained as different dated or structured boundaries rather than made to agree by arithmetic.

    - heading "Planning and approvals" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Sources disagree about when this line's history starts because different bodies mean different things by "planning." The first fully verified institutional milestone is the central government's October 1996 decision to build it as a BOT (build–operate–transfer) concession, and Long Life International Development Co. won that concession in 1998
      - superscript:
        - link "[160]":
          - /url: "#ref-160"
      - text: . The BOT model collapsed on 31 December 2002, when Long Life and the High Speed Rail Bureau agreed to terminate the contract
      - superscript:
        - link "[160]":
          - /url: "#ref-160"
      - text: ". Government took over: MOTC designated the High Speed Rail Bureau as the project's builder on 28 October 2003, and the central government approved the construction plan on 9 March 2004"
      - superscript:

    - paragraph:
      - text: Discussed on
      - link "Taoyuan Airport MRT":
        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/airport-mrt/

    - heading "Construction history" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Construction of the Sanchong–Airport– Zhongli section and its E&M systems formally started 27 February 2006
      - superscript:
        - link "[162]":
          - /url: "#ref-162"
      - text: ; TYMC's own history page instead marks 26 June 2006, the date of a ceremonial groundbreaking presided over by the Premier
      - superscript:
        - link "[161]":
          - /url: "#ref-161"
      - text: — two different milestones in the same year, not a contradiction. DORTS records that Taipei rejected the originally elevated Sanchong–Taipei section on urban-design and land-use grounds; Taipei City agreed to fund the extra cost of underground construction, and that section formally started on 25 September 2006 after its design and construction were assigned to DORTS
      - superscript:
        - link "[162]":
          - /url: "#ref-162"
      - text: . The detailed design ran from March 1998 through 2002, according to the same project chronology
      - superscript:
        - link "[162]":
          - /url: "#ref-162"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The opening date itself moved repeatedly. The earliest announced target was January 2009; by March 2016 it had changed six times
      - superscript:
        - link "[163]":
          - /url: "#ref-163"
      - text: . The fetched report gives that count but not a complete dated list of each change. The line finally opened
      - strong: 2 March 2017
      - superscript:
        - link "[164]":
          - /url: "#ref-164"
      - superscript:
        - link "[162]":
          - /url: "#ref-162"
      - text: . TYMC's chronology records the 99% system-stability test on 20 November 2016, Ricardo's safety certification on 2 December, initial inspection on 3–4 December, final inspection on 29–30 December, the operating permit on 25 January 2017 and trial service from 2 February
      - superscript:
        - link "[161]":
          - /url: "#ref-161"
      - text: .

    - heading "Engineering and contract disputes — two figures confirmed, a widely repeated total not found anywhere" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The main electromechanical contract (ME01) went to a consortium led by the Japanese trading house
      - strong: Marubeni
      - text: (丸紅), with Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Hitachi as named subcontractors. In January 2017, weeks before opening, the High Speed Rail Bureau announced it would impose a
      - strong: NT$2.5 billion delay penalty
      - text: — the contract's maximum, calculated at 0.05% of contract value per day of delay — and had already
      - strong: withheld roughly NT$1.9 billion in performance bonds
      - text: ", over Marubeni's unauthorised subcontracting of the signalling system, which its contract required it to design itself, to a British firm"
      - superscript:
        - link "[165]":
          - /url: "#ref-165"
      - text: . Marubeni's own counter-claim against the Ministry, seeking NT$12.9 billion over repeated design changes, was reported in the same account
      - superscript:
        - link "[165]":
          - /url: "#ref-165"
      - text: . Both of the Bureau's figures were independently corroborated by two further contemporaneous reports naming the same amounts and the same reasons.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: A combined "NT$7.2 billion" total for this dispute circulates widely.
      - text: NT$2.5 billion plus NT$1.9 billion is NT$4.4 billion, not NT$7.2 billion, and no primary or secondary source read for this page — not the three contemporaneous 2017 news accounts, not zh.wikipedia's own article on the line, which contains no Marubeni monetary figures at all — states a combined total of any kind. The NT$7.2 billion figure appeared repeatedly in this research run's own search-engine result summaries, never inside a quoted source sentence, and in one case alongside an unrelated, later, and much smaller 2021 dispute — the Railway Bureau withheld NT$726.93 million from Marubeni that year for missing express-train travel-time, speed and headway targets
      - superscript:
        - link "[166]":
          - /url: "#ref-166"
      - text: — that shares a leading digit and may be the source of the confusion. The two confirmed figures, and Marubeni's name, are published here on the strength of three independent contemporaneous accounts; the total is not, because it could not be found stated anywhere.

    - heading "Rolling stock" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Two fleets, two manufacturers, sharing the same 1,435mm gauge and DC 750V third-rail supply
      - superscript:
        - link "[167]":
          - /url: "#ref-167"
      - superscript:
        - link "[168]":
          - /url: "#ref-168"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The
      - strong: express fleet (2000-type, purple)
      - text: is built entirely by
      - strong: Kawasaki Heavy Industries
      - text: ", delivered 2011–2013 for the 2017 opening: 11 five-car sets, 55 cars, each set four passenger cars plus a dedicated luggage car"
      - superscript:
        - link "[167]":
          - /url: "#ref-167"
      - text: . Transverse seating, overhead luggage racks, WiFi and USB charging are fitted; wireless charging pads are noted in one source as currently suspended, rather than the always-on feature sometimes described
      - superscript:
        - link "[167]":
          - /url: "#ref-167"
      - text: . Capacity is around 855 per set, with 206 seats and eight wheelchair spaces
      - superscript:
        - link "[167]":
          - /url: "#ref-167"
      - text: .
    - paragraph
    - figure "Inside an express (2000-type) train. Cheng-en Cheng from Taichung City, Taiwan, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons":
      - img "Passengers seated in the purple transverse seating of an Airport MRT express train, luggage racks and a route display overhead"
      - text: Inside an express (2000-type) train. Cheng-en Cheng from Taichung City, Taiwan, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons
    - paragraph
    - paragraph:
      - text: The
      - strong: commuter fleet (1000-type, blue)
      - text: "was built under an industrial- cooperation arrangement: Kawasaki built the prototype set and three later sets (101, 118–120); the rest, sets 102–117, were assembled domestically by"
      - strong: Taiwan Rolling Stock Co.
      - text: (台灣車輛股份有限公司)
      - superscript:
        - link "[168]":
          - /url: "#ref-168"
      - text: . There are currently 20 four-car sets, 80 cars, with longitudinal seating for higher standing capacity
      - superscript:
        - link "[168]":
          - /url: "#ref-168"
      - text: . Per-set seating is 188 — one source's own summary prose describes this as "per car," which its own per-car table contradicts (44+47+50+44 seats across the four cars, summing close to 188), so this page publishes the per-set reading
      - superscript:
        - link "[168]":
          - /url: "#ref-168"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: Both fleets run at 100 km/h in service, with a 110 km/h design maximum
      - superscript:
        - link "[167]":
          - /url: "#ref-167"
      - superscript:
        - link "[168]":
          - /url: "#ref-168"
      - text: .

        - /url: /rail/metro/lines/circular-line/
      - text: in the source page's “Incident investigation and engineering findings” section.
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
    - heading "Incident investigation and engineering findings" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Read the report carefully and the first thing to notice is what is
      - emphasis: not
      - text: a finding
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . Its terms of reference recite the allegation it was asked to look at — eleven suspected displacements, a repair initially costed at over NT$400 million, at least a year to fix
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . Those are the reported claims the Control Yuan set out to test, not its conclusions, and they are quoted here as such.
    - heading "The mechanism" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The report's first finding is a construction fault, stated without hedging: the contractor, BES Engineering (中華工程),"
      - strong: did not build to the drawings
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . It milled through the grade-adjustment plate (調坡板) that sits between the girder and the bearing, leaving void space above the locating pin; under the earthquake the pin jumped upward into that void, its base left the interface between the upper and lower plates of the pot bearing, and it lost its ability to resist shear
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The numbers behind that sentence are the heart of the case
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: ":"
    - table:
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Dimension Depth":
          - columnheader "Dimension"
          - columnheader "Depth"
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Milled recess, as shown on the contractor's own shop drawing 5 mm[178]":
          - cell "Milled recess, as shown on the contractor's own shop drawing"
          - cell "5 mm[178]":
            - text: 5 mm
            - superscript:
              - link "[178]":
                - /url: "#ref-178"
        - row "Milled recess, as measured on site by the investigation 41 mm[178]":
          - cell "Milled recess, as measured on site by the investigation"
          - cell "41 mm[178]":
            - text: 41 mm
            - superscript:
              - link "[178]":
                - /url: "#ref-178"
        - row "Void left above the pin 36 mm[178]":
          - cell "Void left above the pin"
          - cell "36 mm[178]":
            - text: 36 mm
            - superscript:
              - link "[178]":
                - /url: "#ref-178"
        - row "Height of the pin itself 40 mm[178]":
          - cell "Height of the pin itself"
          - cell "40 mm[178]":
            - text: 40 mm
            - superscript:
              - link "[178]":
                - /url: "#ref-178"
    - paragraph:
      - text: 36 mm of void plus the 5 mm of engagement the drawing required is 41 mm — the report's own arithmetic — and 41 mm is more than enough to swallow a pin only 40 mm tall
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . The pins were found by the New Taipei City Civil Engineers Association, which jacked the damaged bridges up and discovered them lodged in the upper plate of the bearing or lying on the pier cap where they had fallen
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The section was built under contract CF651B, part of the CF650 section works, and the structures carried a warranty running to 12 March 2026
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: — which is why the timing of the claim against the contractor matters.
    - heading "The shaking was smaller than the design case" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: This is the part most likely to be misread. The viaducts were designed to the Ministry of Transportation and Communications' 2006 railway bridge seismic design code, at a Taipei basin design ground motion of 0.24 g, with an importance factor of 1.2 because metro bridges are classed as important structures — so the minimum design seismic force is 0.288 g, which on the Central Weather Administration's 2020 intensity scale falls in the 6-weak band
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . The "designed for 6-weak" formulation is the report's own arithmetic on 0.24 g × 1.2 followed by a lookup on the 2020 scale, not a design document that says 6-weak
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: What the instruments recorded near the damaged bridges was smaller
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: ":"
    - table:
      - rowgroup:
        - row "Station North–south peak ground acceleration":
          - columnheader "Station"
          - columnheader "North–south peak ground acceleration"
      - rowgroup:
        - row "TAP026, 頂溪國小 224.60 gal[178]":
          - cell "TAP026, 頂溪國小"
          - cell "224.60 gal[178]":
            - text: 224.60 gal
            - superscript:
              - link "[178]":
                - /url: "#ref-178"
        - row "TAP032, 積穗國小 206.77 gal[178]":
          - cell "TAP032, 積穗國小"
          - cell "206.77 gal[178]":
            - text: 206.77 gal
            - superscript:
              - link "[178]":
                - /url: "#ref-178"
        - row "TAP115, 安和國小 223.17 gal[178]":
          - cell "TAP115, 安和國小"
          - cell "223.17 gal[178]":
            - text: 223.17 gal
            - superscript:
              - link "[178]":
                - /url: "#ref-178"
    - paragraph:
      - text: At 積穗國小 the peak ground velocity reached 32.16 cm/s, an intensity of 5-strong, and the peak horizontal acceleration measured there was 0.229 g — below the 0.288 g of the 475-year return-period design earthquake
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: ". New Taipei DORTS said the same thing three weeks after the earthquake: intensity 5-strong at the nearest recording station"
      - superscript:
        - link "[179]":
          - /url: "#ref-179"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The comparison the report itself draws is between seismic microzones rather than between metro lines. The adjacent zones — the DF111 contract range covering Wenshan and Xindian, and the DF113 range covering Sanchong,
      - link "Xinzhuang":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/o18/
      - text: and Banqiao — recorded far lower ground motion in the same earthquake and suffered
      - strong: no bridge damage at all
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . In the DF112 range covering Zhonghe and Yonghe, horizontal peak ground acceleration was around twice its neighbours' and horizontal peak ground velocity around fifteen times
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Which produces the single most quotable line in the document: 「也就是說，輸入比 規範要求小20%的地震，卻得到比預期大50%的力量，顯示出反應譜分析不能反映當地地震反應 的實況」 — an input earthquake 20% smaller than the code requires produced forces 50% larger than expected, showing that response-spectrum analysis does not reflect the local seismic response"
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - heading "The design, and what nobody checked" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The report's second finding is against the design. The structure is described in it as
      - strong: Taiwan's first stacked viaduct
      - text: — 國內史無前例的疊式高架橋 — carried on branching piers through climbing and descending sections, and the finding is that no higher design standard was adopted and no displacement-limiting devices were added to provide a further line of defence, and that this unprecedented structural form went through
      - strong: no external structural review
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Note the word: viaduct, not station. Nothing found in the research behind this page describes stacked"
      - emphasis: stations
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The structural engineers' report the investigation relied on sets out the hierarchy plainly: displacement-limiting devices assist the bearings and resist seismic force, and fall-prevention equipment or sufficient seat length prevents the span dropping — the second and third lines of defence respectively for a bridge bearing system in an earthquake"
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . The line was built with neither of the two backups.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Three further design failures are recorded
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: ":"
    - list:
      - listitem:
        - text: The detailed design consultant, CECI (世曦),
        - strong: double-deducted dead load
        - text: when calculating the bearings' uplift design force, and so underestimated the required uplift resistance
        - superscript:
          - link "[178]":
            - /url: "#ref-178"
        - text: .
      - listitem:
        - text: The pot-bearing detail drawing
        - strong: contradicts itself about the pins
        - superscript:
          - link "[178]":
            - /url: "#ref-178"
        - text: . Note 1 in its lower-left corner gives every pin a height of 40 mm with diameters of 120, 140, 150, 160, 200, 210, 220 and 280 mm; the table on the same drawing gives every pin a diameter of 100 mm with heights of 15, 20 and 25 mm; and neither set matches the pins actually found in the damaged bearings
        - superscript:
          - link "[178]":
            - /url: "#ref-178"
        - text: . The report's own word for this is 令人費解 — baffling.
      - listitem:
        - strong: Nobody senior signed that drawing
        - superscript:
          - link "[178]":
            - /url: "#ref-178"
        - text: . Only the handling officer at Taipei DORTS's third civil works office stamped it; neither the design unit responsible for reviewing it nor DORTS as the approving authority signed at all, which the report finds is a failure to carry out the review and approval the contract's specification chapter on pot bearings required
        - superscript:
          - link "[178]":
            - /url: "#ref-178"
        - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: 888 pot bearings were supplied to the works in total, sampled in six batches against the production schedule and tested at National Taiwan University of Science and Technology's structural mechanics laboratory
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - heading "The plate that nobody in Taiwan inspects" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The third finding is the one most easily missed, and it is the reason the fault survived construction. The grade-adjustment plate is a secondary component between the girder and the bearing; it is designed by the contractor, assembled in the fabrication shop, and concealed once the girder is lifted into place — so it was
      - strong: not an inspection hold point
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The investigation then checked whether it is one anywhere else, and found that it is not: not on the Directorate General of Highways' viaducts, not on the Hualien–Taitung railway works, not on the Tamkang Bridge, not on the Ankeng LRT, not on the Sanying Line, not on the Taichung Metro, not on the Wenhu Line, not on the second phase of the Wanda Line, and not in the Public Construction Commission's inspection checkpoints for steel bridge erection"
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . Taipei DORTS's remedy, dated 13 December 2024 — the day after the line reopened — was to add a pot-bearing inspection flow chart and a sampling standard
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - heading "The seismometer that was told not to report" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The fourth finding concerns an instrument that was installed, worked, and was disconnected from anyone who could act on it. Zhongyuan station has triaxial accelerometer-type seismometers at both ends of its platform level
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . On 28 August 2019 Taipei DORTS's electrical and mechanical systems engineering office wrote to Taipei Rapid Transit Corporation that the seismometer detection signals need not be relayed to the control centre — and from the line's opening in 2020 to the date of the report, the Circular Line control centre held
      - strong: no seismic record from that instrument at all
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The 2019 letter identifies the instruments by the codes
      - code: Y9
      - text: and
      - code: Y13
      - text: ", which are not the codes the stations at those positions carry today; the two numbering schemes remain unreconciled, and the station the report names is Zhongyuan"
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The report also states as fact that when Taipei City Government handed operations to New Taipei City Government on 23 May 2023, New Taipei Metro took the equipment as it stood, and received training on the anemometer only — nothing on the seismic instrumentation
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - heading "The code itself" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The sixth finding is against the ministry. Through years of revision, including the substantially updated 2021 edition of the railway bridge seismic design code, MOTC has never addressed
      - strong: transverse
      - text: "displacement: the rules still deal only with the longitudinal, running direction"
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . The line failed sideways.
    - heading "Who was actually corrected" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: This is worth stating precisely, because the operator of the line and the builder of it are different cities and the two are easily transposed. The formal 糾正 — a correction, the Control Yuan's censure of an agency — was proposed against
      - strong: Taipei City Government
      - text: ", on findings one and three: the construction fault and the supervision gap"
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . Taipei DORTS built the line and supervised its own construction
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: New Taipei City Government and MOTC received 函請檢討改進 — a request to review and improve, and report back — not a correction
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: . Findings two and four went to Taipei City for review, finding four also to New Taipei City, and findings five and six to MOTC
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .

    - heading "Engineering responsibility and dispute" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: On 3 January 2025 New Taipei City Government announced that the two city governments would jointly sue BES Engineering for
      - strong: NT$1.927 billion
      - text: ", on the basis that the contractor had not built to the approved drawings; the same release carries the 40 mm pin, the 5 mm drawing and the 41 mm as-built account of the mechanism"
      - superscript:
        - link "[180]":
          - /url: "#ref-180"
      - text: . The suit was filed on 27 March 2025 at the Taipei District Court
      - superscript:
        - link "[181]":
          - /url: "#ref-181"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: BES has not conceded. It says it 「均依核定施工圖說嚴格執行」 — that it strictly executed the approved construction drawings — and that the milled-through plate and the bearing failure are
      - strong: not
      - text: the main cause of the damage, which it says needs further examination from the direction of structural design strength
      - superscript:
        - link "[182]":
          - /url: "#ref-182"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The litigation outcome, and whether any prosecution followed the Control Yuan's request that New Taipei DORTS pursue liability for public-danger offences
      - superscript:
        - link "[178]":
          - /url: "#ref-178"
      - text: .

    - heading "How far the damage ran" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The primary source is inconsistent with itself, and that is worth publishing rather than smoothing over. The Control Yuan's terms of reference and its opening paragraph put the damage between Banxin and Qiaohe and along the
      - link "Jingping":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y10/
      - text: Road section; the conclusion of its first finding gives the range as Banxin to Jingan; and its own breakdown, quoting New Taipei DORTS, places
      - strong: five displacements between Qiaohe and Zhongyuan, five between Zhongyuan and Banxin, and one near Jingan
      - text: — five plus five plus one, spanning
      - link "Y15":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y15/
      - text: down to
      - link "Y11":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/y11/

    - heading "Where the sources disagree" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Project cost.
      - text: Three official values survive. The October 2014 early-works release gave
      - strong: NT$55.022 billion
      - text: .
      - superscript:
        - link "[190]":
          - /url: "#ref-190"
      - text: The April 2015 NDC-stage release and August 2018 engineering report gave
      - strong: NT$50.5 billion
      - text: ; the report says value engineering used shorter trains, tighter headways, shorter stations, well foundations and U-girders to reduce the earlier NT$55 billion proposal.
      - superscript:
        - link "[191]":
          - /url: "#ref-191"
      - superscript:
        - link "[192]":
          - /url: "#ref-192"
      - text: The live builder page now gives
      - strong: NT$50.200 billion
      - text: .
      - superscript:
        - link "[193]":
          - /url: "#ref-193"
      - text: These are dated project estimates or current programme figures, not interchangeable measurements of final expenditure.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Journey and peak interval.
      - text: In 2014 the city forecast an end-to-end journey of no more than
      - strong: 23 minutes
      - text: and a
      - strong: three-minute
      - text: peak interval.
      - superscript:
        - link "[190]":
          - /url: "#ref-190"
      - text: Opening service was about
      - strong: 30 minutes
      - text: and
      - strong: six minutes
      - text: .
      - superscript:
        - link "[194]":
          - /url: "#ref-194"
      - text: The engineering report's mature design pattern put
      - link "LB01":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb01/
      - text: –
      - link "LB08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb08/
      - text: at 2.2 minutes but
      - link "LB08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb08/
      - text: –
      - link "LB12":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb12/
      - text: at 4.4 minutes.
      - superscript:
        - link "[192]":
          - /url: "#ref-192"
      - text: The sources describe an early forecast, initial operations and a design-year branching pattern respectively; none is substituted for another.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Bade approval.
      - text: The extension page's dated record says the Executive Yuan approved the comprehensive plan on 1 August 2025, while its introduction says the project has not been approved.
      - superscript:
        - link "[195]":
          - /url: "#ref-195"
      - text: The page gives no update date for the stale sentence, so its provenance cannot be reconstructed.

    - paragraph:
      - text: DORTS calls the result 「國內第一條通車的高運量捷運系統」 — the first high-capacity metro line in Taiwan to enter service
      - superscript:
        - link "[206]":
          - /url: "#ref-206"
      - text: ". The last of those three stretches was not built with the rest of the Tamsui line at all: the project record notes against both"
      - link "R08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r08/
      - text: and
      - link "R09":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r09/
      - text: that 「本站工程併入捷運新店線辦理」, the station works were folded into the Xindian line contract
      - superscript:
        - link "[206]":
          - /url: "#ref-206"
      - text: .
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Xinyi section followed fifteen years later, inspected on 13 October and 8 November 2013 and opened on
      - strong: 24 November 2013
      - text: ", against a budget of NT$33.862 billion"
      - superscript:
        - link "[207]":
          - /url: "#ref-207"
      - text: . Its seven-station count includes
      - link "R08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r08/
      - text: and
      - link "R05":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r05/
      - superscript:
        - link "[207]":
          - /url: "#ref-207"
      - text: ", both of which already existed on other lines — so a source giving a smaller number of stations \"opened in 2013\" is counting new stations rather than the project's, not contradicting it."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "The whole thing descends from one decision: the Executive Yuan approved the initial network on 4 April 1986 with a total budget of NT$444.4 billion, and the Tamsui line was let as 13 design contracts and around 120 construction contracts"
      - superscript:
        - link "[206]":
          - /url: "#ref-206"
      - text: . The earliest of them is worth naming — contract CT107, earthworks for
      - link "Beitou Depot":
        - /url: /rail/metro/depots/beitou-depot/
      - text: ", signed on"
      - strong: 19 January 1988
      - text: ", which DORTS itself calls the earliest of them"
      - superscript:
        - link "[206]":
          - /url: "#ref-206"
      - text: .

    - heading "Where the sources disagree" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Dongmen dimensions and shield drives.
      - text: The 2005 DORTS paper reports a box about
      - strong: 217 m × 24.7 m
      - text: ", excavated about"
      - strong: 31.2 m
      - text: ", with Xinyi shield drives of"
      - strong: 1,240.5 m
      - text: and
      - strong: 1,247.0 m
      - text: (about 2,487.5 m combined).
      - superscript:
        - link "[208]":
          - /url: "#ref-208"
      - text: The 2014 DORTS construction paper instead reports about
      - strong: 216 m × 25 m
      - text: ", an excavation of about"
      - strong: 32 m
      - text: ", and drives of"
      - strong: 1,219.3 m
      - text: and
      - strong: 1,225.8 m
      - text: (about 2,445.1 m combined).
      - superscript:
        - link "[209]":
          - /url: "#ref-209"
      - text: The difference is published as a conflict because neither source states why its measuring basis differs.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Route length.
      - text: DORTS's two published figures are 23.8 km for the Tamsui section including the branch
      - superscript:
        - link "[206]":
          - /url: "#ref-206"
      - text: and 6.4 km for the Xinyi section
      - superscript:
        - link "[207]":
          - /url: "#ref-207"
      - text: . They meet end to end at
      - link "R08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r08/
      - text: ", so they sum to 30.2 km with the branch, or 29.0 km for the main line alone — but that sum is this page's arithmetic on two primary figures, not anybody's published length. Chinese Wikipedia's infobox gives"
      - strong: 32.3 km
      - superscript:
        - link "[210]":
          - /url: "#ref-210"
      - text: . Nothing read for this page explains the two-to-three kilometre gap, and the whole-line spec row therefore reads TBC rather than picking one. The Wenhu Line's three lengths turned out to be three correct measurements of three different things; this may be the same, and saying so is not the same as knowing it.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Station count.
      - text: DORTS's 22
      - superscript:
        - link "[206]":
          - /url: "#ref-206"
      - text: and 7
      - superscript:
        - link "[207]":
          - /url: "#ref-207"
      - text: share
      - link "R08":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r08/
      - text: ", which nets to 28 — the number in service today,"
      - link "R02":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r02/
      - text: to
      - link "R28":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r28/
      - text: plus
      - link "R22A":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/r22a/
      - text: . Chinese Wikipedia says 29, counting the unopened
      - code: R01
      - superscript:
        - link "[210]":
          - /url: "#ref-210"
      - text: . Those are compatible once you know what each counts.
    - paragraph:
      - strong: Rolling stock.
      - text: Chinese Wikipedia's line infobox names C301,
      - link "C381":
        - /url: /rail/metro/rolling-stock/c381/
      - text: and C381A
      - superscript:
        - link "[210]":
          - /url: "#ref-210"
      - text: ; its Xinbeitou article names
      - link "C371":
        - /url: /rail/metro/rolling-stock/c371/
      - text: for the branch
      - superscript:
        - link "[211]":
          - /url: "#ref-211"
      - text: . Two articles on one encyclopedia, two fleets. Neither was checked against a TRTC or manufacturer record, so the facts panel names no fleet at all. The obvious reconciliation is obvious enough to be suspicious.

    - 'heading "A genuine conflict: how many social-welfare points, exactly" [level=3]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: Senior (敬老卡) and disability (愛心卡) cardholders get a monthly allowance of social-welfare points, usable across TRTC, NTMC's Circular Line and light rail,
      - link "Maokong Gondola":
        - /url: /rail/cable/lines/maokong-gondola/
      - text: ", and joint bus operators, before falling back to a 40% MRT discount or 50% bus discount once exhausted."
      - superscript:
        - link "[220]":
          - /url: "#ref-220"
      - text: TRTC's own FAQ states this allowance as
      - strong: 600 points a month
      - text: ; NTMC's own FAQ, describing what reads as the identical benefit for the identical population, states

    - paragraph:
      - text: Discussed on
      - link "Taipei Metro ridership":
        - /url: /rail/metro/operations/ridership/
      - text: "in the source page's “TRTC: 2.1 million riders a day, most of the way back from COVID” section."

    - 'heading "TRTC: 2.1 million riders a day, most of the way back from COVID" [level=3]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: TRTC's own FY2025 performance report puts average daily ridership at 2,101,700 — up 3.7% on FY2024's 2,026,843 — split into 2,276,587 on an average weekday and 1,740,170 on an average holiday or weekend.
      - superscript:
        - link "[222]":
          - /url: "#ref-222"
      - text: That figure is 97.2% of the pre-pandemic FY2019 average of 2,163,285, a recovery TRTC states directly rather than leaving a reader to infer it.
      - superscript:
        - link "[222]":
          - /url: "#ref-222"
      - text: "Service quality stayed within the operator's own statutory floors across all five lines: punctuality (arrival within schedule) ranged from 99.69% to 99.93%, and train-availability rates from 91.85% to 95.83%, both comfortably above the 99% and 90% floors respectively."
      - superscript:
        - link "[222]":
          - /url: "#ref-222"
      - text: System reliability, measured in mean distance between failures (MKBF), reached 23.009 million car-kilometres in FY2024 — the best year on record — and 19.678 million in FY2025, the second-best.
      - superscript:
        - link "[222]":
          - /url: "#ref-222"
      - text: A widely repeated shorthand claiming MKBF "exceeds 20 million car-km" holds for FY2024 but not FY2025, which fell just short of that threshold — worth stating precisely rather than rounding up.
    - paragraph:
      - text: "TRTC's cumulative ridership has passed several billion-scale thresholds since the system opened in 1996: 500 million by January 2001, 2 billion by August 2005, 4 billion by April 2010, 5 billion by February 2012, 10 billion by March 2019, 13 billion by November 2023, and 15 billion by 24 June 2026."
      - superscript:
        - link "[223]":
          - /url: "#ref-223"
      - text: TRTC's own operational report, written earlier in 2026, separately states the system had "surpassed 14.5 billion" trips as of that writing — consistent with, not contradicting, the chronicle's later 15-billion milestone a few months on.
      - superscript:
        - link "[222]":
          - /url: "#ref-222"
      - superscript:
        - link "[223]":
          - /url: "#ref-223"

TRTC's FY2025 annual total, calculated here by summing its own two-category table, sits within rounding distance of a different figure attributed to a city-government statistical yearbook, but that yearbook's own tables could not be independently read to confirm the match precisely — not established.
