    - heading "Passenger systems and capacity" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Each car has four externally sliding doors, two per side, driven by DC motors.
      - superscript:
        - link "[231]":
          - /url: "#ref-231"
      - text: Microprocessor controllers monitor direction, speed, obstacle detection and ATC commands.
      - superscript:
        - link "[232]":
          - /url: "#ref-232"
      - text: Door-side lights flash for five seconds before opening, and multi-tone audible warnings provide an equivalent cue before opening and closing.
      - superscript:
        - link "[232]":
          - /url: "#ref-232"
      - text: Four dynamic route displays, four passenger-information screens, two emergency intercoms, CCTV and two extinguishers were specified per car.
      - superscript:
        - link "[231]":
          - /url: "#ref-231"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Capacity has an unresolved primary-source disagreement. The design paper gives 20 seats and 93 people per car at five standing passengers per square metre, which implies 372 per four-car train.
      - superscript:
        - link "[233]":
          - /url: "#ref-233"
      - text: TRTC's current network introduction uses the same five-person standing density but states approximately 386 people per Bombardier train.
      - superscript:
        - link "[234]":
          - /url: "#ref-234"
      - text: The 14-person difference is not explained in either opened page, so both values are published rather than one being chosen.

    - heading "Approved or advancing extensions" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taichung's Blue Line is documented separately as an approved project moving into route construction.
      - superscript:
        - link "[235]":
          - /url: "#ref-235"
      - text: The full project page gives 24.78 km, 20 stations and one depot; current route contracts cover BC11 (B01–B03) and BC12 (B04–B08).
      - superscript:
        - link "[235]":
          - /url: "#ref-235"
      - text: See the
      - link "Taichung Metro Blue Line project page":
        - /url: /rail/projects/taichung-blue-line/
      - text: for the dated approval and procurement record.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taichung's Purple Line remains a feasibility-stage project under central review.
      - superscript:
        - link "[236]":
          - /url: "#ref-236"
      - text: Its full project page gives approximately 16.31 km and 16 planned stations, while the July 2026 release gives the estimated NT$690.87 billion cost.
      - superscript:
        - link "[236]":
          - /url: "#ref-236"
      - superscript:
        - link "[237]":
          - /url: "#ref-237"
      - text: See the
      - link "Taichung Metro Purple Line project page":
        - /url: /rail/projects/taichung-purple-line/
      - text: for its dated review chronology and route boundary.
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taichung's Airport Orange Line feasibility study was approved by the Executive Yuan on 18 August 2026.
      - superscript:
        - link "[238]":
          - /url: "#ref-238"
      - text: The current project page gives approximately 29.23 km and 26 planned stations; see the
      - link "Taichung Airport MRT Orange Line project page":
        - /url: /rail/projects/taichung-orange-line/
      - text: for its approval sequence, forecast boundary and pre-construction status.
      - superscript:
        - link "[238]":
          - /url: "#ref-238"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Orange Line Sea Line extension remains a feasibility-stage project with an interim revised report under review.
      - superscript:
        - link "[239]":
          - /url: "#ref-239"
      - text: Its January public proposal is approximately 16.50 km with 10 stations and branches toward Sanmin Road and Wuqi Fishing Port; see the
      - link "Orange Line Sea Line extension project page":
        - /url: /rail/projects/taichung-orange-sea-extension/
      - text: for the planning boundary, mode debate and source conflicts.
      - superscript:
        - link "[239]":
          - /url: "#ref-239"
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taichung's Chongde–Fengyuan Red Line remains in feasibility review.
      - superscript:
        - link "[240]":
          - /url: "#ref-240"
      - text: Its preliminary scope is approximately 15.42 km with 11 stations and one level-five depot, but the Fengyuan urban section still has two elevated and one underground alternatives.
      - superscript:
        - link "[240]":
          - /url: "#ref-240"
      - superscript:
        - link "[241]":
          - /url: "#ref-241"
      - text: See the
      - link "Taichung Metro Chongde–Fengyuan Line project page":
        - /url: /rail/projects/taichung-red-line/
      - text: for the study chronology, forecast boundary and unresolved route choice.
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Xinyi East Extension is a one-station, approximately 1.4 km extension with tail tracks; its CR580C contract page records a 17 October 2016 start.
      - superscript:
        - link "[242]":
          - /url: "#ref-242"
      - text: DORTS's 2026 priorities describe the construction fences coming down and the extension entering service after preliminary inspection, while its older FAQ gives ROC 115 as the dated completion target.
      - superscript:
        - link "[243]":
          - /url: "#ref-243"
      - superscript:
        - link "[244]":
          - /url: "#ref-244"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Sanying–Bade extension is approved at the comprehensive-planning level but is not presented here as a construction start. The current New Taipei record describes a 4.03 km, three-station route from
      - link "LB12":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/lb12/
      - text: to a jointly built
      - code: LB14
      - text: /
      - link "G04":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/g04/
      - text: ", and records detailed design beginning 1 July 2026."
      - superscript:
        - link "[245]":
          - /url: "#ref-245"
      - text: "Danhai Blue Sea Line Phase 2 has moved further than a sketch but is still a changing project: the original route was 4.4 km, the revised riverside route is 3.32 km, and advance road, utility and track works began in June 2025 while the revised plan continued through review."
      - superscript:
        - link "[246]":
          - /url: "#ref-246"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Railway Bureau's current budget also separates approved projects from municipal route proposals. It includes the
      - code: A14
      - text: Airport MRT station works and the 15.59 km, 13-station Nangang–Badu project, which is planned to connect the Taipei-region metro systems, TRA and HSR; this budget record gives its programme as ROC 113–123.
      - superscript:
        - link "[247]":
          - /url: "#ref-247"

    - paragraph:
      - text: Discussed on

    - heading "Meihe City and the legal dispute" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Meihe City is the region's essential caution against treating joint development as an uncomplicated financing success. New Taipei's official 2014 account says the review lasted more than 15 years, reduced an original 26-building design to 13 buildings, and required greater setbacks and public space after urban-design and environmental review.
      - superscript:
        - link "[250]":
          - /url: "#ref-250"
      - text: A later New Taipei government research report instead describes 16 towers, 2,220 units, about 400,600 m² of floor area, and Rich Development as the selected private developer.
      - superscript:
        - link "[251]":
          - /url: "#ref-251"
      - text: Those are conflicting project descriptions from different official records; the site publishes both rather than choosing one.
      - superscript:
        - link "[250]":
          - /url: "#ref-250"
      - superscript:
        - link "[251]":
          - /url: "#ref-251"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The legal issue is not just a design disagreement. Judicial Interpretation No. 743 states that land expropriated under MRT Law Article 6 cannot be used in the same plan for Article 7 joint development, and that transfer to a third party requires clear legal authority.
      - superscript:
        - link "[252]":
          - /url: "#ref-252"
      - text: The interpretation records the underlying Xindian depot case, the different statutory purposes of expropriation and joint development, and the disagreement among the Control Yuan, executive agencies and courts before the interpretation.
      - superscript:
        - link "[252]":
          - /url: "#ref-252"
      - text: Meihe City is therefore published here as a legal and governance conflict as well as a large-scale station-area project.
      - superscript:
        - link "[252]":
          - /url: "#ref-252"

    - heading "BOT contract and financial disputes" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Railway Bureau describes the project as Taiwan’s first major national infrastructure project promoted through private investment participation.
      - superscript:
        - link "[255]":
          - /url: "#ref-255"
      - text: It records the 23 July 1998 signing of a 35-year construction-and-operation concession and a separate 50-year station-area development concession.
      - superscript:
        - link "[255]":
          - /url: "#ref-255"
      - text: The stated project cost was approximately NT$513.3 billion, with the government responsible for land, the Taipei underground co-construction section, supervision and management, while the concession company funded civil works, stations, core electromechanical systems, operation and maintenance.
      - superscript:
        - link "[255]":
          - /url: "#ref-255"
    - paragraph:
      - text: The original financial model did not remain unchanged. The Railway Bureau says a 27 July 2015 amendment extended the concession to 70 years, cancelled the station-area development contract, returned development land, reduced capital to clear accumulated losses and added NT$30 billion of government investment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[255]":
          - /url: "#ref-255"
      - text: The Control Yuan’s official record names an investigation into whether direct and indirect public investment violated BOT principles.
      - superscript:
        - link "[256]":
          - /url: "#ref-256"
      - text: In a related statement, the Control Yuan says public and state-enterprise entities supplied 37.42% and describes that as a serious departure from the government-zero-investment commitment.
      - superscript:
        - link "[257]":
          - /url: "#ref-257"
      - text: Those are the source’s figures and characterization; this page does not average them into a new ownership percentage.

    - heading "Success and stagnation, in the same programme" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: THSR's own twentieth-anniversary framing draws a sharp contrast. At Qingpu, next to Taoyuan Station, roughly 70% of the local population is now under 45, with new commercial floor space added between 2017 and 2025 equal to about 80% of the area's entire prior office stock.
      - superscript:
        - link "[258]":
          - /url: "#ref-258"
      - text: At Zhubei, next to Hsinchu Station, the under-45 population grew 43.8% — the only one of the twelve station areas to show positive growth in that age band — alongside a fourfold rise in local output value.
      - superscript:
        - link "[258]":
          - /url: "#ref-258"
      - text: THSR's chairman described this as a shift from "movement" to "relocation" to "liveability."
      - superscript:
        - link "[258]":
          - /url: "#ref-258"
    - paragraph:
      - link "Changhua":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/changhua/
      - text: tells a different story. THSR's own twentieth-anniversary figures rank it last of the twelve stations by absolute ridership.
      - superscript:
        - link "[258]":
          - /url: "#ref-258"
      - text: "Since 2014, the county has offered 66.34 hectares of buildable land for sale around the station; 36.76 hectares remained unsold as of the most recent figures read for this page, and the county's own description is blunt: development has fallen short of expectations."
      - superscript:
        - link "[259]":
          - /url: "#ref-259"
      - text: Miaoli tells a related story — two county-owned industrial parcels went to bid 42 times without a single successful sale — though the county was still actively pitching the site to prospective tenants, including Nvidia, as recently as October 2025.
      - superscript:
        - link "[260]":
          - /url: "#ref-260"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "A genuine statistical trap sits inside this same anniversary report:"
      - superscript:
        - link "[258]":
          - /url: "#ref-258"
      - text: Miaoli,
      - link "Yunlin":
        - /url: /rail/thsr/stations/yunlin/
      - text: and Changhua post the
      - emphasis: highest
      - text: ridership-growth multiples of all twelve stations. Both things are true at once — the fastest percentage growth, and the lowest absolute ridership — because an extremely small opening-period base makes any subsequent traffic look like a large multiple. Neither figure should be read as contradicting the other.

    - heading "Elimination by grade separation" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "TRA has been eliminating crossings city by city through grade-separation megaprojects for decades, though this page's confidence in the individual project details is limited: the Railway Bureau's own project pages, the natural primary source, returned no readable content on every fetch attempted. Hualien's own elevation project, covering seven crossings between Hualien and Ji'an, is confirmed by Legislative Yuan records to remain at the feasibility and planning stage, not under construction.

    - heading "Five locomotives, still formally managed" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "TRA's own internal regulation still actively manages five steam locomotives as a tiered rental asset class: CT273 and CK124 in the top \"special-A\" tier, DT668 and CK101 in the \"A\" tier, and the narrow-gauge LDK59 in the \"B\" tier, each with a stated rate for a dynamic (running) rental."
      - superscript:
        - link "[265]":
          - /url: "#ref-265"
      - text: The same regulation bars CT273 and DT668 from the Pingxi, Shen'ao and Jiji lines entirely, and restricts CK101 to static or motionless display on major festival days only, because its original manufacturer has closed and parts and wheels can no longer be sourced.
      - superscript:
        - link "[265]":
          - /url: "#ref-265"
    - paragraph:
      - text: CT273, a 1943 Kawasaki-built CT270-class locomotive based on the Japan Railways C57 design, was TRA's last steam locomotive withdrawn from regular service, in 1984, and was restored to operation in 2014; a 2025 news report, read via search synthesis rather than a full fetch and flagged accordingly for confidence, describes it hauling a summer tourist train between Yuli and Taitung, based at Hualien.
      - superscript:
        - link "[266]":
          - /url: "#ref-266"
      - text: DT668, a 1941 Kawasaki-built DT650-class locomotive and TRA's heaviest steam class, was withdrawn March 1984 and restored to run on the Neiwan Branch Line in November 2011. CK124 was restored to operation in 2001, and LDK59, TRA's preserved narrow-gauge locomotive, in 2011 — both dates from a secondary lead index, not independently verified against a primary source.
      - superscript:
        - link "[267]":
          - /url: "#ref-267"
      - text: "This page does not state where each is currently based with confidence: sources disagree between Changhua Roundhouse and TRA's Fugang depot for both CK101 and DT668, and this page publishes both locations rather than choosing one."

    - heading "A museum, open since 2025" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The National Railway Museum's first phase opened 31 July 2025 at the former Taipei Railway Workshop site, comprising six restored heritage buildings — the Diesel-Electric Workshop, General Administration Building, Technical Training Institute, Materials Testing Lab, Grand Hall and Bathhouse — eight exhibitions, a weekend heritage-train ride over roughly 650 m using restored diesel railcars, and 24 displayed heritage vehicles.
      - superscript:

          - /url: "#ref-268"
      - text: The museum's own current page confirms it remains open in 2026 on the same footprint, Tuesday through Sunday; no source read for this page states a Phase 2 opening date or scope.
      - superscript:
        - link "[269]":
          - /url: "#ref-269"
      - text: The site itself, Taipei Railway Workshop, was designated a national historic monument in 2015; sources disagree on the exact date.

    - heading "What the 2018 Puyuma accident changed" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: The Taiwan Transportation Safety Board's own investigation into the 2018 Puyuma derailment found that ATP had been illegally isolated and the train was travelling over the applicable speed, attributing part of the root cause to TRA's own failure to enforce its existing rules against unauthorised ATP isolation; the report issued 27 recommendations, though the published announcement does not itemise which specifically concern ATP or signalling design as distinct from management and procedure.
      - superscript:
        - link "[270]":
          - /url: "#ref-270"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "In response, TRA built an \"ATP isolation speed-limit system\" that forces a speed cap even when ATP itself is switched off. Sources disagree on both its budget and its cap: one report gives a 60 km/h limit and a NT$245 million budget covering 52 systems across 18 Puyuma and 8 Taroko trainsets;"
      - superscript:
        - link "[271]":
          - /url: "#ref-271"
      - text: another gives a NT$270 million budget.
      - superscript:
        - link "[272]":
          - /url: "#ref-272"
      - text: A separate, earlier report describes an initial ministerial directive for a 65 km/h cap that explicitly did not rule out going lower — consistent with, but not confirmed as, the same rollout. Post-accident operating rules also require drivers to check ATP at both cab ends before departure and require a faulty-ATP train be swapped rather than dispatched.

    - heading "From a failed BOT to a government-built line" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Planning has at least three defensible starting points, and different sources plainly mean different things by it: an October 1989 feasibility study is the earliest date found, though only at secondary strength; in October 1996 the central government decided to build the line under a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) model; and Long Life International Development Co. (長生國際開發) won the BOT bid in 1998."
      - superscript:
        - link "[273]":
          - /url: "#ref-273"
      - text: The BOT arrangement collapsed on 31 December 2002, when Long Life and the then High Speed Rail Bureau agreed to terminate the contract.
      - superscript:
        - link "[273]":
          - /url: "#ref-273"
      - text: "The government took direct responsibility afterward: MOTC designated the High Speed Rail Bureau as the project's construction body on 28 October 2003, and the central government approved the construction plan on 9 March 2004."
      - superscript:
        - link "[274]":
          - /url: "#ref-274"
      - superscript:
        - link "[275]":
          - /url: "#ref-275"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Construction start likewise has more than one dated event rather than one clean answer: New Taipei's project record gives 27 February 2006 for the formal start of the Sanchong–Airport–Zhongli section and its E&M systems, while TYMC's own company history instead records a ceremonial groundbreaking on 26 June 2006, presided over by the Premier."
      - superscript:
        - link "[275]":
          - /url: "#ref-275"
      - superscript:
        - link "[274]":
          - /url: "#ref-274"
      - text: The line opened on 2 March 2017 for stations
      - link "A1":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/a1/
      - text: through
      - link "A21":
        - /url: /rail/metro/stations/a21/
      - text: ", after the originally announced January 2009 target had been publicly revised six times — the specific dates and reasons for each of the six changes are not established by any source read for this page and stay TBC."
      - superscript:
        - link "[274]":
          - /url: "#ref-274"

    - 'heading "The Marubeni dispute: two confirmed figures, one unconfirmed total" [level=3]'
    - paragraph:
      - text: Around the 2017 opening, contemporaneous wire reporting recorded the then High Speed Rail Bureau imposing a NT$2.5 billion delay-penalty cap on contractor Marubeni Corporation (丸紅), the contractual maximum, plus a separate NT$1.9 billion performance bond withheld over Marubeni's unauthorised subcontracting of the signalling system to a British firm — its contract required Marubeni to design that system itself.
      - superscript:
        - link "[276]":
          - /url: "#ref-276"
      - text: Marubeni separately counter-claimed NT$12.9 billion against the Ministry, on the grounds of repeated Bureau-directed design changes.
      - superscript:
        - link "[276]":
          - /url: "#ref-276"
      - text: "No source read for this page states a combined total for the dispute of any kind: NT$2.5 billion plus NT$1.9 billion is NT$4.4 billion, not any commonly-circulated larger figure, and the individual component figures are published here on that basis rather than an unconfirmed total."
    - paragraph:
      - text: "A separate, later dispute in 2021 concerned in-service performance rather than construction delay: the Public Construction Commission recommended withholding NT$726,926,496 from Marubeni for missing three contractual operating standards — express journey time, average speed and train headway."
      - superscript:
        - link "[277]":
          - /url: "#ref-277"

    - heading "A separately reported discount, not verified here" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Existing research on this project's Airport MRT line page separately records a January 2025 cancellation of a NT$10 discount that had applied to single tickets, sourced to a Global Views Monthly (遠見雜誌) article citing the company chairman on rising electricity costs.
      - superscript:
        - link "[280]":
          - /url: "#ref-280"
      - text: Neither of the two ticketing pages read for this report mentions that change, so it is neither newly confirmed nor contradicted here — it remains at the same secondary-source strength already on record. Whether that single-ticket discount cancellation and the season-pass repricing described above form one coordinated fare reform, both taking effect the same day, or are simply two unrelated changes that happened to land together, is not established by any source read and is not assumed either way.

    - heading "How crossing multiple segments is counted" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: "Chinese Wikipedia's article on New Taipei's own city buses gives a worked example of the counting logic. For a corridor running through zones A, B and C, with B as the segment point: riding within one zone, or from A to B, or from B to C, is one segment; riding all the way from A to C is two segments (the single-segment fare, doubled)"
      - superscript:
        - link "[281]":
          - /url: "#ref-281"
      - text: . On a longer corridor with two segment points, A–B–C–D–E, both B and D count as crossing points
      - superscript:
        - link "[281]":
          - /url: "#ref-281"
      - text: . This is an illustrative example rather than a government fare rule in itself, but it does not contradict, and directly illustrates, the primary rule already confirmed above.

    - heading "Bus fares" [level=3]
    - paragraph:
      - text: Taipei and New Taipei buses use segment fares, not one flat price for every journey.
      - superscript:
        - link "[282]":
          - /url: "#ref-282"
      - text: The current passenger table is NT$15 full fare per segment, NT$12 for a student EasyCard segment and NT$8 for elderly, disabled/companion and eligible-child concessions.
      - superscript:
        - link "[282]":
          - /url: "#ref-282"
      - text: Taipei PTO records the latest joint-operation bus operating-rate approval as 1 July 2020 while passenger fares stayed at 15/12/8 and the city subsidised the difference.
      - superscript:
        - link "[283]":
          - /url: "#ref-283"
    - paragraph:
      - text: "This is a measurement conflict, not a price contradiction: operating rate is the regulated cost/revenue figure, while passenger fare is what the rider pays. The historical report records a 1997 bus-rate-related transfer-discount change, but a complete gazette-backed chronology of every passenger-fare adjustment remains TBC."
